title: UK Compliance Landscape — Who Regulates What, and Why
meta: Module 1 · Part 1 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard
learningObjHtml:
Learning Objectives

   
         
  • Name the seven UK regulators and supervisory bodies an accountant interacts with on a daily basis and describe each one's statutory remit.
    •      
  • Distinguish HMRC's role (tax collection, AML supervision of unsupervised agents) from Companies House's role (registry of companies, public record of accounts).
    •      
  • Explain the role of the Financial Reporting Council (FRC), its sub-bodies, and the standards it sets.
    •      
  • List the recognised professional bodies for accountants and bookkeepers and the AML supervision each performs.
    •      
  • Map a typical client engagement to the regulators that will receive filings.
    •      
  • Identify when an accountant becomes “in scope” for AML supervision and the consequences of operating without it.
    •

sections.title: 1.1 Why “compliance” is the centre of gravity for UK accountants
sections.contentHtml:
The UK does not have a single Inland Revenue and Companies Office; it has a layered system of regulators, each with statutory powers, distinct deadlines, and distinct penalty regimes. As an accountant you do not simply “keep books” — you operate as the bridge between your client and these regulators. Failure to meet a deadline triggers automatic penalties, often on a daily basis, and serious failures can result in director disqualification, professional sanction, or criminal prosecution.

 

Compliance has three operational pillars:

 
       
  1. Record-keeping — capturing every business transaction in a form that satisfies HMRC's and (for companies) Companies Act record requirements.
    2.    
  2. Reporting — transforming those records into the statutory returns and accounts each regulator requires, on the deadline they set.
    3.    
  3. Paying — settling liabilities (Income Tax, Corporation Tax, VAT, NI, PAYE, etc.) by the legally specified date.
    4.  
 

The technical work of bookkeeping (debits and credits) is in service of these three pillars. A trial balance is not an end in itself; it is the input to a CT600, an SA100 or a set of FRS 102 accounts. From day one of this course, every ledger entry should be evaluated by the question: “Where will this end up on the statutory return, and is it correctly classified for that purpose?”

sections.title: 1.2 HMRC — His Majesty's Revenue and Customs
sections.contentHtml:
HMRC is the UK's tax authority, formed in 2005 by the merger of Inland Revenue and HM Customs & Excise. It sits as a non-ministerial department of government, responsible to Parliament via the Treasury but not directly part of any minister's portfolio. This independence matters: Parliament sets the law (the Taxes Acts); HMRC administers it.

 

1.2.1 What HMRC actually does

                                                                                 
FunctionDetail & legislative basis
Income Tax collectionIncome Tax (Earnings & Pensions) Act 2003 (ITEPA), Income Tax (Trading & Other Income) Act 2005 (ITTOIA), Income Tax Act 2007 (ITA). Collected via PAYE for employees, Self Assessment for the self-employed and complex cases.
Corporation TaxCorporation Tax Act 2009 (CTA 2009), Corporation Tax Act 2010 (CTA 2010). Filed on form CT600 within 12 months of period end.
VATValue Added Tax Act 1994 (VATA 1994). Quarterly (sometimes monthly or annually) returns filed under MTD.
National InsuranceSocial Security Contributions & Benefits Act 1992; Classes 1, 1A, 1B, 2, 3 and 4 each with a different statutory basis.
Capital Gains TaxTaxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992 (TCGA 1992). UK residential property disposals require a 60-day return separate to Self Assessment.
Inheritance TaxInheritance Tax Act 1984 (IHTA 1984). Form IHT400 filed by personal representatives within 12 months of death.
Stamp Duty Land Tax (England & NI)Finance Act 2003 Part 4. (Wales: LTT — WRA; Scotland: LBTT — Revenue Scotland.)
Customs duties & exciseUK Borders/Customs framework, particularly important post-Brexit for goods movement.
National Minimum Wage enforcementNational Minimum Wage Act 1998. HMRC investigates underpayment and can name & shame employers.
Tax credits / Universal Credit liaisonTax credits being phased out into UC (DWP) but legacy elements still administered.
AML supervisionSupervises tax advisers and accountants who are not supervised by a recognised professional body. See §1.7.
 
    Legal status    

HMRC is established by the Commissioners for Revenue & Customs Act 2005 (CRCA). Its Commissioners (currently a small board) hold delegated statutory power; their officers act “under the care and management of the Commissioners” (CRCA s.5). When you write to HMRC, you are technically writing to an Officer of the Board.

 
 

1.2.2 HMRC's structure and how to interact with it

 

From a practitioner's point of view, HMRC is split into a series of tax silos, each with its own helpline, address and online portal. The silo you need depends on the client and the issue:

                                                   
SiloOnline servicePostal address (current at 2024/25)
Self AssessmentSA online via Government Gateway / Agent Services AccountSelf Assessment, HM Revenue & Customs, BX9 1AS
Corporation TaxCT600 e-filing (third-party software only)Corporation Tax Services, HM Revenue & Customs, BX9 1AX
VATMTD VAT through API-enabled software (Xero, QBO, etc.)VAT Written Enquiries Team, HM Revenue & Customs, BX9 1WR
PAYE / EmployerPAYE Online, RTI submissions via payroll softwarePT Operations North East England, HM Revenue & Customs, BX9 1BX
CISCIS Online for monthly returnsConstruction Industry Scheme, HM Revenue & Customs, BX9 1BX
Agent AuthorisationAgent Services Account (ASA) plus “old” Online Agent Services for SA & CTCentral Agent Authorisation Team, HM Revenue & Customs, BX9 1AU
 
    Working tip    

The “BX9” postcode is not a real geographic location — it routes to HMRC's centralised digital mail-handling. Never address physical post to HMRC's Whitehall headquarters; it will sit in a tray for weeks. Use the BX9 + sub-code for the relevant silo.

 
 

1.2.3 The Government Gateway and Agent Services Account (ASA)

 

Every individual and business that interacts digitally with HMRC needs a Government Gateway account. As an agent you will hold:

 
       
  • A personal Government Gateway for your own Self Assessment.
    •    
  • An Agent Online Services Account — the “old” account — used for filing SA100, CT600 and managing 64-8 authorisations.
    •    
  • An Agent Services Account (ASA) — the “new” account, mandatory for MTD VAT, MTD ITSA, Trust Registration Service, and CGT-on-property reporting.
    •  
 

You authorise an agent relationship by either: (a) the client signing form 64-8 (legacy method, for SA, CT, PAYE, VAT pre-MTD); or (b) the digital authorisation request via the ASA, where the client receives a code from HMRC that they pass to you to enter in your ASA. The digital authorisation has overtaken paper 64-8s for most live filing services.

sections.title: 1.3 Companies House — The Registry
sections.contentHtml:
Companies House (CH) is the registrar of companies in the UK. It is an executive agency of the Department for Business and Trade. Crucially, Companies House is a registry, not a regulator: it records what is filed but historically does not validate the truthfulness of filings beyond formal completeness. The Economic Crime & Corporate Transparency Act 2023 (ECCTA) is now changing that — CH gains identity-verification, query and rejection powers in phased rollouts from 2024 to 2027.

 

1.3.1 What Companies House does

                                                               
FunctionDetail
IncorporationRegisters limited companies (private & public), LLPs, Limited Partnerships, Community Interest Companies (CICs) and Overseas Companies. Form IN01 (paper) or web/software incorporation.
Statutory accountsReceives annual accounts from every active company (full, abridged, micro-entity or filleted). Public on the CH register.
Confirmation StatementAnnual snapshot (form CS01) confirming SIC code, registered office, officers, shareholders and PSC. £34 digital filing fee (£62 paper) from 1 May 2024.
People with Significant Control (PSC) registerPublic register of individuals owning >25% of shares/voting rights or with significant influence over the company.
Director and Secretary appointments / changesForms AP01 (appoint director), TM01 (terminate), CH01 (change details). Must be filed within 14 days of the change.
Share allotments & capital changesSH01 (allotment of shares), SH06 (cancellation), SH19 (statement of capital), and the various return forms for capital reductions.
Charges (security)MR01 to register a fixed/floating charge over company assets within 21 days of creation. Failure to register makes the charge void against a liquidator.
Strike-offVoluntary strike-off via DS01 for solvent dormant companies; compulsory strike-off where filings are overdue.
 
    ECCTA reforms — be aware    

The Economic Crime & Corporate Transparency Act 2023 introduces:

   
         
  • Mandatory identity verification (IDV) for directors, PSCs and people filing on behalf of companies.
    •      
  • Removal of the option to file abridged accounts (only filleted accounts will remain — full accounts must be prepared even if some pages aren't filed publicly).
    •      
  • Mandatory software-only filing (paper and CH WebFiling routes will be phased out).
    •      
  • Enhanced CH powers to query, reject and remove incorrect information.
    •    
   

Rollout is staged 2024–2027. Always check the latest CH transition timetable when advising clients on first-year filings.

 
 

1.3.2 Statutory deadlines — Companies House

                                                   
FilingDeadlinePenalty for missed filing
First accounts (private company)21 months after date of incorporation£150 (≤1 month late) → £1,500 (>6 months); doubled if late in 2 consecutive years
Subsequent accounts (private company)9 months after accounting reference date (ARD)As above
Public company accounts6 months after ARD£750 → £7,500; doubled if late twice
Confirmation statementAnnually, within 14 days of due date (review period)No fine, but company can be struck off and directors can be prosecuted
Director/officer changes14 days from changeCriminal offence; directors prosecutable
Charge registration (MR01)21 days from creationCharge void against liquidator if late; court application required to register out of time

sections.title: 1.4 The Financial Reporting Council (FRC) and its successor ARGA
sections.contentHtml:
The FRC sets UK accounting standards (FRS 100 to FRS 105), audit standards (ISAs UK), corporate governance code, and the actuarial standards. It is in the process of being replaced by the Audit, Reporting and Governance Authority (ARGA) following the post-Carillion Kingman Review. ARGA will have stronger statutory powers including direct sanction of company directors over financial reporting failures.

 

For day-to-day bookkeeping the FRC matters because it owns the financial reporting standards you must apply when preparing accounts:

 
       
  • FRS 100 — framework: which standard applies to which entity.
    •    
  • FRS 101 — reduced disclosure for subsidiaries of IFRS groups.
    •    
  • FRS 102 — the main UK GAAP standard, most clients you will work on.
    •    
  • FRS 102 Section 1A — reduced disclosures for small entities (qualifying as small under Companies Act).
    •    
  • FRS 103 — insurance contracts (specialist).
    •    
  • FRS 104 — interim financial reporting.
    •    
  • FRS 105 — the micro-entities regime: simplest, fewest disclosures, no fair value model.
    •  
 

We will spend modules 29 to 32 on FRS 105, FRS 102 Section 1A and FRS 102 in granular detail, including why each disclosure is required by the standard.

sections.title: 1.5 Professional bodies and AML supervisors
sections.contentHtml:
To call yourself a “Chartered Accountant” you must be a member of a chartered body. These bodies set entry standards, run the qualification, monitor CPD, and supervise members for AML purposes.

                                                                     
BodyDesignationScope
ICAEWACA / FCAInstitute of Chartered Accountants in England & Wales. Full audit-recognised body. Practising certificate required to operate in public practice.
ICASCAInstitute of Chartered Accountants of Scotland. Same scope as ICAEW within Scotland.
Chartered Accountants IrelandACA / FCACross-border (NI / RoI).
ACCAACCA / FCCAAssociation of Chartered Certified Accountants. Audit-recognised. Largest UK body by membership.
CIMAACMA / FCMA, CGMAChartered Institute of Management Accountants. Focus on management accounting; not audit-recognised in the UK.
AATMAAT / FMAATAssociation of Accounting Technicians. Recognised AML supervisor. Ideal for bookkeeping and small-business accounting.
CIOT / ATTCTA / ATTChartered Institute of Taxation / Association of Taxation Technicians — tax-only specialism.
ICBMICB / FICBInstitute of Certified Bookkeepers. Bookkeeping focus; AML supervisor.
IABAIAB / MIABInternational Association of Bookkeepers; AML supervisor.

sections.title: 1.6 The Office for Professional Body AML Supervision (OPBAS)
sections.contentHtml: OPBAS sits within the FCA and supervises the AML supervisors. It does not directly supervise accountants, but it ensures the professional bodies do their AML supervisory job consistently.

sections.title: 1.7 Anti-Money Laundering (AML) supervision — you must be supervised
sections.contentHtml:
Critical legal point    

Under the Money Laundering Regulations 2017 (as amended), any person providing accountancy services or tax services by way of business must be supervised for AML — either by their professional body or, if not in a body, directly by HMRC. Operating without supervision is a criminal offence carrying up to two years' imprisonment (MLR 2017, reg.56).

 
 

HMRC's AML registration costs around £300 per premises per year (2024/25) plus a £40 registration fee and a £150 fit-and-proper test for senior staff. If you are AAT, ACCA, ICAEW etc. you do not additionally register with HMRC for AML — your body covers it. We cover AML in depth in Module 83.

sections.title: 1.8 Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) — data protection
sections.contentHtml: If your business processes personal data (and as an accountant you process names, NINOs, salaries, bank details, addresses), you must register with the ICO (a notification fee, currently £40–£2,900 a year depending on size) and comply with the UK GDPR & Data Protection Act 2018. Module 86 covers this in detail.

sections.title: 1.9 The Pensions Regulator (TPR)
sections.contentHtml: TPR enforces auto-enrolment compliance. Every employer (regardless of size) must auto-enrol eligible jobholders into a qualifying pension scheme, contribute the statutory minimum, and file an annual re-declaration of compliance. Penalties for non-compliance start at £400 fixed and escalate to £10,000/day for the largest employers (Module 23).

sections.title: 1.10 The Charity Commission & OSCR
sections.contentHtml: Charities in England & Wales register with the Charity Commission for England & Wales (CCEW) once income exceeds £5,000 (or any income for CIOs). Scotland uses OSCR; Northern Ireland uses the Charity Commission for Northern Ireland (CCNI). Charity accounts follow the Charities SORP — the Statement of Recommended Practice based on FRS 102 — with extensive narrative disclosures (Trustees' Annual Report). Module 71 covers charity conversion in depth.

sections.title: 1.11 Insolvency Service
sections.contentHtml: Part of the Department for Business and Trade. Investigates bankruptcies, supervises liquidators, oversees director disqualifications, and runs the Bankruptcy Restrictions / Director Disqualification regimes. We meet the Insolvency Service in modules 60–64 (cessation routes).

sections.title: 1.12 Putting it together — a typical client's regulator map
sections.contentHtml:
Imagine you take on a brand-new private limited company — a husband-and-wife consultancy:

                                                                                 
FilingRegulatorFrequency
VAT return (if registered)HMRCQuarterly
RTI / Full Payment SubmissionHMRCOn or before each pay date
Re-declaration of pension complianceThe Pensions RegulatorEvery 3 years
Self Assessment for each directorHMRCAnnual (31 Jan)
P11D (if any benefits in kind)HMRCAnnual (6 Jul)
P60 to each employeevia employer to employeeAnnual (31 May)
Confirmation statementCompanies HouseAnnual
Statutory accountsCompanies House & HMRC (with CT600)Annual
CT600HMRCAnnual (12m after PE)
ICO notificationICOAnnual
Your own AML supervisionProfessional body or HMRCAnnual
 

Eleven distinct compliance points for a tiny consultancy. Multiply across thirty clients and you can see why workflow software (Karbon, Senta, Pixie, etc.) has become essential to practice management.

 
   

Module 1 — Summary

   
         
  • HMRC administers tax (Income Tax, CT, VAT, NI, CGT, IHT). Authority comes from Parliament via the Taxes Acts; HMRC writes guidance but only Parliament makes law.
    •      
  • Companies House is a registry of companies and LLPs. ECCTA 2023 is currently turning it into a more active gatekeeper with identity verification and query powers.
    •      
  • FRC sets accounting and audit standards (FRS 100–105). Being replaced by ARGA with stronger statutory powers.
    •      
  • Accountants must be supervised for AML — by their professional body (ICAEW, ACCA, AAT, etc.) or directly by HMRC. Unsupervised practice is a criminal offence.
    •      
  • Other regulators in the orbit: TPR (pensions), ICO (data protection), Charity Commission/OSCR/CCNI, Insolvency Service.
    •      
  • A typical small-company client triggers a dozen distinct annual compliance points spread across at least four regulators.
    •

sections.title: Knowledge Check
sections.contentHtml:
Knowledge Check
   

Module 1 — End-of-Section MCQ (10 questions)

   

Click the option you believe is correct. Feedback appears immediately. Aim for 8/10.

   
      Q1      
Which of the following is not administered by HMRC?
     
                                     
     
Strike-off (DS01) is processed by Companies House. HMRC may object to a strike-off if tax is owed, but it does not administer the process.
   
   
      Q2      
A new private limited company is incorporated on 14 March 2024. When are its first statutory accounts due at Companies House?
     
                                     
     
First accounts of a private company are due 21 months after incorporation. Subsequent accounts are due 9 months after the accounting reference date (ARD).
   
   
      Q3      
Which standard is most commonly applied to small UK private companies that do not qualify as micro-entities?
     
                                     
     
FRS 102 Section 1A reduces disclosures for entities qualifying as small under the Companies Act size limits while still applying FRS 102 recognition and measurement.
   
   
      Q4      
Operating as a paid bookkeeper without AML supervision is:
     
                                     
     
MLR 2017 reg.56 makes unsupervised practice a criminal offence punishable by up to 2 years' imprisonment.
   
   
      Q5      
The Confirmation Statement (CS01) is filed at:
     
                                     
     
CS01 confirms the registered office, officers, shareholders, PSC and SIC code. Filing fee £34 (digital) from May 2024.
   
   
      Q6      
A “BX9” HMRC postcode refers to:
     
                                     
     
BX9 is a non-geographic mail routing code. Correspondence is sub-routed by the address line (e.g. “Self Assessment”, “Corporation Tax Services”, “PT Operations North East England”).
   
   
      Q7      
Which body is the AML supervisor for AAT-qualified bookkeepers in independent practice?
     
                                     
     
AAT is a recognised AML supervisory body and supervises members in practice. Members do not also need HMRC supervision.
   
   
      Q8      
A fixed charge over a company's premises is created on 1 February. By when must it be registered at Companies House under the standard rule?
     
                                     
     
21 days — CA 2006 s.859A. Out of time, the charge is void against a liquidator and the company would need a court order to register late.
   
   
      Q9      
Which of the following is a non-ministerial department?
     
                                     
     
HMRC is a non-ministerial department reporting to Parliament via the Treasury, established by CRCA 2005. The others are executive agencies or arm's-length bodies.
   
   
      Q10      
Which Act is replacing the FRC with a stronger regulator (ARGA)?
     
                                     
     
The Audit Reform Bill (post-Kingman) creates ARGA. As of 2024/25 the FRC continues to operate while transition occurs.

title: UK Business Structures — Deep Dive
meta: Module 2 · Part 1 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard
learningObjHtml:
Learning Objectives

   
         
  • Compare the seven main UK business structures (sole trader, general partnership, LLP, private limited, public limited, CIC, charity/CIO) on legal personality, liability, taxation, governance, public disclosure and cost.
    •      
  • Calculate the all-in tax cost (Income Tax + NI + Corporation Tax + dividend tax) of a £50,000 / £100,000 / £200,000 profit business under sole-trader vs Ltd vs LLP structures.
    •      
  • Identify the structure that best fits a given client scenario based on liability exposure, profit profile, growth plans and exit strategy.
    •      
  • Explain the regulatory and reporting consequences of each structure.
    •      
  • List the documents constitutionally governing each structure.
    •

sections.title: 2.2 Sole trader — the legal nuts and bolts
sections.contentHtml:
A sole trader (or “self-employed individual”) is a person who carries on a trade, profession or vocation in their own name. There is no legal separation between the person and the business. Their assets and the “business” assets are the same in law — if the business goes bankrupt, the personal assets follow.

 

2.2.1 Registering as a sole trader

 

You must register for Self Assessment with HMRC by 5 October following the end of the tax year in which you started self-employment. Registration is online at gov.uk/register-for-self-assessment; HMRC issues a UTR (Unique Taxpayer Reference) within ~10 working days, and a separate Government Gateway login.

 

2.2.2 Tax footprint of a sole trader

 

Profits from self-employment are charged to:

 
       
  • Income Tax on profits above the Personal Allowance (£12,570 for 2024/25): 20% basic, 40% higher, 45% additional. Personal Allowance tapers away at £1 for every £2 of income above £100,000 — fully eroded at £125,140.
    •    
  • Class 4 NI: 6% on profits between £12,570 and £50,270; 2% above. (Reduced from 9% to 6% from 6 April 2024 in the Spring Budget; check current year for 2025/26.)
    •    
  • Class 2 NI: abolished as a flat-rate weekly charge from 6 April 2024. Voluntary Class 2 contributions remain available for self-employed earning below the Small Profits Threshold (currently £6,725) who wish to maintain a state pension contribution year — £3.45/week (2024/25 rate).
    •  
 
    Worked Example 2.1    

Sarah, freelance graphic designer (sole trader)

   

Year ended 5 April 2025. Trading profit: £40,000. No other income.

                                           
Trading profit40,000
Less Personal Allowance(12,570)
Taxable income27,430
Income Tax (basic 20%)5,486
Class 4 NI: (50,270 − 12,570) × 6% = 2,262 capped to:
(40,000 − 12,570) × 6%		1,646
Total tax & NI7,13217.8% effective
   

Sarah pays this through Self Assessment by 31 January 2026 (along with first Payment on Account for 2025/26).

 
 

2.2.3 Advantages and disadvantages of sole trader status

                                             
AdvantageDisadvantage
Cheapest and simplest to set up — no Companies House feeUnlimited personal liability for business debts
No requirement to publish accounts — complete privacyCannot raise external equity finance
Losses can be offset against other income (sideways loss relief, ITA 2007 s.64)Often perceived as less “professional” than a Ltd by larger customers
Cash basis available if turnover <£150k (mandatory default from 6 April 2024 for new entrants)Profits are taxed each year regardless of withdrawals — no flexibility to defer income recognition like a company can with retained earnings
No Corporation Tax administration; one annual SA100Class 4 NI applies on top of Income Tax — total marginal rate ~28% for basic-rate earners

aiPractice.question: A sole trader has self-employment profits of £45,000 for the tax year 2024/25. Calculate their Income Tax and Class 4 National Insurance liability (assuming they have no other income and are a basic rate taxpayer).

sections.title: 2.3 General Partnership
sections.contentHtml:
Two or more persons (individuals or corporates) carrying on business in common with a view to profit (Partnership Act 1890 s.1). No legal personality in England & Wales (the partnership is not a separate person); each partner is jointly and severally liable for partnership debts.

 

2.3.1 The partnership agreement

 

The PA 1890 provides default rules — equal sharing of profits, equal contribution to capital, no entitlement to remuneration for working in the business, etc. Almost all clients will want to override these by a written Partnership Agreement covering:

 
       
  • Profit-sharing ratio (PSR) and changes in PSR
    •    
  • Capital contributions and interest on capital
    •    
  • Salaries to partners (a P&L charge in commercial accounts but added back for tax)
    •    
  • Drawings limits and policies
    •    
  • Admission of new partners and retirement of existing partners
    •    
  • Dispute resolution
    •    
  • Continuation/dissolution on death of a partner
    •  
 

2.3.2 Tax for a general partnership

 

The partnership itself does not pay tax. It files an SA800 Partnership Tax Return that reports the partnership's profit; that profit is then allocated among the partners according to their PSR for the period and each partner reports their share on form SA104 (partnership pages) within their personal SA100.

 

2.3.3 Limited Partnership (LP) — specialist structure

 

An LP is a partnership with at least one general partner (unlimited liability) and one or more limited partners (limited to capital contribution). LPs are registered at Companies House under the Limited Partnerships Act 1907. Mostly used by private equity / VC funds. Not to be confused with LLP (next).

aiPractice.question:
A general partnership has three partners: Alex, Ben, and Chitra. Their Partnership Agreement specifies a profit-sharing ratio of 50:30:20 respectively. For the year ended 31 December 2023, the partnership made a taxable profit of £120,000. The Partnership Agreement also provides for salaries of £20,000 to Alex and £15,000 to Ben (but none to Chitra), and interest on capital of 5% on their opening capital balances of £80,000, £60,000, and £40,000 respectively.

(a) Calculate each partner's share of the partnership profit for tax purposes.
(b) Explain why the salaries and interest on capital are treated differently for commercial accounts versus for tax purposes.
(c) If the partnership had no written agreement and used the Partnership Act 1890 defaults instead, how would the profit allocation differ?

sections.title: 2.4 Limited Liability Partnership (LLP)
sections.contentHtml:
Created by the Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000. An LLP is a separate legal entity (like a company) but is taxed like a partnership (transparent, members pay IT & NI on their share). Designed for professional firms (law, accountancy) that wanted limited liability without becoming companies.

 

2.4.1 Key LLP attributes

 
       
  • Minimum 2 members; minimum 2 designated members (with statutory filing duties).
    •    
  • No share capital; capital contributions are accounted for as members' loans/equity per the LLP agreement.
    •    
  • Files annual accounts at Companies House (small/micro filing exemptions broadly mirror companies).
    •    
  • Files a confirmation statement annually.
    •    
  • Members are taxed personally on their share of LLP profits as if they were partners (ITTOIA 2005 s.863).
    •    
  • Salaried members rule (ITA 2007 s.863A) deems certain “disguised employees” in LLPs to be employees for PAYE/NI — you must apply the three-condition test annually.
    •

aiPractice.question:
An LLP has four members. Three are equity members with significant capital contributions and management roles. The fourth member receives a fixed salary of £80,000 per year set by the LLP agreement, has no capital contribution, takes no part in management, and their role is to provide specialist technical services on a day-to-day basis under the direction of the other members.

(a) Explain why the salaried members rule under ITA 2007 s.863A might apply to the fourth member.

(b) What are the tax consequences if the salaried members rule applies, compared to normal partnership taxation treatment?

(c) What annual obligation does the LLP have in relation to this determination?

sections.title: 2.5 Private Limited Company (Ltd)
sections.contentHtml:
The workhorse of UK business. Roughly 4.6 million companies on the register. The company is a separate legal person under CA 2006 s.16. Shareholders own; directors manage; their roles and the relationship between them are set out in the company's Articles of Association and (often) a separate Shareholders' Agreement.

 

2.5.1 Constitutional documents

 
       
  • Memorandum of Association — a now-very-short document signed by initial subscribers confirming intention to form a company. Replaced extensively in 2009 by simpler form.
    •    
  • Articles of Association — the company's internal rulebook. The Model Articles for private companies (Companies (Model Articles) Regulations 2008, Sch 1) are the default; can be modified or replaced by bespoke Articles.
    •    
  • Shareholders' Agreement — private contract between shareholders. Often covers pre-emption, drag/tag rights, exit mechanics, valuation. Not filed at Companies House (unlike Articles, which are public).
    •  
 

2.5.2 Tax footprint of a Ltd

 

Two layers of tax:

 
       
  1. Corporation Tax on company profits — 25% main rate above £250,000; 19% small profits rate up to £50,000; marginal relief in between (effective marginal rate ~26.5%).
    2.    
  2. Income Tax on amounts extracted — salary (taxed under PAYE with Class 1 NI primary 8% / secondary 13.8%), or dividends (taxed at 8.75% basic / 33.75% higher / 39.35% additional, with a £500 dividend allowance for 2024/25, reducing to £500 in 2024/25 from £1,000 in 2023/24).
    3.  
 

2.5.3 The salary/dividend mix — the classic owner-managed company question

 

For a director-shareholder, the optimal extraction structure depends on (a) whether they need NI credits, (b) the company's profit level, (c) their other income, and (d) personal allowance interactions. The traditional structure for a single-director company in 2024/25:

 
       
  • Pay a salary equal to the Secondary NI Threshold (£9,100 for 2024/25, raised to £5,000 for 2025/26 with Employer NI changes from April 2025) to maintain a qualifying year for the State Pension without triggering Employer or Employee NI.
    •    
  • Take the rest as dividends out of post-tax retained profits.
    •  
 
    2025/26 watch — Employer NI changes    

From 6 April 2025, the Secondary Threshold drops to £5,000 (from £9,100) and Employer NI rises to 15% (from 13.8%). The classic “£9,100 salary + dividends” strategy needs revisiting from 2025/26 — in many cases a higher salary (up to the Personal Allowance £12,570) becomes optimal because the Employer's Allowance (£10,500 from April 2025, where eligible) covers the resulting Employer NI, and the salary saves Corporation Tax at 19%–25%.

 
 
    Worked Example 2.2    

Director-shareholder — £40,000 profit company (2024/25)

   

Single director-shareholder, no other income, taking £9,100 salary + balance as dividend.

                                                                                     
Profit before director's salary40,000
Less salary(9,100)
Profit chargeable to CT30,900
Corporation Tax @ 19% (small profits rate)(5,871)
Profit available as dividend25,029
Personal tax position:
Salary9,100Personal Allowance covers
Dividend25,029
Less remaining Personal Allowance (12,570 − 9,100)(3,470)
Less Dividend Allowance(500)
Taxable dividend21,059
Dividend tax @ 8.75%1,843
Total tax5,871 + 1,843 = 7,714~19.3% effective
   

Compare Sarah (sole trader, Worked Example 2.1) at £7,132 on £40k profit. The Ltd is slightly more expensive at this profit level — the cross-over typically happens around £30k–£35k profit. The Ltd's value comes at higher profits, when retained earnings can be deferred, and when limited liability is genuinely useful.

sections.title: 2.6 Public Limited Company (PLC)
sections.contentHtml:
A company whose name ends in “plc”. The label means it can offer shares to the public — not that it must, and not that it is listed. Distinct features:

 
       
  • Minimum allotted share capital £50,000, of which 25% must be paid up.
    •    
  • Minimum 2 directors (vs 1 for Ltd) and a company secretary (mandatory).
    •    
  • Accounts due 6 months after ARD (vs 9 months for Ltd).
    •    
  • Cannot file abridged or filleted accounts — full accounts required.
    •    
  • If listed (LSE Main, AIM, AQUIS) — FCA rules apply on top.
    •

sections.title: 2.7 Community Interest Company (CIC)
sections.contentHtml: A limited company (Ltd or company limited by guarantee) with a community/social-purpose lock. Created by the Companies (Audit, Investigations & Community Enterprise) Act 2004. Regulated by the CIC Regulator (a small office within Companies House). Files a CIC34 community-interest report annually with the accounts. Asset lock means assets cannot be distributed to members — if dissolved, must transfer to another asset-locked body.

sections.title: 2.8 Charity, Charitable Incorporated Organisation (CIO) and Charitable Company
sections.contentHtml:
Three principal forms:

 
       
  • Unincorporated charity (charitable trust or association) — trustees personally liable; no separate legal personality.
    •    
  • Charitable company limited by guarantee — legal personality; dual-registered (Companies House + Charity Commission).
    •    
  • CIO — Charitable Incorporated Organisation, created by Charities Act 2011 Part 11. Single regulator (Charity Commission) so no Companies House filing burden. Two flavours: Foundation CIO (members are the trustees) and Association CIO (separate membership body with trustees elected by members).
    •  
 

Charity-specific tax treatment: most income exempt under CTA 2010 Part 11 (trading income exemption) provided used for charitable purposes; non-primary-purpose trading sometimes routed through a wholly-owned trading subsidiary which gift-aids profit up to the parent. Module 71 covers Ltd-to-CIO conversion in detail.

sections.title: 2.9 The choice tree — which structure for which client?
sections.contentHtml:
Client situationRecommended structureRationale
Hobby income, <£10k profit, no liability riskSole traderSimplest, cheapest. No CT or CH filings.
Freelance consultant, £20–£40k profit, low liability riskSole traderTax cost similar; admin cheaper. Revisit at £50k+.
Trades-person (electrician, builder) £30k+LtdSignificant injury or property-damage liability protection worth limited liability cost.
Two-person consultancy with retained profitLtdIncome splitting via dividends; retained profit deferral.
Professional firm (law, accountancy) with multiple senior practitionersLLPLimited liability + tax transparency; easier to admit/retire members than for a Ltd.
Property landlord, single rental propertyGenerally personal nameTax-driven analysis: SDLT 3% surcharge for company purchase, no Section 24 mortgage interest restriction in company, but extra 8% CGT on disposal of corporate. Modelling required.
Property landlord building a portfolio (5+ properties)LtdSection 24 mortgage interest restriction in personal name very expensive at higher rates; companies fully deduct interest.
Social enterprise (community gym, food bank with paid trading)CIC or CIOAsset lock and clear social purpose; CIO if grant-funded mostly; CIC if mostly trading.
Charity raising funds for causeCIOSingle regulator; trustee limited liability; cleaner constitutional framework than charitable trust.
Multi-director SME with VC fundingLtd or PLCShares are the standard investment instrument; partnership structures don't accommodate equity investors.
 
    The £50k profit pivot    

A widely-used rule of thumb: profits up to £30k — sole trader is usually cheaper after software and accountancy costs; £30k–£50k — broadly equivalent; above £50k — Ltd starts to dominate provided the owner does not need to extract every penny each year. If they do extract everything, the dividend-tax layer narrows the advantage. Always model on actual numbers; never advise structurally without modelling.

 
 
   

Module 2 — Summary

   
         
  • Seven principal structures: sole trader, partnership, LLP, Ltd, PLC, CIC, charity/CIO. They differ on legal personality, liability, taxation and disclosure.
    •      
  • Sole trader and partnership offer simplicity and privacy but unlimited personal liability and an Income Tax + Class 4 NI tax footprint.
    •      
  • LLP combines partnership taxation transparency with limited liability — ideal for professional firms.
    •      
  • Ltd provides limited liability and access to dividend extraction at lower combined tax cost above ~£50k profit, at the cost of public filing and Corporation Tax administration.
    •      
  • PLC, CIC and charity forms are specialist — deployed for capital raising, social purpose and tax-exempt purposes respectively.
    •      
  • Always model the after-tax outcome on actual numbers. The 2024/25 to 2025/26 transition (Employer NI changes, dividend allowance erosion, Class 2 abolition) materially shifts the balance.
    •

sections.title: Knowledge Check
sections.contentHtml:
Knowledge Check
   

Module 2 — End-of-Section MCQ (10 questions)

   

Aim for 8/10. Click an option to see the verdict.

   
      Q1      
A sole trader's business assets are, in law:
     
                                     
     
A sole trader has no legal separation from the business; the assets are personal assets and the liabilities are personal liabilities.
   
   
      Q2      
By which date must a new sole trader register for Self Assessment for the tax year 2024/25?
     
                                     
     
Registration for SA is required by 5 October following the end of the tax year of commencement. Filing deadline is the following 31 January, but registration is earlier.
   
   
      Q3      
The Class 4 NI rate on profits between £12,570 and £50,270 in 2024/25 is:
     
                                     
     
Class 4 main rate cut from 9% to 6% from 6 April 2024 (Spring Budget 2024). 2% applies above £50,270.
   
   
      Q4      
A partnership return (SA800):
     
                                     
     
SA800 reports profit; the profit is allocated to partners by their PSR and each partner reports their share on SA104 in their personal SA100.
   
   
      Q5      
Which is true of an LLP?
     
                                     
     
LLPs combine the limited liability of a company with the tax transparency of a partnership.
   
   
      Q6      
The Corporation Tax rate on profits up to £50,000 (single company, 2024/25) is:
     
                                     
     
19% small profits rate applies up to £50k; 25% main rate above £250k; marginal relief in between with effective marginal of 26.5%.
   
   
      Q7      
The dividend allowance for 2024/25 is:
     
                                     
     
£500 for 2024/25 (down from £1,000 in 2023/24 and £2,000 in 2022/23).
   
   
      Q8      
A PLC must file its accounts at Companies House within:
     
                                     
     
PLC accounts: 6 months after ARD. Private companies: 9 months. (First accounts: 21 months from incorporation in either case.)
   
   
      Q9      
A CIC's defining legal feature is:
     
                                     
     
A CIC is a limited company with an asset lock, regulated by the CIC Regulator. It pays Corporation Tax like any company.
   
   
      Q10      
A property investor with 8 buy-to-let properties on residential mortgages and £80k other employment income is most likely better off:
     
                                     
     
Section 24 ITA 2007 restricts mortgage interest relief on residential property to a 20% basic-rate tax credit for individuals; companies deduct it in full. With the investor on higher-rate income, the saving is material.

hookHtml:
A client comes in with the same question every accountant hears: “sole trader or
          ltd?” The honest answer is never a one-liner — it depends on profit profile, liability exposure,
          growth plan, exit intent, and how the owner wants to extract cash. Two builders with identical £80k
          profits can rationally choose differently: one stays sole trader (simpler, full Class 4 NI exposure, unlimited
          liability accepted because the work isn’t litigation-prone); the other incorporates (Corp Tax + dividend
          tax, slightly lower total tax at this band, limited liability against a client who sues over a structural
          defect, professional credibility, easier sale at exit). The wrong structure costs real money — and the
          cost compounds. Pick sole-trader when a Ltd would have saved £4k/year in tax and the owner pays
          £40k of unnecessary tax over a decade. Pick Ltd when sole-trader would have saved £1.5k/year in
          admin and accountancy fees and the owner pays £15k of compliance overhead they didn’t need. Choose
          CIC when a charity would have unlocked Gift Aid and rate relief, or choose a charity when a CIC would have
          allowed dividends to fund the founders. Get the structure right at incorporation and every later decision sits
          on a sound foundation. Get it wrong and you spend years working around it. This module is the seven-structure
          map: sole trader, general partnership, LLP, private limited (Ltd), public limited (PLC), Community Interest
          Company (CIC), and charity/CIO — with the legal personality, liability exposure, tax regime,
          public-disclosure burden, and governance documents that distinguish each.

title: Bookkeeping Fundamentals — Double-Entry from First Principles
meta: Module 3 · Part 1 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard
learningObjHtml:
Learning Objectives

   
         
  • State and explain the accounting equation, including its rearrangements.
    •      
  • Apply the rules of double-entry to record assets, liabilities, equity, income and expenses.
    •      
  • Post compound and reversing journals correctly.
    •      
  • Prepare a trial balance from a list of ledger balances and identify the types of error a TB will and will not detect.
    •      
  • Translate any business event into a journal using the “source → debit → credit → narrative” method.
    •

sections.title: 3.1 What is bookkeeping?
sections.contentHtml: Bookkeeping is the systematic recording of every financial transaction of a business, in chronological order, in a way that allows the business to: (a) know its financial position at any moment (balance sheet); (b) measure its performance over a period (P&L); (c) prove the figures to an external party (HMRC, Companies House, banks, investors); and (d) detect errors and fraud. The discipline is approximately 700 years old — codified by the Italian friar Luca Pacioli in Summa de Arithmetica (1494) — but the underlying logic has not changed since.

sections.title: 3.2 The accounting equation
sections.contentHtml:
Assets = Liabilities + Equity  
 

This is the only equation in accounting. It is true after every single transaction, in every business, in every era. Variations:

 
       
  • Assets − Liabilities = Equity (net worth) — how the balance sheet is normally presented in the UK.
    •    
  • Equity = Capital introduced + Retained profits − Drawings/Dividends — expansion of the equity component over time.
    •    
  • Profit = Income − Expenses — measuring the change in equity from operations between two balance sheet dates (excluding capital introduced/withdrawn).
    •

aiPractice.title: The Accounting Equation in Practice
aiPractice.content: A sole trader starts a business by introducing £10,000 capital (Asset: Bank £10,000; Equity: Capital £10,000). She then buys equipment for £3,000 cash (Asset: Bank £7,000, Equipment £3,000; Equity: Capital £10,000). Next, she borrows £5,000 from the bank (Asset: Bank £12,000, Equipment £3,000; Liability: Loan £5,000; Equity: Capital £10,000). Finally, she makes a profit of £2,000 from trading (Asset: Bank £14,000, Equipment £3,000; Liability: Loan £5,000; Equity: Capital £10,000 + Retained profit £2,000). Notice that Assets (£17,000) always equal Liabilities (£5,000) plus Equity (£12,000) after each transaction.

sections.title: 3.3 Double-entry — the symmetry rule
sections.contentHtml:
Every transaction has at least two equal and opposite entries: one debit and one credit (or several adding to balance). This guarantees the accounting equation remains true. The direction of debit/credit is fixed by the type of account:

                                                   
Account typeIncreaseDecreaseNormal balance
AssetDebitCreditDebit
ExpenseDebitCreditDebit
DrawingsDebitCreditDebit
LiabilityCreditDebitCredit
Equity / CapitalCreditDebitCredit
Income / RevenueCreditDebitCredit
 

Mnemonic: DEAD CLIC — Debits go up for Expenses, Assets, Drawings; Credits go up for Liabilities, Income, Capital.

aiPractice.title: Applying the Symmetry Rule to a Transaction
aiPractice.content: A business purchases equipment for £5,000 on credit from a supplier. Using the symmetry rule, we must record two equal and opposite entries. The asset (Equipment) increases, so we debit it £5,000. The liability (Payable to supplier) increases, so we credit it £5,000. The entry is: Debit Equipment £5,000 / Credit Payables £5,000. Total debits (£5,000) = Total credits (£5,000), so the accounting equation stays balanced: Assets (Equipment +£5,000) = Liabilities (Payables +£5,000). This demonstrates that every transaction always has at least two entries that balance exactly.

sections.title: 3.4 The 8 universal transaction patterns
sections.contentHtml:
Every UK business transaction reduces to one of these eight patterns. Memorise them and you can journalise anything.

 
   
Pattern 1 — Cash sale
   
BankDr 1,200
   
Sales (or Sales + VAT control)Cr 1,200
   
Records receipt of cash and recognition of revenue simultaneously.
 
 
   
Pattern 2 — Credit sale (invoice issued, money not yet received)
   
Trade Debtors (Accounts Receivable)Dr 1,200
   
SalesCr 1,000
   
VAT Output TaxCr 200
   
Recognises receivable and revenue at point of supply (FRS 102 Section 23 / IFRS 15 logic).
 
 
   
Pattern 3 — Receipt from credit customer
   
BankDr 1,200
   
Trade DebtorsCr 1,200
   
Settles the receivable; revenue was already recorded in pattern 2 — do not record sales again.
 
 
   
Pattern 4 — Cash purchase (expense)
   
Stationery (or appropriate expense)Dr 50
   
VAT Input Tax (if recoverable)Dr 10
   
BankCr 60
 
 
   
Pattern 5 — Credit purchase (supplier invoice received)
   
Expense (or Asset, e.g. inventory)Dr 100
   
VAT Input TaxDr 20
   
Trade Creditors (Accounts Payable)Cr 120
 
 
   
Pattern 6 — Payment to supplier
   
Trade CreditorsDr 120
   
BankCr 120
 
 
   
Pattern 7 — Capital introduced by owner
   
BankDr 10,000
   
Capital (sole trader) / Director's Loan / Share Capital (Ltd)Cr 10,000
 
 
   
Pattern 8 — Drawings / Dividend (distribution to owner)
   
Drawings (sole trader) / Dividends Paid (Ltd, charged against retained earnings)Dr 500
   
BankCr 500

aiPractice.question:
A UK sole trader purchases stationery for £84 including VAT (VAT rate 20%), paying immediately by bank transfer. Three days later, she receives an invoice from a supplier for £600 plus VAT for materials to be used in production, with payment due in 30 days. She also receives a cheque for £1,440 from a credit customer who owes exactly this amount.

Write out all three journal entries in full, identifying which of the 8 patterns each one represents.

---

**Rationale:** The section presents all 8 patterns as memorisation content with brief descriptions but no worked examples. A student needs to demonstrate they can:
1. Identify which pattern applies to different scenarios
2. Handle VAT correctly in both cash and credit transactions
3. Distinguish between revenue recognition (pattern 2) and cash receipt (pattern 3)
4. Apply the correct account structure for each pattern

This question consolidates understanding before they move to recording these in actual ledgers.

sections.title: 3.5 Compound journals
sections.contentHtml:
Where a transaction needs more than two postings — e.g. payroll — we use a compound journal:

 
   
Payroll for the month — gross £10,000, tax £1,500, EE NI £700, ER NI £900, net pay £7,800
   
Wages & Salaries (P&L)Dr 10,000
   
Employer's NI (P&L)Dr 900
   
PAYE/NIC liabilityCr 3,100
   
Net wages payable / BankCr 7,800
   
Three credits, two debits — total debits 10,900 = total credits 10,900. Always check.

sections.title: 3.6 The trial balance
sections.contentHtml:
A trial balance lists every ledger account balance with debits in one column and credits in another. The columns must total to the same figure. If they do, you have arithmetic integrity (one of the three checks below).

                                                   
Errors a TB will detectErrors a TB will not detect
One-sided entries (only Dr or only Cr posted)Errors of omission (transaction not recorded at all)
Different amounts on Dr and CrErrors of commission (right side, wrong account)
Casting errors in a single ledgerErrors of principle (e.g. capital expenditure expensed as repair)
Transposition errors that change a side totalCompensating errors (two errors that cancel out)
Original entry errors (wrong amount on both sides)
Reversal errors (Dr and Cr swapped)
 

This is why the trial balance is a necessary but not sufficient check. The other two checks at month-end are: bank reconciliation (proves cash account against external bank statement) and control account reconciliations (proves debtor/creditor control accounts against the underlying sub-ledgers).

 
   

Module 3 — Summary

   
         
  • Accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Equity holds after every transaction.
    •      
  • Double-entry: equal debits and credits per transaction. DEAD CLIC mnemonic.
    •      
  • Eight universal transaction patterns cover the bulk of bookkeeping.
    •      
  • Trial balance proves arithmetic but cannot detect errors of omission, commission, principle, compensation, original entry or reversal.
    •

sections.title: Knowledge Check
sections.contentHtml:
Knowledge Check
   

Module 3 — End-of-Section MCQ (8 questions)

   
      Q1      
A business pays £600 cash for a desk to use in the office (capitalised). Which is the correct journal?
     
                                     
     
An asset is acquired (Dr increases an asset) by paying out cash (Cr decreases an asset). Treating it as an expense would be an error of principle.
   
   
      Q2      
Which type of error will a balanced trial balance not detect?
     
                                     
     
Posting to the wrong account on the right side is an error of commission and the TB still balances.
   
   
      Q3      
A credit sale of £1,200 (incl. 20% VAT) generates which credit to VAT Output Tax?
     
                                     
     
£1,200 ÷ 1.2 = £1,000 net; £1,200 − £1,000 = £200 VAT.
   
   
      Q4      
Drawings are:
     
                                     
     
Drawings reduce the owner's equity. They are not an expense and do not affect profit.
   
   
      Q5      
A receipt from a credit customer is posted as:
     
                                     
     
Sales were recognised when the invoice was raised; the receipt only settles the debtor.
   
   
      Q6      
Equity at year-end equals:
     
                                     
     
Equity moves only via capital introduced/withdrawn (or share issues/buybacks for a Ltd) and retained profit/loss.
   
   
      Q7      
Compensating errors are:
     
                                     
     
Two errors of equal and opposite effect can leave the TB balanced. Only substantive checks (e.g. reconciliations) catch them.
   
   
      Q8      
In double-entry, an increase in a liability is recorded as:
     
                                     
     
Liabilities have a normal credit balance. Increases are credits, decreases are debits.

hookHtml:
A 15th-century Italian friar called Luca Pacioli wrote a 600-page maths book in 1494, and
          a small section — <tspan>Summa de Arithmetica</tspan> — codified the double-entry system that
          every UK SME’s books still run on today. The logic hasn’t changed in 530 years: every transaction
          touches at least two accounts, debits equal credits, and one equation holds true after every single posting:
          <tspan>Assets = Liabilities + Equity</tspan>. Software hides the mechanics — Xero shows you a bank rec,
          QuickBooks shows you a sales invoice — but underneath, every single line is still a debit and a credit.
          Understand the eight universal transaction patterns and you can post anything: a director’s loan
          repayment, a depreciation charge, a deferred revenue release, a wage accrual, a year-end CT provision.
          Don’t understand the patterns and you’ll spend a career copy-pasting from Google searches and
          second-guessing whether sales returns are a debit or a credit (debit). This module is the bedrock: the one
          equation, the five account types, the eight transaction patterns, the trial balance — including what a
          TB does and (critically) doesn’t detect. Skip this and every later module (FRS 102, CT computations,
          journals, year-end adjustments, going-concern reviews) is a struggle.

title: The Chart of Accounts & The General Ledger
meta: Module 4 · Part 1 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard
learningObjHtml:
Learning Objectives

   
         
  • Design a chart of accounts that balances simplicity with the level of analysis needed for VAT, Corporation Tax, payroll and statutory accounts.
    •      
  • Distinguish a control account from a sub-ledger and reconcile between them.
    •      
  • Map every UK statutory account line (per FRS 102 Section 1A formats and the Companies Act Schedule 1) to a chart of accounts code range.
    •

sections.title: 4.1 What is the chart of accounts (COA)?
sections.contentHtml: The chart of accounts is the list of every account in the general ledger, organised by code or category. It is the backbone of the accounting system — everything that gets posted lands in one of these accounts. The COA structure determines how easily you can produce: a P&L (income/expense classification); a balance sheet (asset/liability/equity classification); a VAT return (VAT codes); and statutory accounts (mapped to the Companies Act formats).

sections.title: 4.2 Standard UK COA structure (Xero/QBO defaults)
sections.contentHtml:
Code rangeCategoryExamples
100–199Sales / Revenue200 Sales, 260 Other Income
300–399Cost of Sales310 Materials, 320 Direct Labour
400–599Operating Expenses404 Rent, 408 Utilities, 412 Insurance, 477 Salaries
600–699Finance / Other610 Interest Income, 620 Bank Charges, 625 Loan Interest
700–799Depreciation, Tax Charges710 Depreciation, 760 Corporation Tax
800–899Non-current Assets810 Office Equipment, 820 Plant & Machinery, 850 Motor Vehicles
900–989Current Assets910 Inventory, 920 Trade Debtors, 950 Bank, 960 Petty Cash
990–999Prepayments & Accrued Income995 Prepayments, 996 Accrued Income
1000–1099Current Liabilities1020 Trade Creditors, 1040 VAT Liability, 1050 PAYE/NIC Liability, 1060 Corporation Tax Liability
1100–1199Accruals & Deferred Income1110 Accruals, 1120 Deferred Income
1200–1299Non-current Liabilities1210 Bank Loans, 1230 Hire Purchase
1500–1599Equity1510 Share Capital, 1520 Share Premium, 1530 Retained Earnings, 1540 Director's Loan, 1560 Dividends Paid
 

Note: Xero, QBO, Sage, FreeAgent each use slightly different default code numbers but the categories are universal. When converting clients between platforms, the COA is the first thing to map and the most common source of conversion errors.

sections.title: 4.3 Control accounts and sub-ledgers
sections.contentHtml:
The general ledger contains control accounts (single-line balances summarising sub-ledgers). Examples:

 
       
  • Trade Debtors Control — summary; the underlying sub-ledger has every customer's balance broken out (Aged Debtors Report).
    •    
  • Trade Creditors Control — summary; underlying = supplier balances (Aged Creditors).
    •    
  • VAT Control — summary; underlying = transaction-level VAT detail by tax code.
    •    
  • PAYE/NIC Control — summary; underlying = month-by-month payroll detail.
    •  
 

Control accounts must reconcile to the sub-ledger every period. If they don't, an entry has been posted directly to the control account bypassing the sub-ledger — common in a manual journal that should have been done as a customer credit note instead.

 
   

Module 4 — Summary

   
         
  • The COA is the list of every ledger account, structured by category for reporting.
    •      
  • A control account summarises a sub-ledger; the two must always reconcile.
    •      
  • The COA design predicts whether you can produce a clean VAT return, CT600 and statutory accounts — design it with the end report in mind.
    •

sections.title: Knowledge Check
sections.contentHtml:
Knowledge Check
   

Module 4 — End-of-Section MCQ (5 questions)

   
      Q1      
Trade Debtors Control:
     
                                     
     
It is a single ledger balance summarising the customer sub-ledger; reconciliation is essential.
   
   
      Q2      
A code range of 800–899 is most likely used for:
     
                                     
     
Standard Xero numbering puts non-current assets in 800s.
   
   
      Q3      
Why does COA design matter for VAT?
     
                                     
     
Boxes 6 and 7 of the VAT return need supply-type breakdowns; the COA is where this is captured.
   
   
      Q4      
Director's Loan Account is best classified as:
     
                                     
     
If the director has lent the company money, it is a creditor. If the director owes the company money (overdrawn DLA), it is a debtor with potential s.455 tax consequences (Module 8).
   
   
      Q5      
When migrating from QBO to Xero, the most common issue at the COA level is:
     
                                     
     
Account category mismatches (e.g. an item that was “Cost of Sales” in QBO landing in “Direct Cost” or “Expense” in Xero) are the classic migration issue.

quiz.question: Trade Debtors Control:

options.text: Summarises customer balances; total must equal the aged debtors report
Is only used for VAT-registered businesses

quiz.feedback: It is a single ledger balance summarising the customer sub-ledger; reconciliation is essential.

quiz.feedback: Standard Xero numbering puts non-current assets in 800s.

quiz.question: Why does COA design matter for VAT?

options.text: It doesn't — VAT is determined by the tax code, not the account
Splitting income between standard, zero-rated, exempt and OoS supplies is essential for the VAT return boxes
Because VAT is calculated as a percentage of the COA balance
Only the sales account matters for VAT

quiz.feedback: Boxes 6 and 7 of the VAT return need supply-type breakdowns; the COA is where this is captured.

quiz.question: Director's Loan Account is best classified as:

options.text: An equity-adjacent liability/receivable, depending on whether it is in credit or overdrawn

quiz.feedback: If the director has lent the company money, it is a creditor. If the director owes the company money (overdrawn DLA), it is a debtor with potential s.455 tax consequences (Module 8).

quiz.question: When migrating from QBO to Xero, the most common issue at the COA level is:

options.text: Account categories don't map exactly — opening balances posted to wrong category

quiz.feedback: Account category mismatches (e.g. an item that was “Cost of Sales” in QBO landing in “Direct Cost” or “Expense” in Xero) are the classic migration issue.

title: The Bookkeeping Cycle — From Source Document to Trial Balance
meta: Module 5 · Part 1 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard
learningObjHtml:
Learning Objectives

   
         
  • Sequence the steps in a monthly bookkeeping cycle.
    •      
  • Identify the controls embedded at each step.
    •      
  • Explain how a bank reconciliation works and why it matters.
    •

sections.title: 5.1 The cycle in 9 steps
sections.contentHtml:
1. Capture source documents — collect every invoice, receipt, bank statement, expense claim, payroll record. Source: Dext, supplier portals, bank feeds.
    2.    
  2. Code & post transactions — assign each item to a COA account and a VAT code; post to the ledger.
    3.    
  3. Reconcile the bank — match every line on the bank statement to a posting in the bank ledger; investigate unmatched items.
    4.    
  4. Reconcile control accounts — debtors control to AR ageing; creditors control to AP ageing; VAT control to VAT return draft; PAYE control to payroll summary.
    5.    
  5. Adjusting journals — accruals, prepayments, depreciation, stock movement, payroll accruals, deferred income.
    6.    
  6. Run a trial balance — confirm Dr=Cr; review for unusual balances (negative assets, etc.).
    7.    
  7. Run management accounts — P&L vs budget, balance sheet snapshot, key KPIs.
    8.    
  8. Lock the period — set lock date in software so prior-period postings are blocked.
    9.    
  9. File & archive — store source documents, save management pack, log version.
    10.

sections.title: 5.2 Bank reconciliation in depth
sections.contentHtml:
A bank reconciliation answers: does my cash book agree with the bank's record of my cash? The starting point is the bank statement closing balance. From it, you adjust for unpresented cheques, uncleared lodgements and bank-only items (charges, interest, direct debits not yet recorded), to arrive at the cash book balance. In the cloud-feed era this is largely automated, but the discipline must be understood.

 
    Worked Example 5.1    

Bank Reconciliation as at 31 March 2025

                                           
Bank statement closing balance£12,450
Add: lodgement banked 31/3 not yet credited2,000
Less: unpresented cheques (#241, #243, #244)(1,800)
Adjusted bank balance12,650
Cash book balance per ledger12,650
DifferenceNIL
   

Action: post nothing — the items will clear next period. If the cash book balance had differed (after adjustments), investigate.

 
 
   

Module 5 — Summary

   
         
  • Nine repeating steps every month: capture, code, reconcile bank, reconcile controls, adjust, TB, MI, lock, archive.
    •      
  • Bank reconciliation is the cornerstone control. Never sign off accounts without one.
    •

sections.title: Knowledge Check
sections.contentHtml:
Knowledge Check
   

Module 5 — End-of-Section MCQ (5 questions)

   
      Q1      
An unpresented cheque is one that:
     
                                     
     
Correct — appears in cash book but not yet on bank statement.
   
   
      Q2      
Why lock the period after closing?
     
                                     
     
Lock dates protect the integrity of filed VAT returns and management accounts.
   
   
      Q3      
Which control account would you reconcile to the aged creditors report?
     
                                     
     
Aged creditors = supplier balances = trade creditors control sub-ledger.
   
   
      Q4      
A bank-only item not yet in the cash book is:
     
                                     
     
Bank charges, direct debits, standing orders and bank interest are common bank-only items requiring a journal to bring the cash book up to date.
   
   
      Q5      
A monthly P&L vs budget review is best done:
     
                                     
     
MI is meaningful only after the underlying ledger is corrected for accruals, prepayments, depreciation, etc.

quiz.question: An unpresented cheque is one that:

options.text: Has been received but not banked
Has been written and posted to the cash book but not yet cleared the bank
Has been returned by the bank

quiz.feedback: Correct — appears in cash book but not yet on bank statement.

quiz.question: Why lock the period after closing?

options.text: To prevent backdated postings that would change a published return
It triggers the next period to start

quiz.feedback: Lock dates protect the integrity of filed VAT returns and management accounts.

quiz.question: Which control account would you reconcile to the aged creditors report?
quiz.feedback: Aged creditors = supplier balances = trade creditors control sub-ledger.

quiz.question: A bank-only item not yet in the cash book is:

options.text: A bank charge or direct debit not yet posted

quiz.feedback: Bank charges, direct debits, standing orders and bank interest are common bank-only items requiring a journal to bring the cash book up to date.

quiz.question: A monthly P&L vs budget review is best done:

options.text: After all reconciliations and adjusting journals
Only after VAT return is filed

quiz.feedback: MI is meaningful only after the underlying ledger is corrected for accruals, prepayments, depreciation, etc.

hookHtml:
It’s the 5th of the month. Last month’s books need closing — and
          somewhere in the chaos sit 247 supplier invoices, 18 expense claims, a bank statement with 312 transactions,
          two payroll runs, a VAT return due in three weeks, and a director who’s just dropped a coffee receipt on
          your desk “for the books, ta.” What separates a bookkeeper who closes the month in two working
          days from one still chasing reconciliations a fortnight later isn’t speed — it’s <tspan>the
            cycle</tspan>. A defined nine-step sequence, run the same way every month, with controls embedded at each
          step. <tspan>Capture · code · post · bank rec · control accounts ·
            adjusting journals · trial balance · review · lock</tspan>. Skip a step or do them out
          of order and the errors compound: a missed bank rec hides three duplicate invoices; an un-reconciled VAT
          control silently builds a £4,200 misstatement; an unrun analytical review lets a 14% gross-margin drift
          go unnoticed for a quarter. Run the cycle properly and the trial balance at step 7 is just the natural output
          of having done the previous six. This module is the nine-step monthly close, the controls at each step, and
          the bank reconciliation discipline that catches the issues every other step misses.

sections.title: 6.1 The principal source documents
sections.contentHtml:
DocumentOriginatorPosted into
Sales invoiceYour business → customerSales day book → Sales account + Trade Debtors
Sales credit noteYour business → customerSales returns day book
Purchase invoiceSupplier → your businessPurchase day book → Expense/Asset + Trade Creditors
Purchase credit noteSupplier → your businessPurchase returns day book
Bank statementBankCash book
Cheque counterfoil / paying-in slipInternalCash book
Petty cash voucherInternalPetty cash book
Expense claim with receiptsEmployee → companyExpense ledger / Director's Loan
Payroll summary (P32 / FPS)Payroll softwareWages journal
Loan agreementLenderLoan account + interest expense
HP / lease agreementLenderHP/Lease creditor + asset cost

sections.title: 6.2 What makes a UK VAT invoice valid?
sections.contentHtml:
For input VAT to be recoverable, you need a valid VAT invoice from the supplier. Per VAT Regulations 1995 reg.14, a full VAT invoice must contain:

 
       
  1. An invoice sequential number
    2.    
  2. Date of issue
    3.    
  3. Tax point (time of supply)
    4.    
  4. Supplier's name, address and VAT registration number
    5.    
  5. Customer's name and address
    6.    
  6. Description sufficient to identify the goods/services
    7.    
  7. Quantity / extent of supply
    8.    
  8. Unit price (if applicable)
    9.    
  9. Net amount
    10.    
  10. VAT rate(s) and amount(s) per rate
    11.    
  11. Total VAT charged
    12.    
  12. Gross amount payable
    13.  
 

A simplified VAT invoice (used for retail supplies under £250 incl. VAT) needs fewer fields but must show supplier name/VRN, date, description, rate and the gross amount.

sections.title: 6.3 Retention periods
sections.contentHtml:
RecordsMinimum retentionSource
Self-employed records5 years from 31 January following tax yearTMA 1970 s.12B
Company tax records6 years from end of accounting periodFA 1998 Sch.18 para.21
VAT records6 years (or longer for capital goods scheme — 10 years)VATA 1994 Sch.11 para.6
Companies Act records3 years (private), 6 years (public)CA 2006 s.388
Payroll records3 years from end of tax year (also 6 years for AML purposes if you are an agent)Income Tax (PAYE) Regs 2003 reg.97
Pension auto-enrolment records6 years (4 years for opt-out notices)Pensions Act 2008 / TPR guidance
AML client records5 years from end of business relationshipMLR 2017 reg.40
 
    Practical advice    

Default to 7 years for everything — it covers all the above and aligns with the Limitation Act 1980 (6 years for contractual claims). With cloud storage near-free, longer retention is the safe choice.

sections.title: 6.4 MTD digital records rules
sections.contentHtml:
Under MTD for VAT (and from 2026 onwards, MTD ITSA), records must be kept “digitally” and there must be a “digital link” between every step from source to filed return. Manual re-typing into a spreadsheet between two systems breaks the digital link and is non-compliant. Permitted digital links include:

 
       
  • API connections (the gold standard — Xero/QBO/etc. talking directly).
    •    
  • CSV import/export between systems.
    •    
  • Email of XLS/XLSX files (digital files), where the data is then imported (not retyped).
    •    
  • Linked cells within a spreadsheet (cell A1 in sheet 1 = A1 in sheet 2).
    •  
 

Not permitted: rekeying numbers; copy-paste of values (formula loss); transcribing a paper printout into a spreadsheet.

 
   

Module 6 — Summary

   
         
  • VAT invoice rules (reg.14) determine input tax recoverability.
    •      
  • Retention: 5 years SA, 6 years CT/VAT/CA, 7 years for safety.
    •      
  • MTD requires digital links throughout the workflow — copy-paste breaks the chain.
    •

hookHtml: Three years after a perfectly clean year-end, a client gets a Schedule 36 information notice from HMRC. The enquiry officer wants to see every invoice over £500 for the period, the contracts behind two specific supplier relationships, and the original mileage logs. The client shrugs — “you’ve got it all, right?” — and the bookkeeper’s heart sinks. Because they DON’T have it all. Half the supplier invoices were captured into Dext but the originals were thrown away. The contracts went into a folder that got deleted when someone reorganised the OneDrive. The mileage logs — well, the director kept them in a notebook in the van, and the van got sold last spring. The penalty regime doesn’t care whether you had good books once; it cares whether you can produce them now. UK record-keeping has three overlapping statutory regimes — HMRC, the Companies Act 2006, and the Limitation Act 1980 — with different periods and different categories. Add VAT’s 6-year rule, payroll’s 3-year rule, MTD’s digital-link requirement, GDPR’s retention principle, and AML’s 5-years-after-engagement-ends rule, and the question “how long do we keep this?” has at least five right answers depending on what the document is. This module is the map: every source document, who originates it, what posts it, how long you keep it, and why MTD doesn’t replace the source — it just demands the digital link from source to ledger to return.

title: Cash vs Accruals Basis
meta: Module 7 · Part 1 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard
learningObjHtml:
Learning Objectives

   
         
  • Distinguish cash basis from accruals (traditional) basis.
    •      
  • Identify which businesses must use accruals and which may use cash.
    •      
  • Apply the transition adjustments when moving from cash to accruals (or vice versa).
    •

sections.title: 7.1 The two bases defined
sections.contentHtml:
Cash basis: income is recognised when cash is received; expenses are recognised when paid. No debtors, creditors, accruals or prepayments. Easier for the smallest businesses.

 

Accruals (traditional) basis: income is recognised when earned (invoice raised); expenses recognised when incurred (invoice received), regardless of cash flow. The standard required by FRS 102 / FRS 105 for company accounts and the default for income tax purposes for businesses above the cash basis threshold.

sections.title: 7.2 Cash basis — eligibility (FA 2013, ITTOIA 2005 s.25A onwards)
sections.contentHtml:
Until 5 April 2024 the cash basis was elective for sole traders and partnerships with turnover up to £150,000 (must leave at £300,000). From 6 April 2024 the cash basis is the default for all unincorporated businesses; you must elect out if you want accruals. Turnover thresholds were also abolished. This is a major change brought in by the Spring Budget 2024.

 

Cash basis is not available to: limited companies (must use accruals under FRS); LLPs; partnerships with a corporate partner; farms using herd basis; ministers of religion; managed service companies; Lloyd's underwriters.

sections.title: 7.3 Differences in practice
sections.contentHtml:
ItemCash basisAccruals basis
Sales invoice raised but unpaid at year-endNot income — wait for cashIncome recognised; debtor created
Supplier invoice received but unpaid at year-endNot yet expense — wait for paymentExpense recognised; creditor created
Stock at year-endGenerally not adjusted (purchases expensed when paid)Closing stock asset; reduces cost of sales
Capital expenditureCapital allowances available for cars only; other capital items expensed when paid (cash-basis-specific rule)Capitalised; depreciation in P&L capital allowances for tax
Loan interestRestricted to £500 deduction per year (cash basis cap)Fully deductible on accruals basis
LossesCarried forward only (no sideways relief)Sideways relief available (ITA 2007 s.64)

sections.title: 7.4 Transition adjustments
sections.contentHtml:
When moving from cash to accruals (or accruals to cash), a transition adjustment is required to avoid double-counting or non-counting of income and expenses across the changeover (ITTOIA 2005 ss.232–240).

 
    Worked Example 7.1    

Sole trader switching from cash to accruals

   

Year 1 (cash): Sales received £80,000. Year 2 (accruals): At end of Year 1 there were £8,000 of unpaid sales invoices and £3,000 of unpaid supplier invoices.

   

Transition adjustment in Year 2:

   
         
  • Add £8,000 to income (debtors created on transition date — would never have been counted under cash basis).
    •      
  • Add £3,000 to expenses (creditors created on transition date).
    •    
   

Net adjustment: +£5,000 added to taxable profit in Year 2 — spread over 6 years if on transition to MTD ITSA.

 
 
   

Module 7 — Summary

   
         
  • Cash basis is now the default for unincorporated UK businesses (from 2024/25).
    •      
  • Limited companies must use accruals (FRS 102/105 mandate).
    •      
  • Transition adjustments under ITTOIA 2005 prevent double-counting on basis change.
    •

hookHtml:
A sole trader landscaper finishes a £14,000 garden project in March 2025. They
          invoice on the 28th. The customer pays on the 7th of April. Under <tspan>cash basis</tspan> the £14k
          falls into the 2025/26 tax year (year of receipt). Under <tspan>accruals basis</tspan> the £14k is
          taxable in 2024/25 (year of invoice / earning). Two different tax years, two different tax computations, two
          different payments-on-account profiles — same single invoice. From 6 April 2024 the rules <tspan>flipped
          </tspan>: cash basis is now the DEFAULT for every unincorporated business, regardless of turnover. The old
          £150k threshold is gone. The accruals basis — once standard — is now an election OUT. For
          most very small sole traders that’s fine. For anyone with stock, work-in-progress, large debtors at
          year-end, capital allowances on big assets, or losses they want to offset against general income — the
          cash basis can quietly cost them thousands. And if your client is already on accruals and you flip them (or
          vice versa), the transition adjustments alone can produce a tax shock that wasn’t in any forecast.
          Limited companies are unaffected — FRS 102 / FRS 105 require accruals, full stop. This module is the two
          bases properly defined, who can use what after the 2024 reform, the transition adjustments when moving between
          them, and the “which is better for this specific client?” calculation that should run at every
          year-end review.

title: Dext — Document Capture & Processing
meta: Module 8 · Part 2 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Learning Objectives
