sections.title: 8.1 What Dext is and why we use it
sections.contentHtml:
Dext (formerly Receipt Bank) is a document-capture and pre-accounting platform owned by HG Capital. It ingests source documents (receipts, supplier invoices, bank statements) by mobile photo, email, drive sync or supplier fetch, applies OCR and machine learning to extract data, and pushes the result into the accounting ledger. The value is two-fold: (1) eliminates re-keying — a digital link from source to ledger that satisfies MTD; (2) creates a permanent audit trail attached to each ledger transaction.

 

In a busy bookkeeping practice, Dext typically handles 70–90% of inbound transactions. The remainder come from bank-feed-only items (e.g. card payments without receipt) and direct supplier integrations (Amazon, eBay).

 
   
      Dext · Visual Walkthrough      

Capture & process a receipt — mobile to ledger in 4 clicks

   
   
     
       
Steps
       
             
  1. Open Dext mobile app → tap Camera
    2.          
  2. Snap photo (auto-crops; all corners visible)
    3.          
  3. Upload (auto on Wi-Fi)
    4.          
  4. On desktop Costs Inbox, Dext has OCR'd the receipt
    5.          
  5. Review: Supplier, Date, Total, VAT
    6.          
  6. Assign Account, VAT code, Payment status
    7.          
  7. Click Publish → posts to Xero/QBO + moves to Archive
    8.        
       
Supplier Rules tip
       

After 3 same-supplier items, click Create Rule — Dext auto-codes future invoices. Review quarterly for drift.

sections.title: 8.2 Practice and client account hierarchy
sections.contentHtml:
A Dext Practice account sits above the client accounts. From the Practice dashboard you see all clients, their submission counts, and processing status. Each client account is a separate workspace with its own COA, suppliers, customers and integration. Pricing is per client per month with bands by document volume.

 

8.2.1 Adding a new client

 
       
  1. From the Practice dashboard → Add Client → enter business name and primary contact email.
    2.    
  2. Choose plan tier (Streamline / Optimise / Advance based on document count).
    3.    
  3. Connect to the accounting ledger (Xero / QBO / Sage / FreeAgent / Sage 50). The integration creates an OAuth link and pulls the client's COA, supplier list and tax rates.
    4.    
  4. Set the default VAT rate and the default expense account for new suppliers (typically a holding account such as “Dext to be reviewed”).
    5.    
  5. Set up upload routes (next section).
    6.    
  6. Send the client their personalised email-in address and mobile-app login.
    7.

sections.title: 8.3 Document upload routes
sections.contentHtml:
RouteHow it worksBest for
Mobile appSnap photo → auto-uploads when on Wi-Fi → arrives in InboxReceipts paid by card on the go
Email-inEach client has unique clientname@dext.com address; forwarded emails (or attachments) are processedPDF supplier invoices arriving by email
Cloud drive syncConnect Google Drive, Dropbox or OneDrive folder; new files auto-importSuppliers who upload to a shared folder
Supplier fetchDext logs into supplier portals (BT, EE, Amazon, AWS, etc.) and fetches monthly invoicesRecurring portal-only suppliers
Web upload / drag-dropBulk PDF upload from desktopBookkeeper backfilling old documents

sections.title: 8.4 Processing items in the Inbox
sections.contentHtml:
An item arrives in Costs or Sales Inbox. Dext extracts: supplier, date, total, VAT, currency, and (with line-item add-on) individual lines. The bookkeeper then checks: supplier matches an existing supplier in the ledger; expense account is correct; VAT code is correct; project/tracking categories assigned where used; payment status set to Paid (with bank account selected) or Unpaid.

 

8.4.1 Supplier rules

 

Once you process a supplier the second or third time, click Create Rule to set: this supplier always codes to X account with Y VAT rate, and (if using auto-publish) push to ledger automatically. Rules slash processing time but require periodic review — a supplier can change its supply mix and break the assumption.

 

8.4.2 Multi-line items

 

A typical Amazon invoice contains both VATable goods, zero-rated goods (books) and possibly third-party seller items not yours to recover VAT on. Use the line-item splitter (Optimise/Advance plans) to divide the invoice into rows with separate accounts and VAT codes.

sections.title: 8.5 Publishing to Xero (worked walkthrough)
sections.contentHtml:
1. In Inbox, select the item → review fields → click Publish.
    2.    
  2. Dext creates a Bill in Xero with: contact = supplier; line item = your coded expense; tax rate = your selected VAT code; reference = Dext item number.
    3.    
  3. If marked Paid in Dext, Dext also creates the bank payment matched to the bill.
    4.    
  4. The original receipt PDF is attached to the Bill in Xero (visible in Attachments).
    5.    
  5. The item moves to Archive in Dext.
    6.  
 
    Common error — duplicate publishing    

If a supplier sends the invoice both by email and uploads to a synced drive, two items can land in Dext. Use the Possible Duplicates filter weekly to catch and merge these before publishing.

sections.title: 8.6 Bank statement processing in Dext
sections.contentHtml: Dext will OCR a PDF/scan of a bank statement, extract transactions, and push to your ledger as a feed. Useful for: closed bank accounts where the live feed has been cancelled; old periods being reconstructed; or accounts with no Open Banking support.

sections.title: 8.7 The Practice Dashboard — managing 30+ clients
sections.contentHtml:
Key views: (1) Pending review by client — tells you who needs work; (2) Submission status — who's ahead/behind; (3) Auto-publish health — rules misfiring; (4) Task list — assignable items between team members.

 
   

Module 8 — Summary

   
         
  • Dext digitises source documents and creates a digital link satisfying MTD.
    •      
  • Five upload routes — mobile, email, drive, supplier fetch, web.
    •      
  • Supplier rules and line-items dramatically reduce processing time at scale.
    •      
  • Publishing creates the Bill (or Sales invoice) with the receipt attached for audit.
    •

  • Run the Reports (P&L, Balance Sheet, Aged Receivables, Aged Payables, VAT Return).
    •

sections.title: 9.1 Creating a Xero organisation
sections.contentHtml:
From your Xero Partner dashboard → My Xero → Add an organisation. Enter:

 
       
  • Legal name and trading name
    •    
  • Country (UK)
    •    
  • Currency (GBP)
    •    
  • Industry (sets default COA template)
    •    
  • Time zone (London)
    •    
  • Financial year end
    •    
  • VAT registration status and scheme (Standard / Flat Rate / Cash / Standard with Flat Rate election)
    •    
  • Tax basis (accruals or cash)
    •

sections.title: 9.2 Customising the Chart of Accounts
sections.contentHtml:
Xero ships a standard 200+ account template. Strip it back to what the client actually needs — an over-large COA fragments postings and obscures reporting. Recommended additions for almost every UK COA:

 
       
  • Director's Loan Account (separate per director if multiple)
    •    
  • Wages Control Account (clearing for net pay vs PAYE/NI vs pension)
    •    
  • Dividends Paid (current year, separate from retained earnings)
    •    
  • Sales analysis split by service line
    •    
  • Fixed Asset register categories: Office Equipment, Computer Equipment, Plant & Machinery, Motor Vehicles, Leasehold Improvements
    •

sections.title: 9.3 Bank feeds
sections.contentHtml:
Xero connects to UK banks via Open Banking (regulated PSD2 connection): Lloyds, HSBC, Barclays, NatWest/RBS, Santander, Starling, Monzo, Tide, Revolut, Wise, etc. Authentication uses Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) requiring re-authorisation every 90 days. Tip: set a calendar reminder for 80 days from connection to re-authenticate before the feed lapses.

 

9.3.1 Setting up an Open Banking feed

 
       
  1. Bank Accounts → Add Bank Account → search for the bank.
    2.    
  2. Choose Direct Bank Feed (Open Banking) where available.
    3.    
  3. Authenticate with the client's online banking credentials and SCA.
    4.    
  4. Select which accounts to share with Xero (current, savings, cards).
    5.    
  5. Confirm consent for 90 days.
    6.    
  6. Feed begins to flow — typically backfills 90 days of history.
    7.

sections.title: 9.4 Bank reconciliation in Xero
sections.contentHtml:
Xero presents each bank statement line on the left and proposes a match on the right. Four actions per line:

 
       
  • Match — line matches an existing invoice/bill/payment. Click OK.
    •    
  • Create — no existing record; create a new spend/receive money transaction.
    •    
  • Transfer — line is movement between two of the client's own bank accounts.
    •    
  • Discuss — flag for client/colleague (no posting until resolved).
    •  
 

Bank Rules automate Create for predictable transactions: e.g. “Any line containing ‘TfL Travel’ from this account → spend money to Travel Expenses, VAT N/A”.

 
   
      Xero · Walkthrough X3      

Reconcile a bank line — Match, Create, Transfer or Discuss

   
   
     
       
The 4 actions per line
       
             
  1. Match: line matches an existing invoice/bill → click OK
    2.          
  2. Create: no existing record → fill Account, Tax, Description → OK
    3.          
  3. Transfer: between two of client's own accounts
    4.          
  4. Discuss: flag for client/colleague; no posting until resolved
    5.        
       
Bank Rules
       

Bank Accounts → Bank Rules. Pattern-based auto-fill: e.g. any “TfL Travel” → Spend Money / 471 Travel / VAT N/A / contact TfL.

       
          SCA re-auth           Open Banking re-auth every 90 days. Set a calendar alert at day 80.

sections.title: 9.5 Bills and Sales Invoices
sections.contentHtml:
Bills (purchase invoices) are created either: (a) manually via Business → Bills to pay → New; (b) via Dext publish (Module 8); (c) imported by CSV; or (d) auto-created by a Hubdoc/scan extension. Sales invoices similarly: manual, recurring templates, or via integrations (e.g. WooCommerce, Shopify).

 

9.5.1 Recurring sales invoices

sections.title: 9.6 VAT in Xero
sections.contentHtml:
Xero is a recognised MTD-VAT software. The VAT Return view assembles the 9 boxes from posted transactions. To file: Accounting → Reports → VAT Return → period → Submit to HMRC. First-time filing requires HMRC authorisation via your Government Gateway.

 
   
      Xero · Walkthrough X5      

Submit MTD VAT return (Accounting → Reports → VAT Return)

   
   
     
       
Steps
       
             
  1. Accounting → Reports → VAT Return
    2.          
  2. Pick the period (Q4 1 Jan – 31 Mar)
    3.          
  3. Review 9 boxes; drill into any unusual figure
    4.          
  4. Run Exception Report for late-posted items
    5.          
  5. Reconcile VAT control to Box 5
    6.          
  6. Click Submit to HMRC
    7.          
  7. First time: Government Gateway auth (3-year grant)
    8.          
  8. Save HMRC correlation ID
    9.          
  9. Hard-lock the VAT period
    10.        
       
          Always lock after submit           Otherwise backdated postings flow into “exceptions” in the next return — easy to miss.

sections.title: 9.7 Lock Dates
sections.contentHtml:
Two lock-date levels:

 
       
  • All users lock — prevents anyone (including the bookkeeper) backdating before this date.
    •    
  • Users without Adviser/Standard role — softer lock the bookkeeper can override.
    •  
 

Set the soft lock at month-end after MI is signed; set the hard lock when accounts are filed.

sections.title: 9.8 Key reports
sections.contentHtml:
ReportPurpose
Profit & LossPeriod income vs expense; comparable to prior period or budget
Balance SheetPosition at a date
Aged Receivables DetailCustomer balances split into 30/60/90 day buckets
Aged Payables DetailSupplier equivalent
Bank Reconciliation ReportStatement-balance reconciliation for audit/year-end
VAT Return9-box return ready for MTD submission
Trial BalanceFor year-end accounts production
Account TransactionsDrill-down on a single ledger account for a period
 
   

Module 9 — Summary

   
         
  • Customise the COA at setup; never inherit the default 200-account template untouched.
    •      
  • Use Open Banking feeds and re-authenticate every 90 days.
    •      
  • Reconcile via Match/Create/Transfer/Discuss; automate with Bank Rules.
    •      
  • Set hard lock dates after filings to protect period integrity.
    •

hookHtml: Xero is the platform UK SMEs and their accountants run on — ~4.4m subscribers globally, dominant in the UK SME segment, the default for any practice taking on a new owner-managed company. The strength isn’t any single feature; it’s how the bank feed, the invoice engine, the multi-VAT scheme support, the tracking categories, and the reporting layer plug into each other so a bookkeeper can close a month in hours, not days. The four buttons every Xero user learns first are Match · Create · Transfer · Discuss on the bank-reconciliation screen — and they are the productivity unlock. Match: the system already found the invoice or bill, click Yes. Create: it’s a new transaction, type the supplier and code. Transfer: it’s a movement between two bank accounts you own. Discuss: you don’t know — flag it, ask the director, come back. Plus the discipline pieces: chart-of-accounts customised to the client’s sector (not Xero’s blank default), lock dates set so closed periods can’t be tampered with, tracking categories handling analysis (jobs, departments, branches) without bloating the COA, and the report pack tailored once and reused monthly. This module is the new-org setup, the bank-reconciliation method, the bill / invoice workflow, lock dates and tracking categories, and the reports that turn Xero into a management-accounting platform — not just a bookkeeping system.

Learning Objectives

sections.title: 10.1 QBO at a glance
sections.contentHtml: Intuit's UK product. Three plan tiers (Simple Start, Essentials, Plus) plus QuickBooks Online Advanced for larger SMEs and QuickBooks Online Accountant for practitioners (free with multiple client logins). Strong on banking automation and inventory; sometimes weaker than Xero on multi-currency and project costing.

sections.title: 10.2 New company file
sections.contentHtml:
1. From QuickBooks Online Accountant → Add client → enter details.
    2.    
  2. Choose subscription tier (most UK SMEs land on Essentials or Plus).
    3.    
  3. Set fiscal year end.
    4.    
  4. Set VAT: registration status, VRN, scheme (Standard / Flat Rate / Cash). VAT scheme can be changed later but not retrospectively.
    5.    
  5. Enable MTD: Settings → Taxes → set up MTD → connect to HMRC via Government Gateway.
    6.  
 
   
      QBO · Walkthrough Q1      

Create a sales invoice (+ New → Invoice)

   
   
     
       
Steps
       
             
  1. Click + New in top-left → Invoice
    2.          
  2. Select Customer (or quick-add)
    3.          
  3. Choose Terms (Net 30 etc.)
    4.          
  4. Set Invoice date and Due date
    5.          
  5. Add Product/Service rows; choose VAT code per line
    6.          
  6. Save and send
    7.        
       
          Product/Service setup matters           Each P/S item has a default Income Account + VAT Rate. Set correctly once and every invoice posts right.

sections.title: 10.3 Banking and Bank Rules
sections.contentHtml: QBO's banking screen lists each bank line with Suggested categorisation. Click Add to accept; Find Match to pair to an existing invoice or bill; Transfer for inter-account movements. Bank Rules are powerful: condition-based with multiple criteria (description contains, amount range, account, etc.) and can split a single bank line into multiple categories with VAT rates — useful for things like Amazon (some lines standard, some zero-rated).

sections.title: 10.4 VAT in QBO
sections.contentHtml:
The VAT Centre (Taxes → VAT) shows current return draft, due dates, and exception items. UK VAT codes:

                                                         
CodeMeaning
20.0% SStandard rate sales/purchases
5.0% RReduced rate (domestic fuel, energy-saving materials)
0.0% ZZero-rated (food, books, children's clothes)
ExemptExempt supplies (insurance, education, healthcare)
No VATOut of scope (wages, dividends, MOT pass-through)
20.0% RC SGReverse charge for services (in scope for buyer)
20.0% RC CISDomestic reverse charge for construction (CIS DRC)

sections.title: 10.5 Reports
sections.contentHtml:
Profit and Loss, Balance Sheet, A/R Ageing, A/P Ageing, VAT Liability Report, Transaction Detail by Account, Custom Summary Report. The Custom Summary is QBO's strength: pivot-style report builder for non-standard analysis (e.g. revenue by class × quarter).

 
   

Module 10 — Summary

   
         
  • QBO is a strong alternative to Xero, particularly for inventory-heavy SMEs.
    •      
  • Bank Rules can split a single line and apply different VAT codes — useful for marketplaces.
    •      
  • VAT codes follow standard UK structure (S/R/Z/E/No VAT) plus reverse-charge variants.
    •

sections.title: 11.1 Product range
sections.contentHtml:
ProductPosition
Sage Business Cloud Accounting StartSole trader / micro-business; basic invoicing and bank rec
Sage Business Cloud Accounting StandardMulti-user; full bookkeeping; CIS module
Sage Business Cloud Accounting PlusAdds inventory and multi-currency
Sage 50 Cloud (formerly Sage 50)Desktop product with cloud sync; deep features for £1m+ SMEs

sections.title: 11.2 Workflow basics
sections.contentHtml: Setup mirrors Xero/QBO — choose VAT scheme, set FY end, build COA. Bank reconciliation is via direct bank feed (Open Banking) with the same Match/Create/Transfer pattern. Sage's strength is CIS — the deductions are calculated automatically and the monthly CIS return submission is built in.

sections.title: 11.3 Sage 50 (the desktop legacy)
sections.contentHtml:
Many established UK practices still have clients on Sage 50. Differences from cloud: data lives on the local PC (with optional cloud backup); is more granular but less collaborative; uses tax codes T0–T9 rather than named codes (T1 = standard, T0 = zero, T2 = exempt, T9 = out of scope, T20 = CIS DRC, T21 = CIS DRC zero-rated).

 
   

Module 11 — Summary

   
         
  • Sage's cloud product is fully MTD-compliant and competitive with Xero/QBO at the SME level.
    •      
  • Sage 50 remains widespread in long-established practices; familiarity with T-codes useful.
    •      
  • CIS is a Sage strength.
    •

hookHtml: Sage is the legacy heavyweight of UK accounting software — founded in Newcastle in 1981 and dominant in mid-market UK accounting for two decades before Xero and QBO ate the SME segment. Today Sage runs two parallel products an accountant needs to know: Sage Business Cloud Accounting (the modern SaaS replacement for Sage 50, three tiers: Start, Standard, Plus) for the mid-SME, and Sage 50 Cloud (still desktop-installed with cloud sync) for clients with complex stock, multi-company, or legacy data they refuse to migrate off. A typical practitioner runs at least one of each. The strengths: deep functional coverage in stock and manufacturing; strong CIS handling out of the box; the project costing module is closer to ERP than to Xero or QBO; and the practitioner’s portal (Sage for Accountants ) is genuinely good. The weaknesses: the interface is older-feeling, the third-party app ecosystem is thinner than Xero’s, and migrating data off Sage to Xero/QBO is one of the more painful exercises in practice life. This module is the product range, Sage Business Cloud’s setup and bank reconciliation workflow, Sage 50’s desktop heritage and what makes it still preferable for certain clients, MTD-VAT, and the migration trade-off when a client wants to leave.

title: FreeAgent

Learning Objectives

   
         
  • Position FreeAgent in the UK market — the contractor & freelancer-focused product.
    •

sections.title: 12.1 What is FreeAgent?
sections.contentHtml: UK-built product (Edinburgh) owned by NatWest. Free to NatWest/RBS/Mettle business banking customers; subscription for others. Targets sole traders, contractors and small Ltd companies. Unique: prepares and files SA100 (sole trader) and CT600 (Ltd) directly to HMRC for users meeting eligibility (small companies only; not for groups, not for FRS 102 full).

sections.title: 12.2 Why a contractor would prefer FreeAgent
sections.contentHtml:
• End-to-end: bank rec → invoicing → expenses → MTD VAT → CT600 → final accounts → SA100 in one platform.
    •    
  • Time-tracking and project profitability built in.
    •    
  • Tax forecasting — predicts CT and SA liabilities live based on the year-to-date.
    •    
  • Director's loan account self-management interface.
    •

sections.title: 12.3 Limitations
sections.contentHtml:
• Not designed for large or complex SMEs — limited multi-user, no class tracking, basic inventory.
    •    
  • No FRS 102 full reporting — micro-entity FRS 105 only via the integrated final accounts.
    •    
  • Group/consolidation: not supported.
    •  
 
   

Module 12 — Summary

   
         
  • FreeAgent is the natural choice for owner-managed Ltd contractors and sole-trader freelancers.
    •      
  • Its built-in SA100 and CT600 modules are unique and remove the need for separate tax software at the small end.
    •      
  • Not suitable for complex SMEs — outgrow it at ~£500k turnover or when you add multiple departments.
    •

title: VAT Fundamentals — Registration, Rates, Tax Points & Returns
meta: Module 13 · Part 3 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard
learningObjHtml:
Learning Objectives

   
         
  • State the four VAT rates in the UK and identify supplies that fall in each.
    •      
  • Apply the registration thresholds (compulsory and voluntary) and identify the trigger for backwards/forwards registration.
    •      
  • Determine the tax point of any supply.
    •      
  • Complete a 9-box VAT return from a trial balance.
    •      
  • Calculate output and input VAT for any standard scenario.
    •

sections.title: 13.1 What is VAT, conceptually?
sections.contentHtml:
VAT is a multi-stage transaction tax on the value added at each link of a supply chain. Each VAT-registered business charges output VAT on its sales, recovers input VAT on its purchases, and pays the net to HMRC. The economic burden falls on the final non-VAT-registered consumer; intermediate businesses are tax collectors, not taxpayers, on each transaction.

 

Legislative basis: Value Added Tax Act 1994 (VATA 1994); secondary legislation in the VAT Regulations 1995 (SI 1995/2518); HMRC public notices (Notice 700 series) provide interpretation but are not law.

sections.title: 13.2 The four UK VAT rates
sections.contentHtml:
RateDescriptionExamples
20% standardDefault rate for almost all suppliesMost goods and services; professional services; restaurant meals; clothing for adults; alcohol
5% reducedSpecific listed supplies (VATA Sch 7A)Domestic gas/electricity; energy-saving materials; children's car seats; certain conversions of dwellings
0% zero-ratedListed supplies (VATA Sch 8) — taxable, just at 0%Most food (not catering); books, journals, e-books; children's clothing & footwear; new-build residential construction; passenger transport (10+ seat vehicles); newspapers & magazines
ExemptListed supplies (VATA Sch 9) — outside the scope of VAT charge but block input recoveryInsurance; finance (most); education; health & welfare; postal services; betting & gaming; sale of land/buildings unless opted
 
    Zero-rated vs Exempt — the critical difference    

Both result in £0 VAT being charged on the sale — but the consequence for input VAT recovery differs. Zero-rated sales are taxable supplies; the supplier can fully recover input VAT on costs incurred to make them. Exempt sales are non-taxable supplies; input VAT on costs to make exempt supplies is blocked (subject to partial-exemption rules — Module 18). A VAT-registered insurance broker recovers no input VAT on its overheads; a VAT-registered children's clothing retailer recovers all of it.

 
 

13.2.1 Out of scope (OoS)

 

A separate concept: the supply isn't made in the UK at all (place of supply is overseas), or it isn't a supply for VAT purposes (wages, dividends, statutory fines). OoS items don't appear in Box 6 of the VAT return at all (in most cases — cross-border services to UK businesses can be reverse-charged into Box 6).

sections.title: 13.3 Registration
sections.contentHtml:
13.3.1 Compulsory registration thresholds (2024/25)

 

£90,000 per rolling 12 months of taxable turnover (raised from £85,000 on 1 April 2024). Two tests:

 
       
  1. Historic test — at the end of any month, taxable supplies in the prior 12 months exceed £90,000. Must register within 30 days; effective date is the first day of the month after the breach.
    2.    
  2. Future test — you reasonably expect taxable turnover in the next 30 days alone to exceed £90,000. Effective date is the start of that 30-day period.
    3.  
 

13.3.2 Deregistration threshold

 

£88,000 (raised from £83,000 on 1 April 2024). Voluntary deregistration available when taxable turnover in next 12 months is reasonably expected to be below £88,000.

 

13.3.3 Voluntary registration

 

Available regardless of turnover, including for businesses making zero-rated supplies (often beneficial — can recover input VAT). Not available for businesses making only exempt supplies.

 
    Worked Example 13.1 — Registration date    

A consultancy crosses £90,000 cumulative taxable turnover on 18 May 2025 (a single big invoice tipped it over). What is the VAT registration deadline and effective date?

   
         
  • Threshold breached at end of May 2025 (historic test).
    •      
  • Must notify HMRC by 30 June 2025 (within 30 days of end of breach month).
    •      
  • Effective date of registration: 1 July 2025 (first day of second month after breach).
    •      
  • From 1 July 2025, must charge output VAT on all standard-rated sales.
    •

sections.title: 13.4 The tax point
sections.contentHtml:
The tax point is the date a supply is treated as made for VAT purposes. It determines which VAT return the supply falls into.

                                       
Type of supplyBasic tax pointActual tax point (overrides)
GoodsWhen goods are removed or made available to the customerEarlier of: invoice issued or payment received (if before basic TP); OR invoice issued within 14 days of basic TP (becomes the actual TP)
ServicesWhen the service is performedSame actual TP rules as goods
Continuous servicesEnd of each period covered by an invoiceEarlier of: invoice issued or payment received
Goods on sale or returnEarlier of: customer adopts goods, or 12 months from removal
 

13.4.1 The 14-day rule (in detail)

 

For goods or services where invoice is issued within 14 days of the basic tax point, the actual tax point becomes the invoice date. Most businesses invoice within 14 days, so in practice the invoice date is the tax point. If invoice is issued later than 14 days, the basic tax point applies (unless HMRC agrees a longer period).

sections.title: 13.5 The 9-box VAT return
sections.contentHtml:
BoxContent
Box 1VAT due on sales and other outputs (output VAT charged)
Box 2VAT due on acquisitions from EU member states (now NI-only post-Brexit)
Box 3Total VAT due (Box 1 + Box 2)
Box 4VAT reclaimed on purchases and other inputs (input VAT recoverable)
Box 5Net VAT due to HMRC (Box 3 − Box 4) — payable if positive, repayment if negative
Box 6Total value of sales and all other outputs excluding any VAT (net of VAT)
Box 7Total value of purchases and all other inputs excluding any VAT (net of VAT)
Box 8Total value of dispatches of goods to EU member states (NI-only post-Brexit)
Box 9Total value of acquisitions of goods from EU member states (NI-only post-Brexit)

sections.title: 13.6 Filing & payment deadlines
sections.contentHtml:
• Quarterly returns: filing & payment 1 month and 7 days after the end of the VAT quarter (e.g. Q/E 31 March → 7 May).
    •    
  • Monthly returns: same 1m+7d rule (used by repayment traders).
    •    
  • Annual Accounting Scheme: one return per year + 9 monthly POAs (Module 14).
    •    
  • Payments on Account regime (turnover > £2.3m): monthly POAs based on prior year's liability.
    •

sections.title: 13.7 Output and input VAT calculation basics
sections.contentHtml:
Output VAT on a VAT-exclusive price = price × rate. On a VAT-inclusive price = price × (rate / (1 + rate)). For the standard rate, the inclusive multiplier is 20/120 = 1/6.

 

13.7.1 Input VAT recovery — the four conditions

 
       
  1. The business is VAT-registered.
    2.    
  2. The supply was made to the business (not to the director personally).
    3.    
  3. The business holds a valid VAT invoice (or HMRC-accepted alternative for amounts below £25 / import documentation).
    4.    
  4. The supply is used for taxable business purposes.
    5.  
 

13.7.2 Blocked input VAT

                                             
BlockDetail
Cars (purchase)Generally blocked unless used exclusively for business — narrow exception (taxis, driving school, car hire only)
UK client entertainmentFully blocked. Staff entertaining is recoverable
Goods/services for non-business or private useApportioned
Costs supporting exempt suppliesSubject to partial-exemption rules (Module 18)
Margin Scheme goodsInput VAT on the goods themselves blocked
 
   

Module 13 — Summary

   
         
  • Four rates (20%, 5%, 0%, exempt) and the OoS concept.
    •      
  • Compulsory registration: £90,000 rolling 12-month taxable turnover (2024/25).
    •      
  • Tax point: basic = removal/performance; actual = earlier of invoice/payment, or invoice within 14 days.
    •      
  • 9-box VAT return; filing 1m+7d after quarter end.
    •      
  • Input VAT recoverable only with all 4 conditions met; specific blocks for cars, client entertainment.
    •

hookHtml:
VAT is the UK’s most-administered tax — collected by every registered
          business on every sale, reclaimed on every input, and reported every quarter. Get it wrong and the penalties
          stack up faster than for any other tax. The fundamentals every accountant must hold: the <tspan>four UK rates
          </tspan> (20% standard, 5% reduced, 0% zero-rated, exempt — and the difference between
          “zero” and “exempt” matters enormously); the <tspan>£90,000 registration
            threshold</tspan> (rolling 12-month test PLUS forward look at next 30 days — the two triggers that
          catch every late registration); the <tspan>tax point</tspan> rules that decide which VAT period a supply falls
          into (basic tax point, actual tax point, advance payments, continuous supplies — not always the invoice
          date you’d guess); and the <tspan>9-box return</tspan> that ties it all together. Plus: voluntary
          registration, group registration, de-registration thresholds, retrospective registration when you discover a
          client missed the trigger, and the difference between a VAT invoice (must contain 9 specific items) and a
          simplified one. This module is every fundamental that every other VAT module (schemes, place of supply,
          partial exemption, MTD) builds on.

          “zero” and “exempt” matters enormously); the £90,000 registration
            threshold (rolling 12-month test PLUS forward look at next 30 days — the two triggers that
          catch every late registration); the tax point rules that decide which VAT period a supply falls
          into (basic tax point, actual tax point, advance payments, continuous supplies — not always the invoice
          date you’d guess); and the 9-box return that ties it all together. Plus: voluntary
          registration, group registration, de-registration thresholds, retrospective registration when you discover a
          client missed the trigger, and the difference between a VAT invoice (must contain 9 specific items) and a
          simplified one. This module is every fundamental that every other VAT module (schemes, place of supply,
          partial exemption, MTD) builds on.

title: VAT Schemes — Standard, Cash, Annual, Flat Rate, Margin, TOMS, Retail
meta: Module 14 · Part 3 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard
learningObjHtml:
Learning Objectives

   
         
  • Distinguish the standard scheme from the alternative schemes.
    •      
  • Apply eligibility tests for each.
    •      
  • Calculate VAT under Flat Rate, Cash, Annual, Margin, TOMS and Retail schemes.
    •      
  • Recommend the correct scheme for a given client profile.
    •

sections.title: 14.1 Standard accounting (accruals) scheme
sections.contentHtml: Default scheme. Output VAT accounted for at the tax point of the sale (typically invoice date); input VAT recovered at the tax point of the purchase. Means VAT can be due on a sales invoice before the customer has paid — cashflow burden for businesses with long debtor days.

sections.title: 14.2 Cash Accounting Scheme
sections.contentHtml: Output VAT due when payment received; input VAT recoverable when paid. Solves the cashflow issue. Eligibility: taxable turnover ≤ £1.35m (entry); leave when > £1.6m. Available to most but not for: imports, intra-NI/EU acquisitions, supplies more than 6 months overdue from supplier.

sections.title: 14.3 Annual Accounting Scheme
sections.contentHtml: One annual return + 9 monthly (or 3 quarterly) interim payments based on prior-year liability. Final balancing payment with the return. Same £1.35m / £1.6m thresholds. Combine with Cash Accounting allowed.

sections.title: 14.4 Flat Rate Scheme (FRS)
sections.contentHtml:
You charge customers VAT at standard rates but pay HMRC a fixed flat-rate percentage of your VAT-inclusive turnover. You generally cannot reclaim input VAT (except on capital assets >£2,000 single transaction including VAT).

 

Entry: turnover (excl. VAT) ≤ £150k in next 12 months. Exit: VAT-inclusive turnover > £230k. First-year discount: 1% off published rate.

 

14.4.1 Limited Cost Trader (LCT) — anti-abuse rule

 

If goods cost <2% of VAT-inclusive turnover (or <£1,000/yr), the business is an LCT and pays a punitive 16.5% flat rate. Effectively eliminates FRS benefit for labour-only consultancies.

 
    Worked Example 14.1 — FRS LCT    

IT consultant, turnover £80,000+VAT (£96,000 incl.). Goods spend £200/year. LCT applies (200 < 2% of 96,000 = 1,920).

                         
Output VAT charged16,000
Pay HMRC: £96,000 × 16.5%15,840
Net retained160vs. ~40 under standard with no input VAT — marginal

sections.title: 14.5 Margin Schemes
sections.contentHtml: For dealers in second-hand goods, antiques, art, used cars. VAT calculated on the dealer's margin (sale − purchase price). Input VAT on the goods cannot be recovered.

sections.title: 14.6 TOMS — Tour Operators' Margin Scheme
sections.contentHtml: Mandatory for businesses buying in and reselling travel/accommodation/passenger transport bundled as a package. VAT on the margin. Specialist sector.

sections.title: 14.7 Retail Schemes
sections.contentHtml: For shops with mostly cash B2C sales. Variants: Point-of-sale (modern EPOS), Apportionment (mixed-rate till takings split), Direct Calculation. Allow accounting without per-transaction VAT invoices.

sections.title: 14.8 VAT Group Registration (VATA s.43)
sections.contentHtml:
Bodies corporate under common control may form a single VAT group (one VRN, one return). Internal supplies disregarded. Joint and several liability among members. Care needed with partially-exempt members.

 
   

Module 14 — Summary

   
         
  • Cash Accounting (≤£1.35m) helps cashflow when customers slow-pay.
    •      
  • Annual Accounting reduces admin — 1 return + interim payments.
    •      
  • FRS can save VAT but Limited Cost Trader rules block the benefit for labour-only businesses.
    •      
  • Margin, TOMS, Retail schemes for specialised sectors.
    •      
  • Group registration for commonly-controlled bodies corporate.
    •

hookHtml:
The UK has seven VAT schemes — not one — and choosing the right one for a
          client’s business can save them thousands a year, or hand HMRC money they need not pay. Most accountants
          default to <tspan>Standard accruals</tspan> because it’s the safe choice; but a service business with no
          stock can get a working-capital boost from <tspan>Cash Accounting</tspan>; a tiny consultancy with low costs
          can pay less under <tspan>Flat Rate</tspan>; a second-hand dealer must use the <tspan>Margin Scheme</tspan> or
          pay VAT on the full sale price they never received as profit; a tour operator uses <tspan>TOMS</tspan>; a
          retail shop uses one of the four retail schemes to deal with thousands of unidentifiable till transactions.
          Eligibility is strict for each — turnover caps, scheme-specific tests, “limited cost trader”
          rules for Flat Rate — and the wrong choice is often invisible until the year-end review. This module is
          each scheme, its eligibility, who it’s right for, and the recommendation framework.

title: VAT on Goods — Domestic, Imports, Exports, NI Protocol
meta: Module 15 · Part 3 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard
learningObjHtml:
Learning Objectives

   
         
  • Determine the VAT treatment of goods sold within UK, exported, imported, and moved between GB and NI.
    •      
  • Apply Postponed VAT Accounting (PVA) on imports.
    •      
  • Treat dispatches and acquisitions of goods to/from EU under the Northern Ireland Protocol.
    •

sections.title: 15.1 Domestic supplies
sections.contentHtml: Charge VAT at the appropriate rate (20%, 5%, 0%) per VATA Sch 8/Sch 7A. Standard tax point rules.

sections.title: 15.2 Exports of goods (UK to outside UK)
sections.contentHtml: Zero-rated (Sch 8 Group 7) provided evidence of export within 3 months of supply. Evidence: shipping documents, courier proof of dispatch outside UK. Without evidence, must treat as standard-rated.

sections.title: 15.3 Imports — Postponed VAT Accounting (PVA)
sections.contentHtml:
Default since 1 Jan 2021. Account for import VAT on the VAT return rather than at the border:

 
       
  • Box 1: import VAT (output entry)
    •    
  • Box 4: same import VAT (input entry, subject to recovery)
    •    
  • Box 7: net value of imports
    •  
 

Net cash effect for fully-recovering business: nil. To use PVA, tick on the customs declaration; download monthly Postponed Import VAT Statement (PIVS) from CDS.

sections.title: 15.4 Northern Ireland Protocol — goods only
sections.contentHtml:
NI remains in EU VAT system for goods (not services):

 
       
  • GB ↔ NI: dispatched FROM GB TO NI generally zero-rated; arrival in NI subject to import VAT (PVA available).
    •    
  • NI ↔ EU: continues under EU rules (dispatch zero-rated to EU VAT-registered; acquisition Box 2/Box 9).
    •    
  • NI traders' VRN prefix: XI.
    •

sections.title: 15.5 Distance selling B2C to EU consumers
sections.contentHtml:
Either: register in each EU member state above their distance-selling threshold; use OSS via NI registration; or use a fiscal representative. Specialist area — refer to a VAT specialist.

 
   

Module 15 — Summary

   
         
  • Exports zero-rated with proper evidence.
    •      
  • Imports use PVA — no cashflow drag for fully-recovering businesses.
    •      
  • NI remains in EU VAT for goods; XI VRN prefix.
    •

hookHtml:
Post-Brexit VAT on goods is built around <tspan>four scenarios</tspan> with different
          rules: domestic UK sales (standard tax-point rules); exports from GB to anywhere (<tspan>zero-rated with proof
            of export</tspan>); imports into GB from anywhere (now using <tspan>Postponed VAT Accounting</tspan> to
          avoid the old cash-flow hit); and the Northern Ireland Protocol’s special rules where goods between
          GB↔NI cross a notional VAT border, and NI↔EU continues to use EU acquisition/dispatch mechanics. Get
          the export proof wrong and zero-rating is denied retrospectively. Forget to use PVA on imports and the client
          pays VAT at the border that takes months to reclaim. Treat an NI Protocol acquisition as a normal UK purchase
          and you mis-state Boxes 2 and 9. This module is the four-scenario map: domestic, exports, imports with PVA,
          and NI Protocol — with the proofs, EORI numbers, commodity codes, and 9-box treatment that each
          requires.

title: VAT on Services — Place of Supply & Reverse Charge
meta: Module 16 · Part 3 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard
learningObjHtml:
Learning Objectives

   
         
  • Apply general B2B and B2C place-of-supply rules.
    •      
  • Identify supplies subject to special POS rules.
    •      
  • Apply Reverse Charge for cross-border services received and CIS Domestic Reverse Charge.
    •

sections.title: 16.1 Place of Supply (POS) foundations
sections.contentHtml:
Only supplies made in the UK are within UK VAT. POS rules determine where a service is treated as supplied.

 
       
  • General B2B: POS = where the customer belongs.
    •    
  • General B2C: POS = where the supplier belongs.
    •

sections.title: 16.2 Special POS rules
sections.contentHtml:
ServicePOS
Land-related servicesWhere the land is
Short-term hire of transportWhere vehicle put at customer's disposal
Restaurant & cateringWhere physically performed
Cultural, artistic, sporting (B2C admission)Where carried out
Passenger transportWhere transport takes place
Digital services to non-business EU consumersWhere consumer is — use OSS

sections.title: 16.3 Reverse Charge — services received from overseas (RCSG)
sections.contentHtml:
UK customer self-accounts:

 
       
  • Box 1: VAT as if UK supply (e.g. £1,000 × 20% = £200)
    •    
  • Box 4: same £200 (subject to recovery)
    •    
  • Box 6: net value (£1,000)
    •    
  • Box 7: net value (£1,000)
    •  
 

Net cash nil for fully recovering. Mechanism prevents foreign suppliers undercutting UK suppliers by avoiding UK VAT.

sections.title: 16.4 CIS Domestic Reverse Charge (DRC)
sections.contentHtml:
From 1 March 2021. Applies when ALL of:

 
       
  1. Construction service within CIS scope
    2.    
  2. Both parties VAT-registered
    3.    
  3. Customer CIS-registered
    4.    
  4. Customer NOT the end user
    5.  
 

Subcontractor's invoice shows no VAT, with statement “Reverse charge: customer to pay VAT to HMRC”. Customer enters Box 1 + Box 4.

 
    End-user statements    

Get written confirmation from customer that they are/are not an end user. Without it, default to applying DRC.

 
 
   

Module 16 — Summary

   
         
  • Default B2B services: POS = customer; B2C: POS = supplier.
    •      
  • Special rules for land, transport, cultural, digital B2C.
    •      
  • Reverse Charge mechanism for cross-border B2B services received.
    •      
  • CIS DRC for construction between VAT- and CIS-registered businesses where customer not end user.
    •

sections.title: Knowledge Check
sections.contentHtml:
Knowledge Check
   

Module 16 — End-of-Section MCQ (5 questions)

   
      Q1      
UK consultancy invoices a German company €5,000. UK VAT charged:
     
                                     
     
B2B general rule: POS = customer; outside UK VAT scope.
   
   
      Q2      
UK firm receives £4,000 marketing from US supplier:
     
                                     
     
Reverse charge: equal Box 1 and Box 4; net cash nil.
   
   
      Q3      
CIS DRC does NOT apply when:
     
                                     
     
End-user exclusion — supplier charges VAT normally.
   
   
      Q4      
Land-related services POS:
     
                                     
     
Surveys, valuations, building services follow location of land.
   
   
      Q5      
A subcontractor's CIS DRC invoice shows:
     
                                     
     
No VAT on the invoice, with mandatory DRC statement.

quiz.question: UK firm receives £4,000 marketing from US supplier:
quiz.feedback: Reverse charge: equal Box 1 and Box 4; net cash nil.

quiz.question: CIS DRC does NOT apply when:
quiz.feedback: End-user exclusion — supplier charges VAT normally.

quiz.question: Land-related services POS:
quiz.feedback: Surveys, valuations, building services follow location of land.

options.text: No VAT, with statement that customer pays output tax

quiz.feedback: No VAT on the invoice, with mandatory DRC statement.

hookHtml:
VAT on services lives or dies on one question: <tspan>where is the place of supply?
          </tspan> Because that’s the country whose VAT applies (or whose rules say no VAT at all). The general
          rule splits B2B and B2C. <tspan>B2B</tspan>: place of supply is where the CUSTOMER belongs — so a UK
          marketing agency invoicing a US client doesn’t charge UK VAT, and a UK SaaS company invoicing an EU
          business has the EU business reverse-charge it. <tspan>B2C</tspan>: place of supply is where the SUPPLIER
          belongs — so the UK marketing agency invoicing a US individual DOES charge UK VAT. Then there are the
          special rules: land-related services follow the land, events follow the event, restaurant follows the
          restaurant, electronic services to B2C consumers follow the consumer (MOSS / OSS rules). And the reverse
          charge mechanism: where the customer accounts for the VAT instead of the supplier. Includes cross-border
          services received (DR/CR in both Box 1 and Box 4 = net zero) and the CIS Domestic Reverse Charge for
          construction. Get place of supply wrong and you either charge VAT you shouldn’t (losing competitiveness,
          customer disputes) or fail to charge VAT you should (HMRC assessment later). This module is the framework that
          gets every cross-border service correct.

title: VAT on Land & Property
meta: Module 17 · Part 3 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 17.1 Default treatment
sections.contentHtml: Land and buildings are exempt by default (VATA Sch 9 Group 1). Exemption blocks input recovery on related costs.

sections.title: 17.2 Residential property
sections.contentHtml:
TransactionVAT
Sale or long lease of new dwelling by developerZero-rated
Renting out residential propertyExempt
Construction of new dwellingZero-rated
Conversion of non-residential to residential5% reduced
Renovation of empty dwelling (vacant ≥2 years)5% reduced
Repairs and maintenance to dwellingsStandard 20%

sections.title: 17.3 Commercial property
sections.contentHtml:
TransactionDefaultIf OTT made
Sale of new commercial (<3 years)Standard 20%n/a
Sale of old commercial (≥3 years)ExemptStandard 20%
Lease of commercialExemptStandard 20%
Construction of new commercialStandard 20%n/a

sections.title: 17.4 Option to Tax (OTT)
sections.contentHtml:
Election that converts a specific commercial property/land from exempt to standard-rated. 20-year lock with 6-month cooling-off and 20-year revocation. Notify HMRC on VAT1614A within 30 days. Used to unlock input VAT recovery on property costs.

 

Tenant impact: VAT on rent is an irrecoverable cost for partially-exempt or non-VAT-registered tenants (insurance brokers, banks, charities) — reduces achievable rent.

sections.title: 17.5 Capital Goods Scheme — buildings
sections.contentHtml:
For commercial buildings/refurbishments >£250k (excl. VAT), input VAT recovery monitored over 10 intervals. Annual adjustment if taxable use percentage changes.

 
    Annual adjustment = (Total input VAT × 1/10) × (Current year's taxable% − Original year's taxable%)

sections.title: 17.6 Transfer of a Going Concern (TOGC)
sections.contentHtml:
A sale of a business (or part) as a going concern is OoS for VAT, provided:

 
       
  • Assets sold as a business capable of separate operation.
    •    
  • Buyer uses them in the same kind of business.
    •    
  • If seller VAT-registered, buyer is or becomes VAT-registered immediately.
    •    
  • For property: buyer must opt to tax (and notify) before the relevant date.
    •  
 
   

Module 17 — Summary

   
         
  • Property exempt by default with extensive exceptions.
    •      
  • OTT converts exempt commercial to standard to unlock input recovery — beware tenant impact.
    •      
  • CGS adjusts input recovery over 10 years for property >£250k.
    •      
  • TOGC takes a property transfer outside the scope of VAT if conditions met.
    •

quiz.feedback: 20-year lock with limited revocation windows.

hookHtml:
Property VAT is where almost every accountant’s first instinct is wrong —
          because the default is <tspan>EXEMPT</tspan>, not standard-rated. New residential builds are zero-rated.
          Existing residential lettings are exempt. Most commercial property transactions are exempt by default —
          UNLESS the owner has made an <tspan>Option to Tax</tspan> (a binding 20-year election that locks the property
          at standard rate). The reason a sane person makes that election is they’ve incurred significant VAT on
          the build/refurb and need to reclaim it — the OTT turns an exempt supply into a taxable one so input VAT
          can be reclaimed. Plus three more property-specific mechanisms every accountant must hold: the <tspan>Capital
            Goods Scheme</tspan> (10-year adjustment for buildings >£250k); <tspan>Transfer of a Going Concern
          </tspan> (TOGC — sells the property + tenants together at NO VAT, but strict conditions); and DIY
          housebuilders’ relief. This module is the residential vs commercial split, when OTT helps and when it
          hurts, CGS adjustments, TOGC mechanics, and the trap of changing a property’s VAT status mid-tenancy.

          can be reclaimed. Plus three more property-specific mechanisms every accountant must hold: the Capital
            Goods Scheme (10-year adjustment for buildings >£250k); Transfer of a Going Concern
           (TOGC — sells the property + tenants together at NO VAT, but strict conditions); and DIY
          housebuilders’ relief. This module is the residential vs commercial split, when OTT helps and when it
          hurts, CGS adjustments, TOGC mechanics, and the trap of changing a property’s VAT status mid-tenancy.

title: Partial Exemption
meta: Module 18 · Part 3 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 18.1 Partial-exemption principle
sections.contentHtml: A business making both taxable and exempt supplies cannot recover all input VAT. Direct attribution + residual apportionment.

sections.title: 18.2 The Standard Method (Reg 101)
sections.contentHtml:
1. Direct attribution: assign each input to taxable / exempt / residual.
    2.    
  2. Recovery percentage on residual = Taxable supplies (excl. VAT) / Total supplies (excl. VAT) × 100, rounded UP to nearest whole percent (unless residual VAT > £400k/month).
    3.    
  3. Recover: directly-attributable taxable + (residual × recovery%).
    4.

sections.title: 18.3 De minimis
sections.contentHtml: If total exempt input VAT (direct + share of residual) is below de minimis, all exempt input VAT becomes recoverable. Test: exempt input VAT ≤ £625/month average AND ≤ 50% of total input VAT.

sections.title: 18.4 Annual Adjustment
sections.contentHtml:
Quarterly recovery uses provisional ratios; annual adjustment recalculates using full-year figures and adjusts in the next return after year-end.

 
    Worked Example 18.1 — PE calculation    

Period: taxable supplies £400k; exempt supplies £100k. Input VAT: directly taxable £30k; directly exempt £5k; residual £20k.

   

Recovery% = 400 / 500 = 80%.

   

Recovery = £30k + £20k × 80% = £46k. Blocked = £5k + £4k = £9k. De minimis: £9k > £625 × 3 months = £1,875 → fails. £9k blocked.

 
 
   

Module 18 — Summary

   
         
  • Direct attribution + residual apportionment by taxable/total.
    •      
  • De minimis allows full recovery if exempt input VAT is small.
    •      
  • Annual adjustment reconciles year's quarterly provisionals.
    •

sections.contentHtml:

hookHtml: A business making BOTH taxable AND exempt supplies is partially exempt — and the input VAT it can reclaim is restricted. Input VAT on costs directly attributable to taxable supplies = fully reclaimable. Input VAT directly attributable to exempt supplies = NOT reclaimable. The complication is residual input VAT — rent, utilities, accountancy fees, all the shared costs that can’t be tied to one or the other. That residual VAT gets apportioned using the Standard Method (taxable supplies % of total supplies). Plus the de minimis tests — if exempt input VAT is less than £625/month AND less than 50% of total input VAT, you can reclaim it all anyway. And the annual adjustment — recompute on annual figures at year-end to true up quarterly approximations. Get this wrong and you over-claim (HMRC assessment + penalty) or under-claim (free money to HMRC). This module is the framework that every accountant for a property landlord, charity, financial services business, or healthcare provider must run.

title: VAT Errors, Inspections & Penalties
meta: Module 19 · Part 3 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 19.1 Error correction thresholds
sections.contentHtml:
• Net error ≤ £10,000: correct on next return (Box 1 or Box 4 adjustment).
    •    
  • Net error £10k–£50k or 1% of Box 6 (greater): can still be corrected on next return.
    •    
  • Net error > £50k or 1% of Box 6: report on form VAT652.
    •    
  • Deliberate errors: VAT652 always.
    •

sections.title: 19.2 Points-based penalty regime (post Jan 2023)
sections.contentHtml:
• Late submission: 1 point per missed deadline. Threshold (4 quarterly / 5 monthly / 2 annual) → £200 penalty + £200 each subsequent miss.
    •    
  • Late payment: 0–15 days nil; 16–30 days 3%; 31+ days 6% + daily 10% pa.
    •    
  • Late payment interest: BoE base rate + 2.5% from due date.
    •

sections.title: 19.3 VAT inspections
sections.contentHtml:
HMRC selects on risk profile, random sample or intelligence. Typically 7 days notice. Reviews VAT control reconciliation, sample of sales/purchase invoices, treatment of cars/entertainment/property, apportionment workings.

 
    Practitioner advice    

Always attend the inspection with the client. Pre-inspection: review last 4 returns, identify any “known issues” first, brief client on what to say.

 
 
   

Module 19 — Summary

   
         
  • Errors ≤ £10k correctable on next return; larger or deliberate via VAT652.
    •      
  • Points-based late penalty regime since Jan 2023.
    •      
  • Inspections require active practitioner management.
    •

hookHtml:
When you discover a VAT error six months after the return was filed, the question every
          accountant asks is: <tspan>can I correct it on the next return, or do I have to disclose separately?</tspan>
          The answer comes down to two thresholds — <tspan>£10,000</tspan> net error (or up to <tspan>1% of
            Box 6 turnover, capped at £50,000</tspan>) can be corrected on the next return; above that, mandatory
          disclosure on VAT652. And the new penalty regime since January 2023 changed the whole calculus —
          it’s now a <tspan>points-based system</tspan>: each late filing is a point, hit the threshold for your
          filing frequency (4 quarterly / 5 monthly / 2 annual) and a fixed £200 penalty bites, then every
          subsequent late submission is another £200 until points expire. Plus separate late-payment penalties
          — 2% at day 16, another 2% at day 31, then 4% annualised daily. The carry-over to a VAT inspection: HMRC
          turns up, picks a quarter, and tests every box against the underlying records. Behaviour-based penalties (no
          error / careless / deliberate / deliberate-and-concealed) follow at 30/70/100% of the under-paid tax. This
          module is the error thresholds, the points-based penalty system, the late-payment scaling, and how to manage a
          VAT inspection.

title: Making Tax Digital for VAT
meta: Module 20 · Part 3 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 20.1 Scope
sections.contentHtml: From 1 April 2022, all VAT-registered businesses (regardless of turnover) must comply with MTD VAT. Limited exemption for digital exclusion.

sections.title: 20.2 Digital records required
sections.contentHtml:
• Designatory data (name, address, VRN, scheme).
    •    
  • Adjustments under FRS, partial exemption etc.
    •    
  • For each output supply: time, value, rate.
    •    
  • For each input supply: time, value, VAT recoverable.
    •    
  • Daily Gross Takings (retail scheme).
    •

sections.title: 20.3 Digital links — the chain
sections.contentHtml:
Permitted: API connections; CSV/XML/XLS/XLSX export-import; linked cells in workbook; emailed file then imported.

 

NOT permitted: re-typing; copy-paste of values; transcribing printouts.

sections.title: 20.4 Bridging software
sections.contentHtml: For spreadsheet users (Avalara, BX, VitalTax, Easy MTD VAT). Takes the 9 boxes from a workbook and submits via MTD API.

sections.title: 20.5 Penalties
sections.contentHtml:
Non-MTD compliance: up to £15/day plus standard late penalty regime.

 
   

Module 20 — Summary

   
         
  • All VAT-registered businesses in scope of MTD-VAT.
    •      
  • Digital records of designatory data, supplies and adjustments.
    •      
  • Digital links throughout — re-keying breaks compliance.
    •      
  • Bridging software keeps spreadsheet users compliant.
    •

hookHtml:
Making Tax Digital for VAT — live for everyone VAT-registered since April 2022
          — is two technical requirements packaged as one regime: <tspan>records kept in digital form</tspan>, and
          an <tspan>unbroken digital link</tspan> from source to the figure that lands in each of the 9 boxes on the
          return. A digital record includes the supply’s date, value, and VAT rate, kept in “functional
          compatible software.” A digital link is automated data transfer between software — including
          bridging software for users whose underlying records still live in spreadsheets. <tspan>Re-typing a number
            across systems breaks the link</tspan>. Cut and paste breaks it too (technically). XML, CSV import/export,
          API calls all preserve it. The compliance penalty isn’t huge per-incident but it can be assessed
          alongside any other VAT penalty and adds up. This module is the scope, the “functional compatible
          software” definition, the bridging-software workaround for legacy spreadsheet users, what counts as a
          digital link, the soft-landing periods (now closed), and the practical compliance check every accountant
          should run on each client’s VAT workflow.

title: PAYE Fundamentals — Tax Codes, NI Categories & RTI
meta: Module 21 · Part 4 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 21.1 PAYE in one paragraph
sections.contentHtml: Pay As You Earn is the system by which employers deduct Income Tax and National Insurance from employees' wages and pay them to HMRC each month. Legal basis: Income Tax (PAYE) Regulations 2003 (SI 2003/2682) and the Social Security Contributions & Benefits Act 1992. Since 2013, RTI requires employers to report each pay event on or before the date payment is made.

sections.title: 21.2 Setting up a PAYE scheme
sections.contentHtml:
Register at gov.uk/register-employer. HMRC issues:

 
       
  • Employer PAYE reference (e.g. 123/AB45678)
    •    
  • Accounts Office reference (13 character, e.g. 123PA00012345)
    •  
 

Both required for RTI submissions and for employees' P60s/P45s. Allow 5 working days for issuance.

sections.title: 21.3 Tax codes (2024/25)
sections.contentHtml:
A tax code tells the employer how much tax-free pay an employee gets. Standard code 1257L = £12,570 PA.

                                                                                       
Suffix / PrefixMeaning
LStandard PA
MReceiving 10% of partner's PA (Marriage Allowance recipient)
NTransferring 10% of own PA to partner
TTax code includes adjustments — call HMRC if details needed
K (prefix)Negative allowance — additions to taxable pay (e.g. K475 means add £4,750 to taxable pay/year)
BRBasic Rate (20% on all earnings) — usually a 2nd job
D0Higher Rate (40% on all)
D1Additional Rate (45% on all)
NTNo Tax
0TNo PA — emergency or new starter without P45
S prefixScottish taxpayer — Scottish rates apply
C prefixWelsh taxpayer (Welsh rates currently match English)
 

21.3.1 Cumulative vs Week 1/Month 1

 

Cumulative basis: tax on cumulative pay vs cumulative free pay. New starters or mid-year code changes may be put on W1/M1 (non-cumulative) until the next P6 from HMRC.

Class 1 NI is split between employee (primary) and employer (secondary).

    2025/26 — Employer NI changes    

From 6 April 2025: Secondary Threshold drops to £5,000; Employer NI rises to 15%; Employer's Allowance rises to £10,500 with the £100k payroll cap removed. Re-model salary/dividend mix.

sections.title: 21.5 Employer's Allowance
sections.contentHtml:
Reduces ER Class 1 NI bill by up to £5,000 per tax year (2024/25). Eligibility:

    •    
  • 2024/25: prior year secondary NI bill ≤ £100k (cap removed from 2025/26).
    •    
  • NOT available for sole-director Ltd with no other employees above ST.
    •    
  • Connected employers share one EA.
    •

sections.title: 22.2 SSP detail
sections.contentHtml: Eligibility: AWE ≥ £123/week. Sick 4+ days in a row (incl. non-working days). First 3 days = waiting days (unpaid SSP) unless linked to a previous SSP period within 8 weeks. Max 28 weeks.

sections.title: 22.3 SMP detail
sections.contentHtml: Eligibility: 26 weeks continuous service ending with the 15th week before EWC; AWE ≥ £123 in 8-week period ending 15 weeks before EWC. MATB1 from midwife = evidence. Recovery: 92% standard; 103% Small Employers' Relief.

sections.title: 22.4 EPS recovery
sections.contentHtml:
Payroll software calculates and shows on FPS. EPS Box 11/12 claims recovery monthly, reducing the PAYE bill paid to HMRC.

When an employee goes off sick, becomes a parent, or loses a baby, the employer must pay
          statutory amounts — and can reclaim most of them. The six are: <tspan>SSP</tspan> (statutory sick pay,

          parental), <tspan>SAP</tspan> (adoption), <tspan>SPBP</tspan> (parental bereavement). Get any wrong and the

          you recover 103% of paid statutory pay (the bonus 3% covers your employer NI on it). Standard employers
          reclaim 92%. SSP is NOT reclaimable since 2014 — that’s an unrecoverable cost. The qualifying days
          for SSP, the qualifying week for SMP, the 26-week service requirement, and the SPP/ShPP/SAP windows are all
          eligibility tests an accountant must apply. This module is each payment’s trigger, rate, eligibility,
          qualifying period, and EPS recovery process.

title: Auto-Enrolment Pensions
meta: Module 23 · Part 4 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 23.1 The duty
sections.contentHtml: Pensions Act 2008. Every employer must auto-enrol every “eligible jobholder” into a qualifying pension scheme. Failure: TPR fines from £400 fixed up to £10k/day.

sections.title: 23.2 Worker categories
sections.contentHtml:
CategoryAgeEarningsAction
Eligible jobholder22–SPA≥£10,000/yrAuto-enrol
Non-eligible jobholder16–21 or SPA–74>LEL but <£10,000Right to opt in; ER must contribute
Non-eligible jobholder22–SPA≥LEL but <£10,000Right to opt in
Entitled worker16–74≤LELRight to join (no ER contribution)

sections.title: 23.3 Minimum contributions on qualifying earnings
sections.contentHtml:
Qualifying earnings band 2024/25: £6,240 to £50,270. Total minimum 8%: ER 3% + EE 5% (incl. tax relief).

 
    Worked Example 23.1 — AE on £30k    

QE: £30,000 − £6,240 = £23,760. Total contribution 8% × £23,760 = £1,900.80. ER £712.80; EE £1,188.

sections.title: 23.4 Cyclical compliance
sections.contentHtml:
• Initial declaration of compliance within 5 months of duties start date.
    •    
  • Postponement up to 3 months allowed.
    •    
  • Triennial re-enrolment of opt-outs.
    •    
  • Re-declaration within 5 months of each re-enrolment date.
    •  
 
   

Module 23 — Summary

   
         
  • Eligible jobholders: 22–SPA earning ≥ £10k/year.
    •      
  • Total contribution 8% of QE; ER 3%, EE 5%.
    •      
  • Triennial re-enrolment + re-declaration of compliance to TPR.
    •

          with at least one worker. Every employee is categorised on each pay date (<tspan>eligible</tspan> / <tspan>

title: Benefits in Kind & P11D Reporting
meta: Module 24 · Part 4 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 24.1 What is a BIK?
sections.contentHtml: Non-cash benefit by reason of employment. Taxable on EE under ITEPA 2003; Class 1A NI on ER (13.8% in 2024/25; 15% from 2025/26). Trivial benefits (£50 or under) and certain exempt benefits escape charge.

sections.title: 24.2 Common benefits
sections.contentHtml:
BenefitCash equivalent
Company carList price × CO₂-based AP
Free fuel for company car£27,800 (2024/25) × CO₂-based AP
Beneficial loan > £10,000(Loan × HMRC official rate 2.25%) − interest paid
Living accommodationAnnual value (or rent if higher) + interest charge if cost > £75k
Private medical insuranceCost to ER
Gym membershipCost to ER
Vouchers (non-cash)Cost to ER
Trivial benefit (≤£50, not cash, not contractual)Exempt

sections.title: 24.3 Company car AP table
sections.contentHtml:
CO₂ g/km2024/25 AP (petrol)
0 (electric)2%
1–50 (varies by EV range)2–14%
51–5415%
...incrementing 1% per 5g/km...
170+37% (cap)
 

Diesel non-RDE2: +4% surcharge (capped 37%). RDE2 diesels: no surcharge.

 
    Worked Example 24.1    

BMW 320d (RDE2) £40,000, 130 g/km, AP 30%. CE = £12,000. EE higher-rate tax £4,800. ER Class 1A £1,656.

   

Tesla Model 3 £40,000, 0 g/km, AP 2%. CE = £800. EE tax £320. ER NI £110. Saves ~£5,400.

sections.title: 24.4 Payrolling vs P11D
sections.contentHtml:
• P11D: by 6 July file P11D per EE; P11D(b) for total Class 1A NI; pay Class 1A by 22 July.
    •    
  • Payrolled benefits: register before tax year start; tax collected through PAYE in real time. Still file P11D(b) for Class 1A. Mandatory from April 2026 for most BIK.
    •

sections.title: 24.5 PAYE Settlement Agreement (PSA)
sections.contentHtml:
For minor / irregular / impracticable items. ER pays grossed-up tax + Class 1B NI. Application by 5 July following tax year; payment by 22 October.

 
   

Module 24 — Summary

   
         
  • BIK taxed on EE; ER pays Class 1A NI.
    •      
  • Company car CE = list price × CO₂ AP. Electric on 2% saves thousands.
    •      
  • Trivial ≤£50, mobile, workplace parking exempt.
    •      
  • P11D 6 Jul, Class 1A 22 Jul; payrolling mandatory from April 2026.
    •

          checklist, the new-year setup, and the reconciliation between what HMRC says you owe vs what your books say.

title: Construction Industry Scheme (CIS)
meta: Module 26 · Part 4 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 26.1 Who is in scope?
sections.contentHtml:
• Mainstream contractors: business is construction.
    •    
  • Deemed contractors: non-construction businesses spending > £3m on construction in any rolling 12 months.
    •

sections.title: 26.2 Verification
sections.contentHtml:
StatusDeduction
Gross payment0% — pay in full (subcontractor met turnover, business, compliance tests)
Standard rate20% on labour element
Higher rate30% (unverified or unregistered)

sections.title: 26.3 Calculating the deduction
sections.contentHtml:
CIS on labour only. Strip out: materials, VAT, plant hire (separately invoiced), CITB Levy.

 
    Worked Example 26.1 — CIS deduction    

Subcontractor invoice: Labour £4,000, Materials £1,200, VAT £1,040 (20% on £5,200). Standard 20% deduction.

                                                 
Gross invoice6,240
Less: materials(1,200)
Less: VAT(1,040)
Labour4,000
CIS @ 20%(800)
Net to subcontractor5,440
CIS to HMRC by 22nd of following month800
 
 
   
      BrightPay · Walkthrough P4      

Process a CIS subcontractor payment with VAT DRC

   
   
     
       
Steps
       
             
  1. Add subcontractor: CIS → New Subcontractor
    2.          
  2. Enter UTR + NI (sole trader) or UTR + CRN (Ltd)
    3.          
  3. Verify with HMRC — instant API
    4.          
  4. HMRC returns: 0% gross / 20% std / 30% higher
    5.          
  5. When invoiced: separate Labour / Materials / VAT / Plant hire
    6.          
  6. CIS deduction calculated on labour element only
    7.          
  7. Process payment — net paid; CIS withheld
    8.

hookHtml:
The Construction Industry Scheme is HMRC’s way of taxing subcontractor payments at
          source — designed in the 1970s to combat the cash economy in construction and still essential today.
          Every <tspan>contractor</tspan> (anyone whose business is construction, or who spends > £3m on
          construction in any rolling 12-month period) must deduct CIS at one of three rates from <tspan>subcontractor
          </tspan> payments and pay it across to HMRC monthly: <tspan>20%</tspan> if verified standard, <tspan>30%
          </tspan> if unregistered, or <tspan>0% gross payment status</tspan> for established subcontractors who pass
          HMRC’s tests. Subcontractors then reclaim the deductions through their own returns — via tax
          credit (sole traders/partnerships) or against PAYE liability (Ltd companies). Plus the <tspan>CIS Domestic
            Reverse Charge</tspan> for VAT (M16) creates a second layer of complexity on the same transactions. Get it
          wrong and contractor faces penalties for under-deduction PLUS interest, AND the subcontractor over-pays tax
          that’s painful to reclaim later. This module is contractor vs subcontractor classification,
          verification, the three deduction rates, gross payment status tests, monthly CIS300 returns, the contractor
          pay/subcontractor reclaim flow, and the VAT reverse charge interaction.

title: The Year-End Process
meta: Module 27 · Part 5 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 27.1 Why year-end exists
sections.contentHtml: CA 2006 s.396 requires “a true and fair view” of profit/loss for the financial year and the state of affairs at year-end. Year-end transforms running ledger into a complete, corrected, statutory set.

sections.title: 27.2 The 11-step year-end workflow
sections.contentHtml:
1. Pre-year-end review (1–2 months before): aged debtors/creditors stale items, fixed asset register, stock count plan.
    2.    
  2. Period close: final pay run, recurring journals, lock VAT period.
    3.    
  3. Trial balance produced from accounting software.
    4.    
  4. Reconcile balance sheet — every BS line has a working paper.
    5.    
  5. Adjusting journals — accruals, prepayments, depreciation, stock, payroll, deferred income, dividend, CT, bad debts, DLA.
    6.    
  6. Tax computation in TaxCalc / IRIS / Alphatax; agree CT charge with directors.
    7.    
  7. Draft accounts in accounts production software.
    8.    
  8. Internal QA: senior reviews TB, comparatives, lead schedules, disclosures.
    9.    
  9. Client sign-off: directors review draft, sign accounts (CA s.414).
    10.    
  10. iXBRL tag & submit: Companies House and HMRC (with computations + CT600).
    11.    
  11. Archive working papers — 6 years (FA 1998 Sch 18 para 21).
    12.

sections.title: 27.4 Materiality
sections.contentHtml:
Audit benchmarks: 5% PBT, 1% turnover, 1–2% total assets — auditor selects most appropriate. Non-audit SME: ~£100 per item or 0.5% turnover whichever lower. Don't agonise over immaterial items.

 
   

Module 27 — Summary

   
         
  • Year-end transforms the running ledger into compliant statutory accounts.
    •      
  • 11-step workflow from pre-review to archive.
    •      
  • 9 mandatory balance sheet reconciliations.
    •      
  • Materiality keeps effort proportionate.
    •

hookHtml:
Year-end is when the running ledger gets transformed into a complete, corrected, <tspan>
            statutory set of accounts</tspan> that satisfies Companies Act 2006 s.396’s “true and fair
          view” requirement. It’s the most-scrutinised event in the accounting year — the accounts get
          filed to Companies House (public record), the CT600 derives from the same figures, and a year-end mistake is
          propagated downstream into every related filing. The professional year-end is an <tspan>11-step workflow
          </tspan>: pre-year-end review (1-2 months ahead so issues can still be fixed), period close, trial balance
          extract, all the year-end adjusting journals (M28), control account reconciliations, fixed asset
          additions/disposals/depreciation, stock count + valuation, going-concern review, tax computation, draft
          accounts, approval and signing. Standard reporting framework depends on size — <tspan>FRS 105</tspan>
          for micro (M29), <tspan>FRS 102 Section 1A</tspan> for small (M30), <tspan>FRS 102 full</tspan> for
          medium/large (M31). The discipline that separates senior from junior: <tspan>cut-off testing</tspan>, lead
          schedules for every balance sheet line, formal sign-off, and the working papers file that survives a Sch 36
          enquiry years later. This module is the framework that every later year-end module builds on.

hookHtml:
A cash-basis ledger and an accruals-basis ledger can diverge by tens of thousands of
          pounds at year-end — and FRS 102 s.2.36 demands the <tspan>accruals basis</tspan> for every company set
          of accounts (only the smallest unincorporated traders may opt for cash basis tax filing). Year-end adjusting
          journals are the bridge: the nine standard adjustments that take a software-extracted trial balance and
          convert it into a true-and-fair P&L and balance sheet. Each journal has a recognition rule behind it
          — <tspan>accruals</tspan> from s.2.36, <tspan>depreciation</tspan> from s.17 (systematic basis matching
          consumption of economic benefit), <tspan>stock</tspan> from s.13 (lower of cost and NRV), <tspan>bad debt
            provisions</tspan> from s.11 (expected credit loss), and <tspan>CT</tspan> from s.29 (current tax payable on
          taxable profit). The discipline that separates a clean year-end from a messy one: <tspan>every adjusting
            journal reverses on day 1 of the new period</tspan>, so the new year’s P&L starts at zero and the
          same accrual isn’t recognised twice. Get the nine right, and the rest of the year-end (lead schedules,
          disclosure notes, tax comp) flows naturally.

hookHtml:
FRS 105 is the UK GAAP framework for the smallest companies — the <tspan>
            micro-entity regime</tspan> introduced by SI 2013/3008 and embedded in Companies Act 2006 Part 15. To
          qualify, the company must meet two of three thresholds for two consecutive years (or its first year): turnover
          ≤ £632k, total assets ≤ £316k, and average employees ≤ 10 — <tspan>thresholds
            rising approximately 50% for accounting periods starting on or after 6 April 2025</tspan>. What makes FRS
          105 attractive: <tspan>minimal disclosure</tspan> — no directors’ report, no notes-by-line, no
          fair value remeasurement, no deferred tax, no revaluation. The filed accounts are essentially a stripped-down
          balance sheet and P&L plus two footnotes (director advances/credits and off-balance-sheet commitments).
          But FRS 105 excludes any company in an ineligible group, any PLC, financial institution, or charity. The
          accounts are also <tspan>not subject to true and fair override</tspan> if prepared in the format prescribed by
          FRS 105 — though they must still give a true and fair view. This module covers qualification,
          what’s in a FRS 105 set, the typical journal differences from FRS 102, and when a micro-entity should
          consider electing into FRS 102 1A anyway (for example, when bank covenants require fuller disclosure).

sections.title: 30.4 Why each major disclosure exists
sections.contentHtml:
Accounting Policies
   

Source: FRS 102 s.10 + s.8.4. Why: Many areas allow policy choice (depreciation method, FV vs cost, grants). Users need to know choices to interpret figures and compare to peers.

 
 
   
Going Concern
   

Source: FRS 102 s.3.8 + ISA UK 570. Why: Accounts assume continuation 12+ months. If at risk, users must be warned — liquidation valuations would be materially different.

 
 
   
Significant Judgements & Estimates
   

Source: FRS 102 s.8.6/8.7. Why: Many figures depend on management estimates (useful lives, bad debt, fair values). Users need to identify the “hot spots”.

 
 
   
Tangible Fixed Asset Movement
   

Source: FRS 102 s.17.31 + CA 2006 Sch 1. Why: Capex investment, write-downs, depreciation policy — assess cash needs and replacement cycle.

 
 
   
Creditors split <1yr / >1yr
   

Source: CA 2006 Sch 1 + FRS 102 s.4.5. Why: Liquidity assessment — what's payable next 12 months vs longer-term.

 
 
   
Director's Loans & Advances
   

Source: CA 2006 s.413. Why: Statutory transparency on transactions between company and officers — risk of value extraction. Lenders and minority shareholders need this.

 
 
   
Related Party Transactions
   

Source: FRS 102 s.33. Why: Non-arm's-length transactions can transfer value to a related party. Disclosure deters and exposes.

 
 
   
Average Employee Number
   

Source: CA 2006 Sch 1 para 87. Why: Statutory size benchmark + scale indicator.

 
 
   
Post-Balance-Sheet Events
   

Source: FRS 102 s.32. Why: Adjusting events reflected in BS; non-adjusting events disclosed for user awareness even though no figures changed.

  • Section 1A: full FRS 102 R&M, reduced disclosures.
    •      
  • Mandatory disclosure list per Appendix C (~16 items).
    •      
  • Each disclosure ties to CA mandate or FRS 102 user-protection rationale.
