hookHtml:
Section 1A is the most-used disclosure regime in UK practice — the regime that sits
          between FRS 105’s austerity and full FRS 102’s heavy disclosure burden. It applies to <tspan>small
            companies</tspan> (turnover ≤ £10.2m, assets ≤ £5.1m, employees ≤ 50 — <tspan>
            rising to £15m / £7.5m / 50 from 6 April 2025</tspan>) that want or need to use full FRS 102
          recognition and measurement but qualify for reduced disclosure. The trick of Section 1A: <tspan>full
            recognition and measurement of FRS 102 still applies</tspan> — investment properties revalued,
          deferred tax recognised, financial instruments classified into basic/non-basic, going concern assessment
          formally done — but the disclosures filed are reduced to the “Appendix C” list of <tspan>~30
            mandatory items</tspan>. Section 1A also permits <tspan>filleted accounts</tspan> (P&L and related notes
          withheld from public filing), and from 2026 the ECCTA changes mean small companies will no longer be able to
          file BS-only abridged accounts — the filed pack must include the full P&L. This module walks through
          the Section 1A format, the 30+ Appendix C disclosures, accounting policy choices, the small-company audit
          exemption (CA 2006 s.477) and the typical Section 1A vs full FRS 102 trade-offs. It is the bread-and-butter
          framework of UK SME accounting.

sections.title: 31.4 The 2026 amendments — major changes
sections.contentHtml:
Effective for accounting periods starting on/after 1 January 2026:

 
       
  • s.23 Revenue: 5-step model (identify contract → POs → transaction price → allocate → recognise) aligned with IFRS 15.
    •

    •    
  • Restate comparatives; recalculate covenants, bonuses, KPIs.

sections.contentHtml:

    •

    •    
  • KPIs (financial and non-financial)
    •

    •    
  • Climate-related financial disclosures (CFD) — large + PIE

sections.contentHtml:

hookHtml:
Every line in a set of accounts is there because a <tspan>specific law or standard
            mandates it</tspan> — Companies Act 2006, FRS 102 (with Section 1A for small entities), FRS 105 for
          micros, or sector SORPs for charities/pensions. A senior accountant doesn’t copy a previous year’s
          notes; they reason from <tspan>source → trigger → content</tspan>. Note 1 (Statement of Compliance)
          exists because FRS 102 s.3.3 + CA 2006 s.474 require users to know <tspan>which framework governs the figures
          </tspan>. Note 2 (Significant Accounting Policies) exists because FRS 102 s.10.7 demands disclosure of any
          policy “relevant to an understanding of the financial statements.” The related party note exists
          because CA 2006 s.413 requires director loans/credits to be public, and FRS 102 s.33 extends that to all
          related parties. The going concern note exists because s.3.8 imposes a 12-month forward assessment. This
          module reasons through <tspan>every note</tspan> in a typical small-company set, gives the exact statutory or
          framework reference, and explains why the disclosure protects the user of the accounts. Master this and you
          can defend every note in an audit, an enquiry, or a peer review — and you can prune anything that
          isn’t required, keeping the disclosure pack lean.

sections.title: 33.1 What iXBRL is
sections.contentHtml: Inline eXtensible Business Reporting Language. Machine-readable tags inside human-readable XHTML accounts. HMRC requires iXBRL with every CT600. Companies House: voluntary now, mandatory from 2027 under ECCTA.

sections.title: 33.2 Taxonomies
sections.contentHtml:
• UK GAAP (FRS 102) taxonomy

  • FRS 105 (micro) taxonomy
    •    
  • UK IFRS taxonomy
    •    
  • Charities taxonomy
    •    
  • Detailed P&L (DPL) taxonomy — line-by-line for HMRC, separate from statutory accounts
    •

sections.title: 33.3 Two-stage tagging
sections.contentHtml:
Software (TaxCalc, IRIS, Sage, BTC) auto-tags. The accountant reviews:

 
       
  1. Statutory accounts tags — every BS, P&L, notes line
    2.    
  2. DPL tags — detailed P&L for HMRC alongside CT600
    3.  
 

HMRC rejects submissions with missing/incorrect mandatory tags.

 
   

Module 33 — Summary

   
         
  • iXBRL = machine-readable layer on accounts.
    •      
  • Different taxonomies for FRS 102, FRS 105, IFRS, Charities, DPL.
    •      
  • Software auto-tags; accountant reviews.

hookHtml:
Every set of UK statutory accounts is filed in <tspan>iXBRL</tspan> — Inline
          eXtensible Business Reporting Language — a hybrid format that delivers a <tspan>human-readable XHTML
            document with machine-readable tags embedded inside</tspan>. HMRC has mandated iXBRL for every CT600 since
          2011; Companies House currently accepts it voluntarily but <tspan>ECCTA 2024 makes iXBRL mandatory for all
            filings from 2027</tspan>. The tags come from <tspan>taxonomies</tspan> — the UK GAAP (FRS 102 / FRS
          105) taxonomy, the Charities SORP taxonomy, the IFRS taxonomy, the DPL (Detailed Profit & Loss) extension.
          A tagged P&L line for “Turnover” isn’t just text — it carries an XBRL element id,
          a context (period and entity), a unit (GBP), and possibly footnotes. Quality matters: HMRC’s automated
          checks reject filings with missing mandatory tags, and a poor tag job triggers manual review and enquiry risk.
          Modern accounts software (CCH, IRIS, TaxCalc, Sage, Xero Tax) auto-tags 70-90% of items; the
          accountant’s job is to <tspan>review, correct, and complete</tspan> the tagging before submission. This
          module covers the iXBRL standard, the UK taxonomies, the auto-tag workflow, the most-commonly-missed tags, and
          the audit trail for review.

hookHtml:
Filing accounts with Companies House is the <tspan>final mechanical step</tspan> of the
          year-end cycle — but it’s also the step where most penalty letters land. Private companies must
          file within <tspan>9 months of year-end</tspan>; public companies within <tspan>6 months</tspan>. Miss the
          deadline and the penalty escalates: £150 (within 1 month), £375 (1-3 months), £750 (3-6
          months), £1,500 (over 6 months) — doubled if you also missed the prior year. Filing routes have
          collapsed to <tspan>software-API</tspan> for almost everyone: TaxCalc, IRIS, CCH, Xero Tax, Sage, FreeAgent
          all submit directly via the Companies House software filing API, returning an immediate accept/reject.
          WebFiling and paper routes are being phased out by ECCTA 2024. The big regulatory change is <tspan>ECCTA 2024
          </tspan> — the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act — which from 2026 ends abridged and
          filleted accounts for small companies (the filed pack must include the full P&L), introduces <tspan>
            identity verification</tspan> for directors and PSCs, and gives Companies House new powers to reject
          suspicious filings. This module walks through the mechanics: which forms file when, the small/dormant
          exemptions still permitted, the deadline calculator, late penalty mechanics, the ECCTA changes coming live in
          2025/26, and how to handle resubmissions and corrections via <tspan>second filing</tspan> mechanism.

sections.title: 35.1 The basics
sections.contentHtml:
• Tax on UK company profits (CTA 2009 + CTA 2010).
    •    
  • Period: an Accounting Period (AP) — typically the company's accounting period; long period >12 months split into 12-month AP + remainder.
    •    
  • CT600 within 12 months of end of AP.
    •    
  • Pay 9m+1d after AP end (non-large); large companies (taxable profits >£1.5m) pay quarterly Instalments (QIPs).

sections.title: 35.2 Rates 2024/25 & 2025/26
sections.contentHtml:
Profit bandRate
Up to £50,000 (Small Profits Rate)19%
£50,001 – £250,000 (Marginal Relief)Effective marginal 26.5%
Above £250,000 (Main Rate)25%

sections.title: 35.3 Marginal Relief
sections.contentHtml:
Marginal Relief = (Upper limit − Augmented profits) × (Augmented profits ÷ Total taxable profits) × 3/200  
 

Compute CT at 25% then deduct MR.

 
    Worked Example 35.1 — Marginal Relief    

Profit £150,000. Single company, no associates.

                               
CT @ 25%37,500
MR: (250,000 − 150,000) × (150,000/150,000) × 3/200(1,500)
CT due36,000
Effective rate24.0%

sections.title: 35.4 Associated companies
sections.contentHtml: £50k/£250k limits divided by number of associated companies (51% group, common control). Reintroduced from 1 April 2023.

hookHtml:
Corporation Tax is the levy on UK company profits, governed by the <tspan>Corporation Tax
            Act 2009</tspan> (income/expense) and the <tspan>Corporation Tax Act 2010</tspan> (rates, reliefs, groups).
          The basis period is the <tspan>Accounting Period (AP)</tspan> — usually the company’s year-end,
          but a long period (>12 months) splits into a 12-month AP plus a remainder AP, each with its own CT600 and
          computation. From 1 April 2023 the regime returned to a <tspan>two-rate structure</tspan>: <tspan>19%
            small-profits rate</tspan> for profits ≤ £50k, <tspan>25% main rate</tspan> for profits ≥
          £250k, and <tspan>marginal relief</tspan> tapering between (effective marginal rate ~26.5%). Augmented
          profits include franked investment income and associated-company thresholds are divided by (1 + number of
          associates) — a critical trap for groups and family holdings. The filing/payment chain: <tspan>file
            CT600 within 12 months</tspan> of period end, <tspan>pay 9 months and 1 day</tspan> for non-large companies,
          or <tspan>quarterly instalments (QIPs)</tspan> for large (taxable profits >£1.5m) and very large
          (>£20m). This module is the conceptual scaffold for everything in Part 6 — the language of CT,
          the deadlines, the rate map, and the framework you carry into every CT600 you ever prepare.

hookHtml:
Accounting profit is not taxable profit. The <tspan>CT computation</tspan> bridges the
          two via two columns — <tspan>add backs</tspan> (items expensed in accounts but disallowed for tax) and
          <tspan>deductions</tspan> (items allowed for tax that aren’t in the P&L, or that are tax-free income
          to back out). The classic add-backs: <tspan>depreciation</tspan> (replaced by capital allowances under CAA
          2001), <tspan>goodwill amortisation</tspan> (generally disallowed since FA 2002), <tspan>client entertaining
          </tspan> (CTA 2009 s.1298), <tspan>fines and penalties</tspan> (not wholly & exclusively trade), <tspan>
            political donations</tspan>, and capital expenditure expensed in error. Deductions: capital allowances on
          qualifying P&M (replacing depreciation), pension contributions paid (s.196 FA 2004), and statutory
          reliefs. The <tspan>“wholly and exclusively” test</tspan> (CTA 2009 s.54) is the workhorse
          principle — if expense isn’t wholly and exclusively for trade purposes, it’s disallowed. Get
          this column right and the rest of the computation flows; get it wrong and HMRC discovery-window risk follows
          you for 6 years. This module covers every standard add back, every standard deduction, the
          wholly-and-exclusively test in practice, and the structured pro-forma that every CT computation should follow.

hookHtml:
Capital allowances are the <tspan>tax substitute for depreciation</tspan> — the
          system by which the cost of qualifying capital expenditure on plant and machinery (P&M) is written off
          against taxable profits, governed by the <tspan>Capital Allowances Act 2001</tspan>. The core toolkit: <tspan>
            Annual Investment Allowance (AIA)</tspan> at 100% on the first £1m of qualifying P&M (any
          business); <tspan>Full Expensing</tspan> at 100% with no cap on new main-pool P&M (companies only,
          permanent from April 2023); <tspan>50% First-Year Allowance</tspan> on new special-rate P&M (companies);
          <tspan>Writing-Down Allowances (WDA)</tspan> at 18% main pool / 6% special rate (reducing balance), and a
          <tspan>structures and buildings allowance (SBA)</tspan> at 3% straight-line. Special rules apply to <tspan>
            cars</tspan> (CO2-banded WDA, no AIA), <tspan>integral features</tspan> (lifts, electrical, A/C —
          special pool), and <tspan>short-life assets</tspan>. Get capital allowances right and the CT charge drops
          materially; get them wrong and you either overpay tax or trigger a balancing charge on disposal. This module
          walks through the full toolkit, the pool mechanics, the qualifying-cost rules, the AIA-allocation strategy,
          and the standard worked example you’ll use on every CT computation.

sections.title: 38.1 The new schemes (from 1 April 2024)
sections.contentHtml:
Old SME and RDEC schemes merged. Two routes now:

 
       
  • Merged scheme: 20% above-the-line expenditure credit. Net cash benefit ~16.2% for profitable cos.
    •    
  • ERIS: Enhanced R&D Intensive Support — for loss-making SMEs with R&D ≥ 30% of total expenditure. 86% additional deduction (so 186% total); payable credit at 14.5%; net cash up to ~27% of qualifying spend.
    •

• SME R&D: 86% additional deduction; payable credit 10%
    •

    •

sections.contentHtml: Activities seeking advance in science or technology through resolution of scientific/technological uncertainty. Not: routine work, commercial uncertainty alone, marketing.

• Staff costs (proportionate to time on R&D)

title: Loss & Group Relief
meta: Module 39 · Part 6 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 39.1 The five trading loss reliefs
sections.contentHtml:
ReliefSectionEffect
Current yearCTA 2010 s.37(3)(a)Loss against total profits of same AP
Carry backCTA 2010 s.37(3)(b)Against total profits of preceding 12 months
Extended carry backFA 2021 s.183-year carry back, capped (mostly expired)
Carry forwardCTA 2010 s.45A onwardsAgainst future total profits (post-Apr 2017 losses; LRR)
Group reliefCTA 2010 Part 5Surrender to 75% group company

sections.title: 39.2 Loss Relief Restriction (LRR) — c/f losses
sections.contentHtml:
From 1 April 2017:

 
       
  • £5m Deductions Allowance per group, used freely
    •    
  • Losses above allowance restricted to 50% of remaining profit
    •  
 

So £20m profit + £20m b/f losses = offset £5m + 50%×£15m = £12.5m → £7.5m taxable.

sections.title: 39.3 Group relief — 75% group
sections.contentHtml: Parent owns ≥75% of subsidiary's ordinary share capital, ≥75% beneficial entitlement to distributable profits and assets on winding-up. Losses surrendered between members applied against overlapping AP.

sections.title: 39.4 Other losses
sections.contentHtml:
• Capital losses: only against capital gains; carry forward indefinite; cannot be group-relieved.
    •    
  • Property business losses: ring-fenced.
    •    
  • Loan relationship deficit: similar 5 reliefs but ring-fenced.
    •

sections.title: 39.5 Anti-avoidance
sections.contentHtml:
CTA 2010 s.673 — losses denied if major change in nature of trade within 5 years of change in ownership. Prevents “loss buying”.

 
   

Module 39 — Summary

   
         
  • 5 routes for trading losses: CY, 12m carry back, c/f, group relief, extended carry back.
    •      
  • LRR caps c/f use above £5m group allowance to 50% remaining profit.
    •      
  • 75% group: capital, profit, asset rights.
    •      
  • Capital losses ring-fenced.
    •      
  • Anti-avoidance on change of ownership + change in trade.

hookHtml:
Losses are the most valuable asset on a CT balance sheet you can’t see. The UK
          system gives <tspan>five separate trading-loss reliefs</tspan> (CTA 2010 s.37 and onward): <tspan>current year
          </tspan> against total profits (s.37(3)(a)), <tspan>12-month carry back</tspan> (s.37(3)(b)), <tspan>carry
            forward</tspan> against total profits from 1 April 2017 (post-reform s.45A — previously trading-only),
          <tspan>terminal loss relief</tspan> for cessation (3-year carry back, s.39), and <tspan>group relief</tspan>
          — surrendering losses to a 75%-owned consortium or group member (CTA 2010 Part 5). The <tspan>
            Restriction</tspan>: from 1 April 2017, brought-forward losses can only relieve up to £5m of profits
          plus 50% of the excess — a major restriction for large groups. <tspan>Group relief</tspan> rules (75%
          group, 75% consortium) require both companies UK-resident or chargeable to CT and run on a <tspan>strict
            ownership test</tspan>. Trading losses, non-trading loan relationship deficits, property losses, and
          management expenses all have their own carry-forward and surrender rules — this module maps every
          relief, every restriction, and the decision tree for “which relief should I claim and in what
          order?”

          UK Self Assessment client files annually, supplemented by source-specific pages (SA102 employment, SA103
          self-employment, SA104 partnership, SA105 UK property, SA106 foreign, SA108 capital gains, SA109 residence).
          The legal hook is <tspan>TMA 1970 s.8</tspan>: any person who receives a notice to file must file. Filing

            October</tspan> (paper) and <tspan>31 January</tspan> (online), with <tspan>balancing payment</tspan> and

          £100 immediate, £10/day after 3 months (max £900), then 5% or £300 at 6 and 12 months.

          triggers POAs for the following year. This module walks the structure, who must register, when registration is
          triggered, the income/allowances flow, and the end-to-end software workflow.

title: SA104 — Partnership Income

hookHtml:
Partnerships are <tspan>transparent for tax</tspan> — the partnership itself
          doesn’t pay tax; each partner’s share of profit is taxed on their own personal return. Two filings
          are required: the <tspan>SA800</tspan> partnership return (with a nominated partner submitting profit
          allocation) and each partner’s <tspan>SA104</tspan> supplementary on their SA100. Partners can be
          individuals (SA104) or companies (CT600 share). The <tspan>salaried members rule</tspan> (ITA 2007 s.863A) is
          critical for LLPs: if a member meets all three tests (Disguised Salary >80% of pay-out, no significant
          influence, contribution <25% of pay-out), they’re deemed employee for PAYE/NI — expensive
          surprise from HMRC re-classifications. <tspan>Basis-period reform</tspan> equally applies to partners:
          tax-year basis from 2024/25, transition profit spread, overlap profits used up. <tspan>Corporate partners
          </tspan> trigger TCGA 1992 special rules and SI 2014 PIE (partnership income element) anti-avoidance. <tspan>
            Mixed-membership rules</tspan> (ITA 2007 s.850C) catch profit-shifting between non-corporate and corporate
          partners. This module walks SA104, SA800 mechanics, LLP salaried members test, mixed membership, and the
          partner-vs-employee distinction that HMRC scrutinises closely.

hookHtml:
The <tspan>SA109</tspan> reports residence and domicile status — the gatekeeper for
          whether the UK taxes a person on <tspan>worldwide income</tspan> or only on <tspan>UK source</tspan>. The
          <tspan>Statutory Residence Test (SRT)</tspan> in <tspan>FA 2013 Schedule 45</tspan> is a 3-tier flow:
          automatic overseas (under 16 days, or under 46 if non-res in 3 prior years, or full-time overseas work) →
          automatic UK (183+ days, only home in UK, or full-time UK work) → sufficient ties test combining family,
          accommodation, 90-day, work, and country ties. <tspan>Split-year treatment</tspan> applies in years of
          arrival/departure with 8 cases. The big news: the <tspan>non-dom remittance basis abolished from 6 April 2025
          </tspan> — a 200-year-old regime replaced by a 4-year FIG (Foreign Income & Gains) regime for new
          arrivals plus transition rules. <tspan>Deemed domicile</tspan> rules (15/20 years UK residence) made many
          non-doms tax-resident for IHT already; the FIG regime now ends the income-tax shelter too. This module walks
          SRT mechanics with worked examples, split-year, FIG regime, transition rules (50% rebasing election, TRF), and
          the SA109 boxes that report all of it.
hookText:
The SA109 reports residence and domicile status — the gatekeeper for
          whether the UK taxes a person on worldwide income or only on UK source. The
          Statutory Residence Test (SRT) in FA 2013 Schedule 45 is a 3-tier flow:
          automatic overseas (under 16 days, or under 46 if non-res in 3 prior years, or full-time overseas work) →
          automatic UK (183+ days, only home in UK, or full-time UK work) → sufficient ties test combining family,
          accommodation, 90-day, work, and country ties. Split-year treatment applies in years of
          arrival/departure with 8 cases. The big news: the non-dom remittance basis abolished from 6 April 2025
           — a 200-year-old regime replaced by a 4-year FIG (Foreign Income & Gains) regime for new
          arrivals plus transition rules. Deemed domicile rules (15/20 years UK residence) made many
          non-doms tax-resident for IHT already; the FIG regime now ends the income-tax shelter too. This module walks
          SRT mechanics with worked examples, split-year, FIG regime, transition rules (50% rebasing election, TRF), and
          the SA109 boxes that report all of it.

title: Choosing a Structure — The Decision Framework
meta: Module 49 · Part 8 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 49.1 The five key questions
sections.contentHtml:
1. Liability: how much could the business lose to creditors? Higher = limited structure.
    2.    
  2. Profit profile: low / lumpy / steadily growing? Higher and growing = company often beats sole trader.
    3.    
  3. Privacy: do owners care about public accounts? Sole trader = total privacy; Ltd = public.
    4.    
  4. Capital: equity finance needed? Investors expect shares, not partnership interests.
    5.    
  5. Exit: planning sale within 5–10 years? BADR (10% CGT) needs trading-company structure for 2 years pre-disposal.
    6.

sections.title: 49.2 The £30k–£60k pivot zone
sections.contentHtml:
The “sole trader vs Ltd” tax math typically inverts somewhere between £30k and £60k profit. Below: sole trader cheaper after software/accountancy. Above: Ltd dominates IF profit can be retained or extracted as dividends.

 
    Worked Example 49.1 — £80k profit comparison (2024/25)                                                                          
Sole TraderLtd (£9.1k salary + dividend)
Profit80,00080,000
Salary deducted—(9,100)
Profit before CT—70,900
CT @ 19%/marginal—~14,290
Profit available as dividend—56,610
IT on profit (sole trader)17,432—
Class 4 NI (sole trader)2,841—
IT on dividend—~5,400
Total tax20,273~19,690
Net to owner59,72760,310
   

Tiny difference at £80k. From 2025/26 the Ltd's advantage erodes due to ER NI changes — re-model.

sections.title: 49.3 Beyond tax — qualitative factors
sections.contentHtml:
• Bank lending: Ltd more credible to lenders
    •    
  • Customer perception: large customers prefer Ltd suppliers
    •    
  • DLA flexibility: Ltd allows owner to lend money in/out
    •    
  • Pension funding: Ltd can pay employer pension contribution for owner-director
    •    
  • Spousal income split: Ltd shares can be issued to spouse
    •    
  • Risk separation: trade litigation stays in the company
    •

sections.title: 49.4 Six valid reasons NOT to incorporate (yet)
sections.contentHtml:
1. Profit too low — Ltd costs outweigh tax savings
    2.    
  2. Significant losses expected — sole trader can sideways-relief; Ltd losses ringfenced
    3.    
  3. Need to pull all profit out — dividend/salary tax narrows the gap
    4.    
  4. Privacy critical — sole trader figures aren't public
    5.    
  5. Trade involves regulated activity that Ltd would complicate
    6.    
  6. Likely cessation in 1-2 years — incorporation + closure within 2 years can lose BADR
    7.  
 
   

Module 49 — Summary

   
         
  • Decision driven by 5 questions: liability, profit, privacy, capital, exit.
    •      
  • Tax math typically tips around £30k–£60k profit.
    •      
  • Qualitative factors often more important than marginal tax saving.
    •      
  • 6 valid reasons to delay incorporation.
    •

          <tspan>tax exposure</tspan>, <tspan>liability shield</tspan>, <tspan>privacy posture</tspan>, <tspan>capital
            flexibility</tspan>, and <tspan>compliance burden</tspan> for years. The five canonical options: <tspan>sole
            trader</tspan> (zero set-up, full liability, SA only), <tspan>partnership</tspan> (joint & several
          liability, SA800 + SA104s), <tspan>LLP</tspan> (limited liability + tax transparency, accounts public),
          <tspan>private Ltd</tspan> (limited liability, CT regime, public accounts), and <tspan>PLC</tspan>
          (listed-ready, full disclosure). The decision turns on five questions: liability appetite, profit profile
          (low/lumpy/growing), privacy concerns, capital plans (need shares?), and operational complexity. Tax-driver
          heuristics: <tspan>profits <£30k</tspan> typically sole trader wins (no double tax, no public
          accounts), <tspan>£30-50k</tspan> grey zone (depends on extraction), <tspan>>£50k</tspan> Ltd
          usually wins via salary+dividend optimisation, <tspan>>£1m</tspan> Ltd essential for capital
          allowances and growth investors. Many advisors choose poorly because they default to “Ltd” without
          modelling. This module is the framework, the worked example, and the cheat-sheet for first-meeting client
          conversations.

hookHtml:
Sole-trader setup is deceptively simple — <tspan>no registration with Companies
            House</tspan>, no Articles, no shareholders, no minutes — but the tax compliance still requires
          precision. The legal status: the trader IS the business — no separate legal person, full personal
          liability for debts and creditors. <tspan>Step 1 register for Self Assessment</tspan> via <tspan>CWF1</tspan>
          by 5 October after the tax year of commencement (or face failure-to-notify penalty up to 100% of tax due).
          HMRC issues a <tspan>UTR</tspan> in ~10 days, plus <tspan>NIC Class 4 registration</tspan> (Class 2 abolished
          from 24/25 for profits above small-profits threshold). <tspan>Step 2</tspan>: <tspan>activate Government
            Gateway</tspan>. <tspan>Step 3</tspan>: separate <tspan>business bank account</tspan> (strongly recommended,
          not legally required). <tspan>Step 4</tspan>: VAT registration if turnover > £90k threshold
          (2024/25). <tspan>Step 5</tspan>: PAYE registration if hiring employees. <tspan>Step 6</tspan>: choose <tspan>
            cash basis</tspan> (default from 24/25 reform) or <tspan>accruals</tspan> election. <tspan>Step 7</tspan>:
          <tspan>basis period reform</tspan> — new sole traders now report on tax-year basis from day one. Cheap
          to set up, cheap to run, but full IT + Class 4 NIC on profits. This module covers each setup step, the
          registration mechanics, MTD ITSA delayed timeline, and the year-1 checklist every sole trader needs.

hookHtml:
A general partnership exists the moment <tspan>two or more persons carry on a business in
            common with a view of profit</tspan> (<tspan>Partnership Act 1890 s.1</tspan>). No registration with
          Companies House needed — but partnership setup needs care because <tspan>joint and several liability
          </tspan> exposes every partner personally to the debts and acts of every other partner. The <tspan>Partnership
            Agreement</tspan> overrides the default 1890 rules (equal shares of profit, equal capital, no salaries)
          — without one, the defaults govern, often badly. <tspan>Step 1</tspan>: draft the agreement covering
          profit/loss share (PSR), capital contributions, drawings, salaries, admission/retirement, dispute resolution,
          dissolution. <tspan>Step 2</tspan>: register the partnership with HMRC via <tspan>SA400</tspan> (gets
          partnership UTR). <tspan>Step 3</tspan>: each partner registers individually for SA via <tspan>SA401</tspan>.
          <tspan>Step 4</tspan>: nominate a partner to handle the SA800 submission. <tspan>Step 5</tspan>: open a
          partnership bank account with all partners on the mandate. <tspan>Step 6</tspan>: VAT, PAYE, and other
          registrations as needed. <tspan>LLP setup</tspan> follows a parallel but more formal process — register
          with Companies House via LL IN01, member agreement (binding), and account-filing obligations apply. This
          module covers both routes, the salaried-members trap from M45, and the year-1 checklist.

hookHtml:
An LLP — <tspan>Limited Liability Partnership</tspan> — is the hybrid form:
          <tspan>legal person</tspan> like a company (sues, owns assets, contracts), but <tspan>tax-transparent</tspan>
          like a partnership (members taxed on their share). Created by <tspan>Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000
          </tspan>. The big draw: <tspan>limited liability</tspan> for members, but with <tspan>partner-style profit
            allocation flexibility</tspan> — ideal for solicitors, accountants, architects, investment managers.
          <tspan>Setup steps</tspan>: (1) draft the <tspan>Member Agreement</tspan> (LLPA 2000 defaults are very sparse
          — without an agreement, all members share profit equally and consent to all decisions); (2) file <tspan>
            LL IN01</tspan> at Companies House (£50, ~24h); (3) appoint <tspan>at least 2 designated members
          </tspan> with statutory duties (sign accounts, appoint auditors, file CS01); (4) register with HMRC via
          <tspan>SA400</tspan> + each member via <tspan>SA401</tspan>; (5) open bank account. <tspan>Critical traps
          </tspan>: the <tspan>salaried members rule</tspan> (M45 — ITA 2007 s.863A) can re-classify members as
          employees; <tspan>annual accounts public</tspan> at CH (FRS 105/102 framework); <tspan>ECCTA 2024 identity
            verification</tspan> applies to all members. <tspan>LLP vs Ltd</tspan> calculus: LLP wins where
          partner-style allocation flexibility matters AND members are individuals (corporate members trigger
          mixed-membership). This module covers setup, post-incorp checklist, designated member duties, ECCTA
          implications, and the LLP vs Ltd decision.

          SA400 + each member via SA401; (5) open bank account. Critical traps
          : the salaried members rule (M45 — ITA 2007 s.863A) can re-classify members as
          employees; annual accounts public at CH (FRS 105/102 framework); ECCTA 2024 identity
            verification applies to all members. LLP vs Ltd calculus: LLP wins where
          partner-style allocation flexibility matters AND members are individuals (corporate members trigger
          mixed-membership). This module covers setup, post-incorp checklist, designated member duties, ECCTA
          implications, and the LLP vs Ltd decision.

title: Charity Registration
meta: Module 54 · Part 8 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 54.1 Choosing the form
sections.contentHtml:
• Unincorporated charity — trustees personally liable; no separate legal personality.
    •    
  • Charitable company limited by guarantee — dual-registered (CH + Charity Commission).
    •    
  • CIO — single regulator (Charity Commission). Foundation CIO (members = trustees) or Association CIO (separate membership).
    •

sections.title: 54.2 The CIO route (most common for new charities)
sections.contentHtml:
1. Draft constitution (CC model templates).
    2.    
  2. Confirm objects exclusively charitable (Charities Act 2011 s.3 — 13 purposes).
    3.    
  3. Identify 3+ trustees (unrelated, willing, fit).
    4.    
  4. Apply online to Charity Commission (~6–12 weeks).
    5.    
  5. Receive Charity Number.
    6.    
  6. Register with HMRC for charity tax exemptions (online HT2).
    7.    
  7. Open bank account (charity bank, CAF Bank, Co-op).
    8.    
  8. Bookkeeping with Charities SORP (FRS 102).
    9.    
  9. Annual: accounts + Trustees' Annual Report; Annual Return to CC.
    10.

sections.title: 54.3 Tax treatment
sections.contentHtml:
• Most income exempt under CTA 2010 Part 11 if used for charitable purposes
    •    
  • Gift Aid: 25% gross-up on cash donations from UK taxpayers
    •    
  • Trading exemption: small-scale or in furtherance of objects exempt; non-primary trading often via wholly-owned trading subsidiary
    •    
  • VAT: not automatically exempt; partial exemption common; specific reliefs (advertising, fundraising)
    •    
  • Business rates: 80% mandatory relief on premises used for charitable purposes
    •  
 
   

Module 54 — Summary

   
         
  • CIO is the modern default.
    •      
  • CC registration ~6–12 weeks; HMRC tax exemption separate.
    •      
  • Charities SORP (FRS 102 + extensive narrative).
    •      
  • Most income exempt; trading subsidiaries for non-primary trading.
    •

title: Sole Trader → Ltd Company Incorporation
meta: Module 55 · Part 8 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 55.1 The 9-step process
sections.contentHtml:
1. Form the new Ltd (Module 52).
    2.    
  2. Value the business assets: tangible (book value), inventory (cost), debtors (face value), goodwill (see 55.2).
    3.    
  3. Sale agreement: written contract sole trader → Ltd transferring assets and goodwill.
    4.    
  4. VAT TOGC: if VAT-registered, structure as TOGC (Module 17) to avoid VAT on transfer.
    5.    
  5. CGT: s.162 incorporation relief: where consideration is wholly shares, s.162 applies automatically to defer entire gain on goodwill into share base cost. Mixed consideration → partial s.162 (relief proportional to share value / total consideration).
    6.    
  6. HMRC notify cessation: file final SA103 marking cessation.
    7.    
  7. VAT: VAT68 to transfer VRN to Ltd, OR sole trader deregisters and Ltd applies for new VRN.
    8.    
  8. Bank, contracts, insurance, suppliers: novate or reissue in Ltd's name. Some (commercial leases, finance) require landlord/lender consent.
    9.    
  9. Open BS of Ltd: post asset transfer journal.
    10.

sections.title: 55.2 Goodwill — the technically tricky bit
sections.contentHtml:
Goodwill = value beyond identifiable assets. On incorporation, technically a CGT disposal at MV (s.18 TCGA 1992 — connected-party at MV).

 

Two main treatments:

 
       
  • Pure share consideration → s.162 incorporation relief: gain rolled into share base cost; no immediate CGT. Required: all assets transferred to Ltd in exchange for shares.
    •    
  • Mixed (shares + cash/DLA): s.162 partial (£ shares ÷ £ total × gain). The cash/DLA portion of gain is taxable now but BADR may apply (10% up to £1m lifetime) provided 2-year qualifying trade.
    •

sections.title: 55.3 Goodwill amortisation in Ltd
sections.contentHtml: Acquired goodwill amortised under FRS 102 s.18/s.19 (presumed 10-year life). However goodwill amortisation generally non-deductible for CT since 2002 (FA 2002 reform). From April 2019 narrow corporate intangibles regime allows 6.5% write-down where goodwill acquired alongside “qualifying IP” — most plain incorporations don't qualify.

sections.title: 55.4 Other transfer considerations
sections.contentHtml:
• Trading stock: transfer at higher of cost or MV (TCGA s.161). MV creates P&L credit in sole trader's final accounts.
    •    
  • Plant & machinery: usually elect TWDV transfer to avoid balancing charge/allowance (CAA 2001 s.266).
    •    
  • Property: SDLT applies on land at MV between connected parties (FA 2003 s.53). Often property left in personal name and licensed to Ltd to avoid SDLT.
    •    
  • VAT TOGC: meet conditions or face VAT on entire asset transfer.
    •    
  • DLA: if Ltd buys assets but doesn't pay cash, the unpaid balance is a credit to Director's Loan — drawable tax-free as repayment of loan in future.
    •

sections.title: 55.5 Loss treatment on transition
sections.contentHtml:
• Sole trader losses: carried forward to set against future income from same trade — but the trade has ceased! Limited use; can elect under s.86 ITA 2007 to relieve against income from new Ltd only if consideration ≥80% shares.
    •    
  • Capital losses: remain personal; no transfer.
    •

sections.title: 55.6 Practitioner's incorporation checklist
sections.contentHtml:
1. “Is incorporation worth it” tax model on actual numbers?
    2.    
  2. 2 years' trade for BADR eligibility?
    3.    
  3. Goodwill valuation defensible?
    4.    
  4. VAT TOGC structuring confirmed?
    5.    
  5. Property treatment decided?
    6.    
  6. Sale agreement drafted/signed?
    7.    
  7. Final sole trader SA filed (cessation noted)?
    8.    
  8. New Ltd opening BS posted?
    9.    
  9. DLA / share base cost recorded?
    10.  
 
   

Module 55 — Summary

   
         
  • Sole trader → Ltd is a CGT event on goodwill at MV (s.18 TCGA).
    •      
  • s.162 defers gain if wholly shares; partial if mixed.
    •      
  • BADR may cover taxable portion at 10% (2-year qualifying period).
    •      
  • TOGC for VAT; elect P&M at TWDV; consider leaving property in personal name.
    •      
  • Goodwill amortisation in Ltd usually non-deductible.
    •      
  • Final sole trader SA marks cessation.
    •

sections.title: Knowledge Check
sections.contentHtml:
Knowledge Check
   

Module 55 — End-of-Section MCQ (5 questions)

   
Q1      
s.162 applies fully when consideration is:
     
                                     
     
Wholly shares → automatic full s.162.
   
   
Q2      
Connected-party CGT base for goodwill:
     
                                     
     
Connected-party transactions deemed at MV.
   
   
Q3      
Goodwill amortisation in Ltd:
     
                                     
     
Add back; narrow 6.5% corporate intangibles regime exception since 2019.
   
   
Q4      
P&M transfer election:
     
                                     
     
Avoid balancing issues by electing TWDV.
   
   
Q5      
Property transfer between sole trader and Ltd:
     
                                     
     
Connected-party SDLT at MV; often property left out and licensed.

quiz.feedback: Wholly shares → automatic full s.162.

quiz.question: Connected-party CGT base for goodwill:
quiz.feedback: Connected-party transactions deemed at MV.

quiz.question: Goodwill amortisation in Ltd:
quiz.feedback: Add back; narrow 6.5% corporate intangibles regime exception since 2019.

quiz.question: P&M transfer election:

options.text: Election to transfer at TWDV (CAA s.266)

quiz.feedback: Avoid balancing issues by electing TWDV.

quiz.question: Property transfer between sole trader and Ltd:

options.text: SDLT at MV (connected parties, FA 2003 s.53)

quiz.feedback: Connected-party SDLT at MV; often property left out and licensed.

hookHtml:
Sole-trader-to-Ltd is the <tspan>most common UK transition</tspan> — and the most
          commonly botched. Done badly: <tspan>triggers CGT</tspan> on goodwill transfer, <tspan>leaves stranded VAT
          </tspan>, creates inefficient extraction structures, <tspan>wastes loss relief</tspan>, and creates years of
          compliance pain. Done well: preserves trading losses via election (CTA 2010 s.86), secures BADR eligibility on
          later disposal, transfers stock at value, creates tax-efficient extraction (salary + dividends + pension) from
          day one. The <tspan>9-step process</tspan>: (1) prepare cessation accounts, (2) value the business (goodwill +
          tangible assets), (3) incorporate Ltd, (4) execute the sale agreement (assets + goodwill in return for shares
          + DLA credit), (5) transfer trade + employees (TUPE), (6) handle VAT (transfer-as-going-concern or new
          registration), (7) terminate sole trader registrations, (8) start company compliance cycle, (9) elect for loss
          carryover (s.86). <tspan>Critical tax mechanics</tspan>: <tspan>CGT on goodwill</tspan> — usually
          triggered as market value disposal, but <tspan>incorporation relief (TCGA s.162)</tspan> defers if whole
          business transferred for shares; <tspan>SDLT</tspan> on property; <tspan>VAT TOGC</tspan> rules (no VAT
          charged if conditions met); <tspan>DLA</tspan> mechanism credits the trader for net assets transferred. This
          module walks every step, the s.162 vs s.165 election choice, and the TUPE/employee considerations.

title: Partnership → LLP / Partnership → Ltd
meta: Module 56 · Part 8 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 56.1 General partnership → LLP
sections.contentHtml:
Mostly painless. Both tax-transparent. Steps:

 
       
  1. Form the LLP, mirroring partnership members and PSR.
    2.    
  2. Draft LLP Agreement.
    3.    
  3. Transfer assets at book value (no CGT — partnership treated as continuing).
    4.    
  4. VAT68 to transfer VRN.
    5.    
  5. Notify clients/suppliers.
    6.    
  6. Final SA800; new SA800 starts for LLP.
    7.  
 

HMRC treats as continuation of trade (provided members substantially same) — no balancing charges, no goodwill CGT.

sections.title: 56.2 Partnership → Ltd
sections.contentHtml:
Mechanically similar to sole trader → Ltd, but each partner makes a CGT disposal of their partnership share.

 
       
  1. Form Ltd; share allocation typically mirrors PSR.
    2.    
  2. Each partner's share of business assets transferred at MV.
    3.    
  3. s.162 if all-shares; partial if mixed.
    4.    
  4. BADR may cover taxable goodwill at 10% (each partner's £1m lifetime).
    5.    
  5. Final SA800; cessation; new CT600 for Ltd.
    6.    
  6. Novate partnership creditors/contracts.
    7.  
 
   

Module 56 — Summary

   
         
  • GP → LLP: tax-transparent, treated as continuation.
    •      
  • Partnership → Ltd: each partner's share = CGT disposal; s.162 / BADR available.
    •

hookHtml:
Partnership-to-LLP is mostly painless — both are <tspan>tax-transparent</tspan>
          — while partnership-to-Ltd involves the harder transition from transparency to a separate taxable entity
          with all the goodwill, CGT, and TUPE issues. <tspan>Partnership → LLP</tspan>: form the LLP mirroring the
          partnership’s membership and PSR, then HMRC’s <tspan>concession D33</tspan> generally treats it as
          continuation (no cessation, no transfer-pricing, no CGT). Existing partnership assets <tspan>continue at
            carrying value</tspan>; capital allowance pools <tspan>roll over</tspan>; trading losses can be claimed
          against LLP members on the same continuation basis. <tspan>Partnership → Ltd</tspan>: now a real
          transition — treated like sole-trader-to-Ltd for each partner. Each partner’s share of partnership
          goodwill triggers CGT (s.162 incorporation relief available if whole business for shares), partnership assets
          transferred at market value with possible balancing charges, trading losses survive via election (CTA 2010
          s.86), CSCH (Capital Account Sale-and-Buy-Back) sometimes useful. <tspan>SDLT</tspan> on property, <tspan>VAT
            TOGC</tspan> for new Ltd. <tspan>LLP → Ltd</tspan>: same mechanics, plus dealing with LLP wind-down at
          Companies House. Critical: <tspan>profit-sharing changes can trigger CGT on goodwill</tspan> — structure
          carefully. This module covers each route with worked examples and the partnership-agreement amendments needed
          pre-transition.

title: Sole Trader Cessation
meta: Module 58 · Part 9 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 58.1 Final SA103 — special items
sections.contentHtml:
• Tick “ceased trading”; enter cessation date
    •    
  • Final accounts to cessation date
    •    
  • Closing stock at MV (TCGA s.161)
    •    
  • Balancing CA charge / allowance
    •    
  • Outstanding debtors → post-cessation receipts taxed as income from previous trade
    •

sections.title: 58.2 Capital allowances on cessation
sections.contentHtml: Pools closed. Disposal proceeds vs TWDV: balancing allowance (proceeds < TWDV) or balancing charge (proceeds > TWDV).

sections.title: 58.3 Loss reliefs
sections.contentHtml:
• Terminal loss relief (ITA 2007 s.89): last 12 months of trading loss carried back 3 years (latest first), set against profits of same trade.
    •    
  • CY / 12m carry back / sideways s.64 also available.
    •

sections.title: 58.4 VAT deregistration
sections.contentHtml:
Within 30 days of ceasing taxable supplies (VAT7).

 
       
  • Deemed self-supply: assets retained > £6,000 (excl. VAT) — output VAT due on stock + capital assets retained
    •    
  • Final VAT return covers period to dereg date
    •    
  • VAT427 for post-dereg input VAT recovery (4 years for some items)
    •

sections.title: 58.5 Other compliance
sections.contentHtml:
• PAYE: close scheme, final FPS marked final, P45s
    •    
  • CIS: deregister
    •    
  • HMRC notify cessation
    •    
  • Insurance: PII run-off (~6 years)
    •  
 
   

Module 58 — Summary

   
         
  • Final SA103 with cessation date.
    •      
  • Closing stock at MV; balancing CA on cessation.
    •      
  • Terminal loss relief: last 12m carry back 3 years.
    •      
  • VAT deregister 30 days; deemed self-supply on retained assets >£6k.

          <tspan>ceased-trading box ticked</tspan> + cessation date, final accounts run to the cessation date, plus
          several special items: <tspan>balancing charge or allowance</tspan> on disposal of P&M (CAA 2001 s.55),
          <tspan>terminal loss relief</tspan> (ITA 2007 s.89 — 3-year carry-back), <tspan>post-cessation receipts

          retirement, ill-health, business failure, sale to third party, incorporation (covered separately in M55),
          death of trader. <tspan>Order of post-cessation actions</tspan>: (1) stock disposed/transferred, (2) debtors
          collected/written off, (3) creditors settled, (4) P&M disposed with balancing entries, (5) VAT7 within 30

meta: Module 59 · Part 9 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 59.1 Steps
sections.contentHtml:
1. Final SA800 with cessation flag
    2.    
  2. Each partner files SA100 + SA104
    3.    
  3. Terminal loss relief per partner (s.89)
    4.    
  4. VAT deregistration if applicable
    5.    
  5. PAYE closure
    6.    
  6. Final settlement of partnership assets/liabilities
    7.    
  7. Distribution per capital accounts
    8.

sections.title: 59.2 Goodwill on dissolution / sale
sections.contentHtml:
Each partner has CGT disposal of their share of goodwill. BADR available (10%, £1m lifetime each).

 
   

Module 59 — Summary

    •

hookHtml:
Partnership cessation has TWO layers: <tspan>the partnership itself winds up</tspan>
          (final SA800 with cessation flag, partnership UTR deregistered), and <tspan>each partner has their own
            cessation event</tspan> (final SA104 inside their SA100, terminal loss relief calculated per partner). For
          LLPs, add a third layer: <tspan>LLP wind-down at Companies House</tspan> via LL DS01 strike-off or formal
          liquidation. Common scenarios: <tspan>full dissolution</tspan> (all partners leave, business stops), <tspan>
            partial change</tspan> (one partner retires, remaining partners continue — <tspan>not a cessation
          </tspan> if at least one continues), <tspan>conversion to sole trader</tspan> (one partner buys out others
          — partnership ceases, sole trader emerges), <tspan>conversion to Ltd</tspan> (handled in M56). <tspan>
            Capital account settlement</tspan> — each partner’s capital + reserves + share of goodwill paid
          out, often phased; CGT on disposal of capital interest; <tspan>BADR available</tspan> if 2-year ownership +
          whole/most of business interest. <tspan>Terminal loss relief</tspan> (ITA 2007 s.89) applies separately to
          each partner’s share. <tspan>VAT, PAYE, public-register dereg</tspan> all required. This module walks
          the partnership-level mechanics, per-partner mechanics, LLP wind-down, and the “continuation vs
          cessation” test that determines which path applies.

title: Ltd Strike-Off (DS01) — Voluntary Dissolution
meta: Module 60 · Part 9 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 60.1 Eligibility (CA 2006 s.1003)
sections.contentHtml:
• SOLVENT, dormant or simple-affairs Ltd
    •    
  • Not traded or changed name in last 3 months
    •    
  • Not subject to insolvency proceedings
    •    
  • No agreement with creditors (e.g. CVA)
    •

sections.title: 60.2 Process
sections.contentHtml:
1. Settle all known creditors (HMRC for VAT/CT/PAYE).
    2.    
  2. Distribute remaining assets BEFORE applying for strike-off.
    3.    
  3. Final CT600 (period to cessation of trade).
    4.    
  4. Final VAT return; deregister.
    5.    
  5. Close PAYE; final FPS.
    6.    
  6. File DS01 (£33 fee online from May 2024); signed by majority of directors.
    7.    
  7. CH publishes notice in The Gazette; if no objection within 2 months, strike-off complete.
    8.    
  8. Notify creditors, shareholders, employees within 7 days of DS01.
    9.

sections.title: 60.3 £25,000 capital distribution rule (CTA 2010 s.1030A)
sections.contentHtml:
• Pre-strike-off distributions ≤ £25k → capital (CGT, often BADR 10%)
    •    
  • > £25k → income dividend (8.75/33.75/39.35%)
    •    
  • For larger capital extraction → MVL is the route
    •

sections.title: 60.4 HMRC objection
sections.contentHtml: HMRC objects to strike-off if tax outstanding. Always check HMRC clearance before DS01.

sections.title: 60.5 Restoration if struck off in error
sections.contentHtml:
CH (administrative, 6-year limit) or court (CA 2006 s.1024 / s.1029) restoration.

 
   

Module 60 — Summary

   
         
  • DS01 for solvent simple closure; £33 fee.
    •      
  • Settle creditors and distribute assets first.
    •      
  • £25k capital cap (s.1030A); above use MVL.
    •      
  • HMRC objects if tax outstanding.
    •

hookHtml:
Voluntary strike-off via <tspan>DS01</tspan> (Companies Act 2006 s.1003) is the cheapest,
          simplest route to close a Ltd company — a £33 form to Companies House, 2-3 months of public-notice
          period, then dissolution. But it’s strictly limited to <tspan>solvent, simple-affairs companies</tspan>:
          not traded in the last 3 months (no recent name change), no insolvency proceedings pending, no CVA, no
          creditors agreements. The killer constraint: <tspan>distributable reserves <£25k</tspan> for
          tax-efficient distribution via “ESC C16-style” mechanism — over £25k requires <tspan>
            MVL</tspan> (M61) instead. Even with low reserves, <tspan>TCGA s.1030A</tspan> from FA 2012 limits the
          £25k cap to genuine distributions; anti-avoidance rules (TAAR — <tspan>ITTOIA 2005 s.396B</tspan>)
          catch “phoenix” arrangements where shareholders restart the same trade within 2 years. The 5-step
          process: (1) clear creditors and tax liabilities, (2) distribute reserves, (3) file DS01 + send copies to
          interested parties (creditors, employees, shareholders, pension trustees), (4) wait 2-3 months for objection
          window, (5) confirmation of strike-off. Director duties continue throughout. This module walks eligibility,
          the £25k cap mechanics, BADR availability, anti-phoenixing rules, post-dissolution issues (bona vacantia
          for missed assets), and the strike-off vs MVL decision.

title: Members' Voluntary Liquidation (MVL)
meta: Module 61 · Part 9 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 61.1 When MVL is the route
sections.contentHtml:
• Solvent (Declaration of Solvency by directors; debts payable in 12 months)
    •    
  • Distributable funds > £25,000
    •    
  • Shareholders want capital treatment (CGT/BADR) over dividends
    •

sections.title: 61.2 Process
sections.contentHtml:
1. Directors prepare Declaration of Solvency (sworn).
    2.    
  2. Members pass special resolution to wind up + appoint IP as liquidator.
    3.    
  3. Notice in Gazette.
    4.    
  4. IP gathers assets, settles creditors, distributes surplus to members.
    5.    
  5. Final meeting; IP files final account at CH.
    6.    
  6. Company dissolved 3 months after final account.
    7.

sections.title: 61.3 Tax treatment
sections.contentHtml:
Distributions = CAPITAL:

 
       
  • BADR 10% up to £1m lifetime if conditions met
    •    
  • AEA £3,000 (2024/25)
    •    
  • Higher CGT 20% otherwise
    •

sections.title: 61.4 TAAR (Targeted Anti-Avoidance Rule, 2016)
sections.contentHtml:
Distribution re-classified as income dividend if:

 
       
  1. Recipient connected (5%+)
    2.    
  2. Recipient continues same/similar trade within 2 years
    3.    
  3. Reasonable to assume one main purpose is income tax avoidance
    4.  
 

Genuine retirement / sale: not affected.

sections.title: 61.5 IP costs
sections.contentHtml:
£1,500–£5,000 typical. BADR savings on £500k distribution can be £100k+.

 
   

Module 61 — Summary

   
         
  • MVL: solvent, >£25k, capital tax treatment.
    •      
  • Declaration of Solvency by directors; IP appointed.
    •      
  • TAAR re-classifies as dividend if owner continues similar trade within 2 years.
    •      
  • IP costs £1.5k–£5k; BADR savings often substantial.
    •

sections.contentHtml:

hookHtml:
MVL — Members’ Voluntary Liquidation — is the <tspan>tax-efficient exit
            route</tspan> for solvent companies with reserves above the <tspan>£25k strike-off cap</tspan>. All
          distributions to shareholders are treated as <tspan>capital</tspan> not income — meaning <tspan>BADR at
            10%</tspan> (rising to 14% April 2025, 18% April 2026) on the entire reserves, vs dividend tax at
          33.75-39.35%. On £500k of reserves that’s ~£100k saved. Process: directors sign <tspan>
            Declaration of Solvency</tspan> (debts paid within 12 months — criminal offence if false), 75%
          shareholders pass resolution to wind up, appoint <tspan>Insolvency Practitioner (IP)</tspan> as liquidator. IP
          fees: typically <tspan>£3-7k</tspan> — worth it if BADR savings > fees. IP takes control,
          settles creditors, distributes net assets to shareholders. <tspan>TAAR (ITTOIA s.396B)</tspan> still applies
          — same trade within 2 years recharacterises distribution as dividend, killing BADR. <tspan>Pre-MVL
            planning</tspan>: clear DLAs, recover R&D refunds, manage employment status of director-shareholders.
          Process timeline: 2-6 months typically, occasionally longer if HMRC clearance needed. This module covers
          eligibility, IP appointment, the £25k threshold decision vs strike-off, TAAR avoidance, BADR mechanics,
          and post-MVL compliance.

title: Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation (CVL)
meta: Module 62 · Part 9 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 62.1 When CVL applies
sections.contentHtml: Insolvent company — debts cannot be paid. Directors choose voluntary liquidation rather than wait for creditor petition.

sections.title: 62.2 Process
sections.contentHtml:
1. Directors decide insolvent.
    2.    
  2. Members resolve to wind up.
    3.    
  3. IP appointed (often by directors, with creditor approval).
    4.    
  4. S.100 creditors' meeting within 14 days.
    5.    
  5. Liquidator settles creditors in statutory order:      
             
    1. Liquidator's costs & expenses
      2.        
    2. Secured creditors (fixed charge)
      3.        
    3. Preferential creditors (employees up to £800 each; HMRC for VAT/PAYE/NI since Dec 2020)
      4.        
    4. Secured (floating charge) with prescribed part for unsecureds
      5.        
    5. Unsecured creditors (pro rata)
      6.        
    6. Members
      7.      
       
    6.    
  6. Final account; dissolution.
    7.

sections.title: 62.3 Director consequences
sections.contentHtml:
• Disqualification (CDDA 1986) if conduct “unfit”: 2–15 years
    •    
  • Wrongful trading (IA 1986 s.214): personal liability if knew/should have known
    •    
  • Fraudulent trading (IA 1986 s.213): personal liability + criminal
    •    
  • Personal guarantees crystallise
    •  
 
   

Module 62 — Summary

   
         
  • CVL: insolvent voluntary liquidation; director-initiated.
    •      
  • Statutory order of creditor payment.
    •      
  • HMRC moved to preferential status for VAT/PAYE/NI from Dec 2020.
    •      
  • Wrongful/fraudulent trading risks personal liability + disqualification.
    •

hookHtml:
CVL is the <tspan>insolvent-company exit</tspan> — directors recognise the company
          can’t pay its debts and voluntarily choose liquidation rather than wait for a <tspan>creditor petition
          </tspan> (compulsory liquidation under IA 1986 s.124). Insolvency tests: <tspan>cash-flow</tspan> (can’t
          pay debts as they fall due) and <tspan>balance-sheet</tspan> (liabilities exceed assets). <tspan>Critical
            timing</tspan>: from the moment of insolvency, <tspan>wrongful trading</tspan> liability begins (IA 1986
          s.214) — directors personally liable for additional losses if they continue trading when no reasonable
          prospect of avoiding liquidation. Process: directors call <tspan>board meeting</tspan> → appoint <tspan>
            insolvency practitioner</tspan> → convene <tspan>shareholders’ meeting</tspan> (75% to wind up)
          → hold <tspan>creditors’ meeting</tspan> within 14 days (s.100) → IP nominated by creditors
          becomes liquidator. <tspan>Director conduct review</tspan> follows: any breach of duty (wrongful trading,
          fraudulent trading s.213, preference payments, transactions at undervalue s.238) can result in personal
          liability AND <tspan>director disqualification</tspan> up to 15 years (CDDA 1986). <tspan>HMRC preferential
            creditor</tspan> status restored from 1 Dec 2020 for VAT, PAYE/NIC, CIS — HMRC ranks ahead of
          floating-charge holders. This module walks the insolvency tests, the timing-critical director duties, the CVL
          process, and post-CVL disqualification risks.

title: Compulsory Liquidation
meta: Module 63 · Part 9 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 63.1 What it is
sections.contentHtml:
Court-ordered winding up. Petition typically by:

 
       
  • Creditor (most common; debt > £750 + statutory demand)
    •    
  • Company itself
    •    
  • HMRC (for unpaid VAT/PAYE/CT)
    •    
  • Shareholder (rare)
    •

sections.title: 63.2 Process
sections.contentHtml:
1. Creditor files winding-up petition at court.
    2.    
  2. Hearing ~6–8 weeks later.
    3.    
  3. Court issues winding-up order; Official Receiver becomes liquidator.
    4.    
  4. Investigation of director conduct.
    5.    
  5. If asset realisations > OR fees, IP appointed.
    6.    
  6. Distribution per statutory order.
    7.

sections.title: 63.3 Effect
sections.contentHtml:
• Bank accounts frozen
    •    
  • Trading must cease
    •    
  • Director powers cease
    •    
  • Director conduct investigated
    •  
 
   

Module 63 — Summary

   
         
  • Court-ordered; usually creditor-initiated.
    •      
  • OR initially liquidator; IP if assets sufficient.
    •      
  • Director conduct investigated.
    •

hookHtml:
Compulsory liquidation is <tspan>court-ordered winding up</tspan> — the involuntary
          version of CVL, triggered by a <tspan>winding-up petition</tspan> (IA 1986 s.122). The most common petitioner
          is a <tspan>creditor</tspan>: any debt >£750 + statutory demand unpaid for 21 days = grounds for
          petition. Other petitioners: <tspan>the company itself</tspan> (rare — CVL is faster), <tspan>directors
          </tspan> (joint), <tspan>shareholders</tspan> (under just-and-equitable ground), <tspan>HMRC</tspan>
          (significant tax debt), <tspan>The Secretary of State</tspan> (public interest under CDDA 1986). Process:
          petition filed at <tspan>High Court</tspan> (or county court for smaller companies), advertised in <tspan>The
            Gazette</tspan>, hearing within ~8 weeks. Court appoints <tspan>Official Receiver</tspan> initially
          (Insolvency Service officer), who may then appoint a private IP. <tspan>From petition to liquidation order
          </tspan>: company assets effectively frozen, transactions can be voided (s.127), bank accounts often frozen by
          banks. Directors have <tspan>21-day window</tspan> to convert to CVL or otherwise dispose. <tspan>Director
            conduct review</tspan> typically more aggressive than CVL given creditor petition. Same post-liquidation
          regime as CVL (SoCID2, CDDA 1986, phoenix rules). This module covers petition mechanics, the s.127 freeze,
          conversion options, the OR’s role, and what to do when a winding-up petition arrives.

title: Administration & CVA
meta: Module 64 · Part 9 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 64.1 Administration (IA 1986 Sch B1)
sections.contentHtml:
• Court protection while administrator restructures or sells as going concern
    •    
  • Moratorium on creditor action
    •    
  • 3 statutory objectives (in order): rescue going concern; better creditor result; realise assets to pay secured/preferential
    •    
  • 12-month duration (extendable)
    •    
  • Pre-pack sale (sale to connected party arranged before administration) — controversial
    •

sections.title: 64.2 CVA (IA 1986 Part I)
sections.contentHtml:
• Compromise with creditors — pay reduced amounts over time
    •    
  • 75% creditor approval (by value)
    •    
  • Binds all unsecured creditors
    •    
  • Trading continues; equity preserved
    •    
  • Suitable when business viable but burdened by historical debt
    •  
 
   

Module 64 — Summary

   
         
  • Administration: moratorium + IP-led restructuring; 3 statutory objectives.
    •      
  • CVA: 75% creditor approval; trading continues.
    •      
  • Pre-pack: sale arranged pre-appointment.

hookHtml:
Administration and CVA are the <tspan>rescue tools</tspan> — alternatives to
          liquidation when the business has <tspan>rescuable value</tspan>. <tspan>Administration</tspan> (IA 1986 Sch
          B1) puts the company under court protection while an <tspan>administrator</tspan> (licensed IP) restructures
          or sells it as a going concern. The big benefit: <tspan>moratorium</tspan> — creditor action halted, no
          winding-up petition can be presented, no security can be enforced without consent. Three statutory purposes
          ranked: <tspan>(1) rescue as going concern</tspan>, (2) better result for creditors than liquidation, (3)
          realise property to distribute to secured/preferential creditors. <tspan>CVA</tspan> (IA 1986 Part 1) —
          <tspan>Company Voluntary Arrangement</tspan> — is a deal between company and creditors: typically pay
          reduced amount over 3-5 years instead of full debt. Approved by <tspan>75% by value of creditors</tspan>.
          Continues trading throughout. Cheaper than administration but limited: no moratorium except the 28-day
          “Part A1 moratorium” introduced by CIGA 2020. <tspan>CIGA 2020 reforms</tspan> introduced the
          <tspan>Restructuring Plan</tspan> (Part 26A CA 2006) for larger restructurings with <tspan>cross-class
            cramdown</tspan>. <tspan>Pre-pack administration</tspan>: sale of business arranged before administration
          begins, often to connected party — requires SIP 16 statement + new viability statement under SoCV
          regulations 2021. This module covers administration mechanics, CVA structure, CIGA changes, and when each tool
          applies.

hookHtml:
Final accounts on cessation differ from ordinary year-end accounts in critical ways:
          <tspan>going-concern basis no longer applies</tspan>, so <tspan>FRS 102 s.3.9</tspan> requires the <tspan>
            break-up basis</tspan> — assets at <tspan>net realisable value</tspan>, liabilities at <tspan>
            settlement amount</tspan>. For <tspan>sole traders/partnerships</tspan>: closing stock at <tspan>market
            value</tspan> (FA disposed of in S.1 of CTA 2010 / equivalent for unincorporated), <tspan>balancing capital
            allowance</tspan> entries on disposed P&M, debtors at recoverable value, write off uncollectible,
          partnership capital accounts settled. For <tspan>Ltd companies</tspan>: prepare to <tspan>cessation date
          </tspan> (often mid-year), include final period AP for CT600, mark balance sheet “Prepared on a break-up
          basis” if appropriate, <tspan>recognise liabilities at amounts likely to settle</tspan> (provisions for
          dilapidations, redundancy, contingent claims), <tspan>reverse deferred tax</tspan> as no future profits,
          include <tspan>going-concern note</tspan> explaining cessation basis. The auditor (if applicable) gives a
          <tspan>modified going concern opinion</tspan> — usually emphasis of matter with cessation paragraph.
          Cessation-cost provisions: <tspan>redundancy</tspan> (when constructive obligation arises, IAS 37 / FRS 102
          s.21), <tspan>lease exit / dilapidations</tspan>, <tspan>warranty obligations</tspan>, <tspan>contract
            termination</tspan>. <tspan>Asset write-downs</tspan> — impairment of intangibles, goodwill, PP&E
          to recoverable amount. This module walks the break-up basis, the disclosures required, the auditor
          implications, and the bridge to CT600 / SA105 / SA800 closure.

title: Capital Distributions & BADR
meta: Module 66 · Part 9 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 66.1 Capital vs income on closure
sections.contentHtml:
RouteTreatmentTax rate
DS01 ≤£25kCapital10%/20% with AEA & BADR
DS01 >£25kDividend8.75/33.75/39.35%
MVLCapital10% BADR (subject to TAAR)
CVL distribution to members (rare)Capital10%/20%

sections.title: 66.2 BADR conditions
sections.contentHtml:
• Disposing of: trading company shares, sole trader / partnership business, or shares in personal company on cessation
    •    
  • For shares: 5%+ ordinary share capital + voting + 5%+ profit/asset entitlement, AND officer/employee, all for ≥2 years
    •    
  • Trading company (not investment) — most common dispute area
    •    
  • Lifetime limit £1m (cut from £10m March 2020)
    •

sections.title: 66.3 Worked example — MVL with BADR
sections.contentHtml:
Worked Example 66.1    

Owner-director MVL. Distributable cash £400,000. Original share cost £1,000. 100% holding, 5 years qualifying.

                                     
Distribution400,000
Less: cost(1,000)
Less: AEA(3,000)
Chargeable gain396,000
BADR @ 10%39,600
   

Compare dividend treatment: ~39.35% AR ≈ £157k. BADR saves ~£117k.

 
 
   

Module 66 — Summary

   
         
  • DS01 ≤£25k = capital; >£25k = dividend.
    •      
  • MVL = capital, BADR available subject to TAAR.
    •      
  • BADR: 10% up to £1m lifetime; 5%+ shareholding, 2-year qualifying.
    •

hookHtml:
The <tspan>capital vs income</tspan> treatment of distributions on company closure
          determines the tax bill — potentially saving owners <tspan>40% of every distribution £</tspan>.
          Capital treatment (10% BADR up to £1m, 18% non-BADR) beats dividend tax (33.75-39.35%) at all but the
          lowest income bands. The routing decision: <tspan>strike-off DS01</tspan> — capital up to £25k,
          income above (s.1030A); <tspan>MVL</tspan> — full capital treatment with BADR (subject to s.396B TAAR);
          <tspan>share buy-back</tspan> — capital treatment if conditions met (CTA 2010 s.1033-1043); <tspan>
            liquidation as part of sale</tspan> — capital. <tspan>BADR conditions</tspan>: 2-year ownership period
          + 5% shareholding + officer/employee status throughout + qualifying business (s.169I TCGA). <tspan>BADR rates
          </tspan>: 10% currently — <tspan>rising to 14% from 6 April 2025, 18% from 6 April 2026</tspan>.
          Lifetime limit £1m. <tspan>TAAR (ITTOIA s.396B)</tspan>: same trade within 2 years recharacterises
          distribution from capital to dividend — killing BADR and adding 30 percentage points of tax. Planning
          rules: <tspan>clean break</tspan>, document genuine retirement intent, allow time gap before any new venture,
          careful clearance applications for borderline cases. This module covers each capital-distribution route, BADR
          mechanics, TAAR avoidance, the timing decision pre-April-2025 BADR-rate-rises, and the practical decision
          framework.

title: Ltd → Sole Trader (Disincorporation)
meta: Module 67 · Part 10 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 67.1 Why disincorporate
sections.contentHtml:
• Simplification — owner tired of CT, CH filings
    •    
  • Profits dropped below break-even (Module 49)
    •    
  • Cost of compliance exceeds tax saving
    •    
  • Owner doesn't need limited liability
    •

sections.title: 67.2 No clean tax route
sections.contentHtml:
Unlike sole trader → Ltd (s.162 incorporation relief), there is no equivalent reverse relief. Disincorporation Relief (2013–2018) expired.

 

Ltd transferring business to director triggers:

 
       
  • CGT on goodwill at MV (s.18 TCGA — connected parties)
    •    
  • Balancing CA charge on P&M
    •    
  • Stock at MV
    •    
  • VAT issues (TOGC may apply)
    •    
  • Distribution to shareholder (capital if MVL, dividend if direct)
    •

sections.title: 67.3 Practical steps
sections.contentHtml:
1. Value business assets and goodwill.
    2.    
  2. Decide route: MVL (capital + BADR) or wind-down + DS01 (capital ≤£25k).
    3.    
  3. Sole trader registers for SA.
    4.    
  4. Ltd transfers assets to sole trader at MV.
    5.    
  5. Apply VAT TOGC if applicable.
    6.    
  6. Final CT600 covers period to cessation.
    7.    
  7. Distribution to shareholder.
    8.    
  8. CH closure (DS01 or post-MVL dissolution).
    9.    
  9. Sole trader operates from new VRN (or transferred VRN).
    10.

sections.title: 67.4 Practical reality
sections.contentHtml:
Many owners either: (a) leave Ltd dormant rather than disincorporate; or (b) MVL for capital extraction at BADR, then continue as sole trader if TAAR doesn't apply.

 
   

Module 67 — Summary

   
         
  • No reverse equivalent of s.162 — disincorporation is taxed.
    •      
  • Disincorporation Relief (2013–2018) not renewed.
    •      
  • Common route: MVL distribution + sole trader continues if TAAR allows.
    •      
  • Alternative: leave Ltd dormant.
    •

hookHtml:
Disincorporation — reversing a Ltd back to a sole trader — is the <tspan>rare
            but tax-expensive transition</tspan> that catches advisors out. Common reasons: simplification (owner tired
          of CT, accounts, CH filings), profits dropped below break-even (M49), client decided incorporation
          didn’t suit, regulatory change. The big problem: there’s <tspan>no equivalent of s.162
            incorporation relief in reverse</tspan>. Disincorporation triggers: <tspan>CGT on transfer of company assets
          </tspan> to shareholder at market value, <tspan>balancing charge</tspan> on P&M disposed (CAA 2001 s.55),
          <tspan>VAT TOGC</tspan> only if conditions met, <tspan>income tax on undistributed reserves</tspan> as
          dividends, <tspan>BADR if conditions met</tspan>. The <tspan>Disincorporation Relief</tspan> (FA 2013) was a
          limited time-window relief (2013-2018, never extended) — expired and not available now. <tspan>Order of
            operations</tspan>: clear DLAs, distribute distributable reserves, transfer assets to shareholder at MV,
          formally cease Ltd trade, strike-off or MVL, register sole trader (CWF1). <tspan>Cost-benefit</tspan>: often
          the “de-incorporation tax cost” exceeds the long-term compliance saving — clients commonly
          keep dormant Ltd or change to non-trading instead. This module covers the mechanics, the absent
          reverse-relief, the practical decision tree, and alternatives like dormancy.

title: Sole Trader → Partnership
meta: Module 68 · Part 10 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 68.1 Steps
sections.contentHtml:
1. Draft Partnership Agreement.
    2.    
  2. Register partnership for SA (SA400).
    3.    
  3. New partners register for SA.
    4.    
  4. Sole trader brings assets in at agreed values (often book value).
    5.    
  5. Final SA103; first SA800 starts on conversion.
    6.    
  6. VAT: notify HMRC change of legal entity.
    7.    
  7. PAYE/CIS continue under partnership.
    8.    
  8. Update bank, contracts, insurance.

sections.title: 68.2 Tax
sections.contentHtml:
• Sole trader contributes assets at MV → CGT disposal of share given up to other partners.
    •    
  • Partial disposal calc — only share given up is a disposal; retained share is not.
    •    
  • If new partner is spouse: no gain / no loss (TCGA s.58).
    •    
  • Goodwill share given up: BADR may apply if 2-year qualifying.
    •  
 
   

Module 68 — Summary

   
         
  • Partial CGT disposal of share given up.
    •      
  • Spouse partnership: no gain / no loss.
    •      
  • SA400 + each partner's SA101.

hookHtml:
Sole-trader-to-partnership is the <tspan>tax-light transition</tspan> — both
          regimes are tax-transparent, both file SA. The sole trader brings their <tspan>existing trade</tspan> into a
          new partnership with one or more incoming partners. <tspan>Critical tax point</tspan>: this is treated as a
          <tspan>cessation of sole trader trade</tspan> + commencement of partnership trade, but <tspan>basis-period
            continuation</tspan> generally applies (no balancing charges if assets pass at carrying value). However, the
          incoming partner <tspan>acquires a share of goodwill at market value</tspan> — potential CGT for the
          original sole trader if a market-value consideration is received. The <tspan>5 setup steps</tspan>: (1) draft
          Partnership Agreement covering PSR, salaries, drawings, dispute resolution; (2) register partnership for SA
          via SA400 (gets partnership UTR); (3) each new partner registers for individual SA via SA401; (4) nominate a
          partner for SA800 filing; (5) update VAT registration (VAT68 transfer or new). <tspan>Final SA103 for sole
            trader</tspan> closes the unincorporated trade; <tspan>first SA800</tspan> with SA104s for all partners.
          Basis-period reform (M42) applies — tax-year basis from 24/25. Common scenarios: bringing in spouse or
          child (income-splitting), bringing in service partner for capital injection, professional firm formalising
          existing arrangement. This module covers the mechanics, the goodwill mechanics, basis continuation, and the
          Partnership Agreement essentials.

title: Partnership → Ltd (cross-reference Module 56)
meta: Module 69 · Part 10 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard
hookHtml:
The partnership-to-Ltd route is comprehensively covered in M56; this module is the
          <tspan>quick-reference recap</tspan> emphasising the partner-specific mechanics. Each partner makes a <tspan>
            CGT disposal of their partnership interest</tspan> — goodwill, premises, intangibles, all transferred
          to Ltd at market value. <tspan>Section 162 incorporation relief</tspan> defers CGT if consideration is <tspan>
            wholly shares</tspan>; <tspan>section 165 gift relief</tspan> available where shares are gifted; <tspan>BADR
          </tspan> may cover any taxable element (10%, rising 14%/18%). <tspan>Process</tspan>: final SA800 cessation
          with all partners’ allocations, incorporate Ltd with shares allocated per partner’s
          pre-incorporation share, sale agreement transferring assets+goodwill, TUPE for employees, VAT TOGC, deregister
          partnership UTR, each partner files final SA104. <tspan>Critical timing</tspan>: align partnership year-end
          with incorporation date to simplify final allocation; consider basis-period reform position; <tspan>LLP
            wind-down</tspan> at Companies House via LL DS01 strike-off if LLP. <tspan>Loss preservation</tspan>: CTA
          2010 s.86 allows trading losses to carry forward into the Ltd if same trade continues. <tspan>Reserve
            distribution timing</tspan>: capital accounts settled BEFORE or AFTER incorporation — pre-incorp
          better for clean ledger but post-incorp can be DLA-credit mechanism. This module sketches the structure; deep
          mechanics in M56.
