title: Group Restructuring
meta: Module 70 · Part 10 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 70.1 Why create a group
sections.contentHtml:
• Risk separation (trading sub, IP sub, property sub)
    •    
  • Sale optionality
    •    
  • JV vehicle
    •    
  • Investor protection (Holdco shares simpler)
    •    
  • BADR optimisation
    •

sections.title: 70.2 Holdco over existing TradingCo (share-for-share, s.135)
sections.contentHtml: Existing shareholders transfer their shares in TradingCo to a new HoldCo in exchange for new HoldCo shares. HoldCo shares inherit base cost — no immediate CGT (s.135 exchange relief). HMRC clearance (s.138) advisable.

sections.title: 70.3 Inter-group asset transfers — TCGA s.171
sections.contentHtml: Transfers of capital assets between members of a 75% group: no gain / no loss. Allows asset reorganisation without CGT.

sections.title: 70.4 Stamp Duty
sections.contentHtml:
• 0.5% Stamp Duty on share transfers
    •    
  • FA 1930 s.42 group relief: 75% group transfers exempt
    •    
  • FA 1986 s.75 reconstruction relief
    •

sections.title: 70.5 Substantial Shareholding Exemption (SSE)
sections.contentHtml:
Corporate parent disposing of 10%+ shares in trading subsidiary held 12+ months: gain exempt from CT (TCGA Sch 7AC). Major incentive for grouping pre-sale.

 
   

Module 70 — Summary

   
         
  • s.135 share-for-share creates HoldCo without CGT trigger.
    •      
  • s.171 inter-group asset transfers no gain / no loss.
    •      
  • Stamp Duty group relief s.42 FA 1930.
    •      
  • SSE exempts qualifying corporate disposals.
    •

title: Ltd → Charity / CIO Conversion
meta: Module 71 · Part 10 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 71.1 Why convert
sections.contentHtml: Trading entity wants public-benefit purpose; tax exemption; grant funding eligibility; legacies.

sections.title: 71.2 Two routes
sections.contentHtml:
1. Convert Ltd into charitable company limited by guarantee — change Articles, cancel share capital (CA 2006 Part 17 Ch 10), register with Charity Commission. Complex.
    2.    
  2. Establish new CIO and transfer assets/business across — usually simpler. Old Ltd then strikes off.
    3.

sections.title: 71.3 Tax consequences
sections.contentHtml:
• Ltd → CIO at MV would normally trigger CGT (no s.171 — CIO not a corporate group member)
    •    
  • Gift to charity exempt from CGT (TCGA s.257) — disposal at no gain / no loss
    •    
  • Part-gift / part-sale: gift element exempt; sale element at MV
    •    
  • Stock gift may be deductible (CTA 2010 Pt 6)
    •    
  • VAT TOGC if applicable
    •

sections.title: 71.4 Process
sections.contentHtml:
1. Establish CIO (Module 54).
    2.    
  2. Asset valuation; decide what transfers.
    3.    
  3. Asset transfer agreement.
    4.    
  4. HMRC clearance for tax treatment if material.
    5.    
  5. VAT TOGC structuring.
    6.    
  6. Final CT600 for Ltd; cessation.
    7.    
  7. Ltd strike-off (DS01).
    8.    
  8. CIO operates under Charities SORP.
    9.

sections.title: 71.5 Trustee considerations
sections.contentHtml:
Existing directors typically become founding CIO trustees. Different duties; CC guidance mandatory reading.

 
   

Module 71 — Summary

   
         
  • Common route: new CIO + asset transfer + Ltd strike-off.
    •      
  • CGT exemption under s.257 TCGA on gift to charity.
    •

    •      
  • Existing directors become founding trustees.

hookHtml:
Ltd-to-charity is the <tspan>mission-shift transition</tspan> — a trading Ltd
          becomes a registered charity to access <tspan>tax exemption</tspan>, <tspan>Gift Aid</tspan>, <tspan>grant
            funding eligibility</tspan>, and <tspan>legacies</tspan>. Two routes: (1) <tspan>convert existing Ltd to CLG
          </tspan> — change articles to charitable purposes, register with CC + HMRC, may need court order; (2)
          <tspan>incorporate new CIO + transfer trade</tspan> — simpler, common preferred route post-2013. The
          critical issue: <tspan>existing shareholders cannot benefit</tspan> after conversion — charitable
          purpose means no private benefit. <tspan>Disposal of shares</tspan> by founders to charity: TCGA s.257
          gift-to-charity relief (no CGT) + income-tax relief (s.431 ITA) for the donor. <tspan>Property transfer
          </tspan>: SDLT relief if transferred to charity for charitable purposes (FA 2003 Sch 8). <tspan>Asset transfer
            to CIO</tspan>: structured carefully to maintain HMRC charity tax status; <tspan>trading subsidiary</tspan>
          often retained for revenue-generating activities. <tspan>Compliance shift</tspan>: from CT600 + CH accounts to
          <tspan>CC online return</tspan> + Charities SORP accounts. <tspan>Trustees</tspan> appointed (fit-and-proper
          test). <tspan>VAT</tspan>: charities have partial exemption + reduced rate access. This module covers both
          routes, the share-disposal mechanics, the asset transfer, and the year-1 compliance calendar.

title: Sale of Business — Asset Sale vs Share Sale
meta: Module 72 · Part 10 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 72.1 The two structures
sections.contentHtml:
Asset SaleShare Sale
What's soldIndividual assets + goodwillShares in the company
SellerThe companyShareholders
Tax on sellerCT on company gain + then dividend/distributionCGT (often BADR 10%) direct
BuyerPicks specific assets, leaves liabilitiesInherits everything (known + contingent)
Buyer's CT baseHigher cost base — CAs, goodwill amortisation if applicableInherits company's existing tax base
VATTOGC availableVAT exempt (sale of shares)
Stamp dutySDLT on land; nil on goodwill0.5% on shares
Typical preferenceBuyerSeller

sections.title: 72.2 Negotiating
sections.contentHtml: Sellers push for share sale (BADR 10% vs ~30% effective on asset sale + dividend). Buyers push for asset sale (clean assets, cost base for CA/amortisation). Common middle: share sale + comprehensive warranties & indemnities, plus price adjustment.

sections.title: 72.3 Earn-outs
sections.contentHtml:
Marren v Ingles principle:

 
       
  • Estimated value included in disposal proceeds at sale date
    •    
  • Difference on actual receipt = separate disposal of chose in action
    •    
  • s.279A election to defer where contingent becomes “ascertainable” later
    •

sections.title: 72.4 Loan notes / QCBs
sections.contentHtml:
Qualifying Corporate Bonds defer gain until QCB redeemed. BADR can apply on subsequent disposal.

 
   

Module 72 — Summary

   
         
  • Asset sale: company taxed; shareholder then taxed on extraction. Buyer-friendly.
    •      
  • Share sale: shareholder direct CGT/BADR. Seller-friendly.
    •      
  • Stamp duty: 0.5% shares; SDLT on land in asset sale.
    •      
  • Earn-outs: Marren v Ingles + s.279A election.
    •      
  • Loan notes / QCBs can defer gain.
    •

hookHtml:
The <tspan>asset-sale vs share-sale</tspan> decision in M&A is the most consequential
          structuring choice for both buyer and seller — affecting tax cost, deal complexity, liability transfer,
          and consideration mechanics. <tspan>Asset sale</tspan>: buyer cherry-picks specific assets + assumes specific
          liabilities — seller’s Ltd retains residual exposure, leftover cash, the legal entity. <tspan>Tax
            for asset sale</tspan>: seller faces double-tax friction (CT on gains in Ltd, then dividend/MVL tax on
          extraction); buyer gets <tspan>step-up</tspan> on asset base costs + new CA pools + goodwill amortisation
          deduction (post-1 April 2002 goodwill). <tspan>Share sale</tspan>: buyer acquires the company itself —
          gets all assets + ALL liabilities (warranties + indemnities cover unknown risks). <tspan>Tax for share sale
          </tspan>: seller gets single-tax (CGT on shares, BADR available); buyer inherits historic base costs, no
          step-up, but no double-tax. <tspan>SSE</tspan> (M70) applies if seller is corporate. <tspan>Buyer typically
            prefers asset sale</tspan> (control over what’s taken, step-up, no historic liabilities); <tspan>
            seller typically prefers share sale</tspan> (cleaner exit, single tax, BADR). <tspan>Deal structuring
          </tspan>: warranties, indemnities, completion accounts, locked-box, escrow, deferred consideration, earn-outs.
          <tspan>SDLT</tspan> on property in asset sale; <tspan>VAT TOGC</tspan> for asset sales of going concerns. This
          module covers the comparison, mechanics, and the inevitable negotiation tension.

title: Demergers
meta: Module 73 · Part 10 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 73.1 Three statutory routes
sections.contentHtml:
1. Distribution-in-specie (s.1075 CTA 2010): split group's trading subs into two Holdcos owned by original shareholders.
    2.    
  2. Reduction of capital demerger (CA 2006 s.641): court-confirmed capital reduction.
    3.    
  3. Liquidation demerger (s.110 IA 1986): liquidator splits the trade.
    4.

sections.title: 73.2 Use case
sections.contentHtml: Owner-managed group has Trading Co A and Trading Co B; founders want to separate so daughter takes A, son takes B. Demerger creates two Holdcos owned separately, without an immediate CGT trigger.

sections.title: 73.3 Conditions
sections.contentHtml:
Statutory demerger (s.1075) needs HMRC clearance + conditions about trading nature and post-demerger holding. Failure → distribution treated as income dividend.

 
   

Module 73 — Summary

   
         
  • Three demerger routes: distribution-in-specie, capital reduction, liquidation s.110.
    •      
  • HMRC clearance and trade-nature conditions required.
    •

hookHtml:
Demergers split a single corporate group into two or more <tspan>independently-owned
            entities</tspan> — typically to separate trading and investment activities, prepare for sale of one
          business, resolve shareholder disputes, or unlock SSE eligibility. Three statutory routes: <tspan>(1)
            Distribution-in-specie demerger</tspan> (CTA 2010 s.1075-1086) — HoldCo distributes shares in
          subsidiary to its shareholders; <tspan>(2) Capital reduction demerger</tspan> (CA 2006 s.641-653) —
          court-confirmed reduction creates demerger reserve to distribute; <tspan>(3) Liquidation demerger</tspan>
          (TCGA s.137) — HoldCo liquidates, assets distributed to new HoldCos via s.110 IA 1986. Tax treatment
          <tspan>requires careful structuring</tspan>: distribution-in-specie generally tax-neutral if conditions met
          (TCGA s.139); shareholders deemed to dispose of original shares + acquire new shares with cost-basis split;
          <tspan>HMRC clearance</tspan> mandatory via SP3/16 advance assurance. <tspan>Stamp duty</tspan>: usually
          relieved via CTA s.77 reconstruction relief. <tspan>SDLT</tspan>: relieved for group transfers if within 75%
          group at relevant times. <tspan>Anti-avoidance</tspan>: Transactions in Securities rules (ITA s.684), TAAR.
          <tspan>Common scenarios</tspan>: trading + investment split, family disputes splitting family co, partial
          divestment ahead of trade sale. This module sketches each route, tax mechanics, clearance requirements, and
          the typical demerger timeline.

title: Reconstructions
meta: Module 74 · Part 10 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 74.1 What it is
sections.contentHtml: CTA 2010 s.939 — transfer of trade between commonly-owned companies where same shareholders own original and new, and new company carries on the same trade.

sections.title: 74.2 Tax
sections.contentHtml: Trading losses can transfer to new company (subject to anti-avoidance — change in nature restrictions). CA pools transfer at TWDV.

sections.title: 74.3 Stamp Duty / SDRT relief
sections.contentHtml:
FA 1986 s.75/76 reliefs for genuine reconstructions on share transfers.

 
   

Module 74 — Summary

   
         
  • CTA 2010 s.939 reconstruction: trade transferred between commonly-owned cos.
    •      
  • Trading losses can transfer subject to anti-avoidance.
    •      
  • FA 1986 s.75/76 stamp duty relief.
    •

hookHtml:
A <tspan>reconstruction</tspan> moves a trade and assets from one company to another
          <tspan>without losing tax continuity</tspan> — the recipient carries on the same trade and shareholders
          are substantially identical. Legal hook: <tspan>CTA 2010 s.939 (continuation of trade)</tspan> and <tspan>CTA
            2010 s.940A-947 (transfer of trade)</tspan> set out the relief, which lets the recipient inherit the
          transferor’s trading-loss position, capital allowances pools, and various other tax attributes. <tspan>
            Stamp duty relief</tspan>: CTA 2010 s.77 reconstruction relief on the share-for-share exchange. <tspan>SDLT
          </tspan>: FA 2003 Sch 7 reconstruction relief on property transfers. <tspan>CGT relief</tspan>: TCGA s.139
          covers business reconstructions where shares are issued. <tspan>Typical uses</tspan>: moving trade between
          group companies, hive-down of trade to a new sub before sale, reorganisation prior to listing, separating
          trade from non-trading assets. <tspan>Conditions to qualify</tspan>: <tspan>same shareholders</tspan>, <tspan>
            same trade continues</tspan>, <tspan>consideration substantially in shares</tspan>, <tspan>commercial reason
          </tspan>. <tspan>HMRC clearance</tspan> via SP3/16 again advisable. <tspan>Distinguishing from demerger
          </tspan>: reconstruction preserves single-entity outcome (trade moves but ownership doesn’t change);
          demerger creates separate ownerships. This module covers the relief framework, conditions, common scenarios,
          and the “hive-down + sale” case study.

title: IR35 / Off-Payroll Working Rules
meta: Module 75 · Part 11 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

sections.title: 75.1 What IR35 is
sections.contentHtml: Anti-avoidance: prevents individuals avoiding employee taxes by interposing a personal service company (PSC). If the engagement “would be employment” absent the PSC, IR35 applies — full PAYE/NI on deemed employment income.

sections.title: 75.2 Status tests (Ready Mixed Concrete v MoP 1968)
sections.contentHtml:
1. Personal Service: must the worker do the work, or can they substitute?
    2.    
  2. Mutuality of Obligation (MOO): ongoing offer/accept obligation?
    3.    
  3. Control: how, what, when, where over the work?
    4.  
 

Plus secondary: financial risk, equipment, exclusivity, integration, intention.

sections.title: 75.3 Who decides status
sections.contentHtml:
• Pre-April 2017 private sector: worker (via PSC).
    •    
  • Public sector since April 2017: client (SDS — Status Determination Statement).
    •    
  • Private sector since April 2021: medium/large clients determine; small clients = worker still decides.
    •

sections.title: 75.4 If inside IR35
sections.contentHtml:
• Fee payer (client/agency) deducts PAYE/NI on deemed direct payment to worker
    •    
  • Employer NI applies (fee payer = NI employer)
    •    
  • Worker offsets deemed employment income against PSC income to avoid double tax
    •

sections.title: 75.5 CEST
sections.contentHtml:
HMRC's status check tool. HMRC stands by results if answers honest. Many disputes; tribunals have overturned.

 
   

Module 75 — Summary

   
         
  • IR35 prevents disguised employment via PSCs.
    •      
  • Tests: Personal service, MOO, Control + secondary.
    •      
  • Determination: medium/large clients in private sector since April 2021.
    •      
  • Inside IR35 → fee payer deducts PAYE/NI.
    •

hookHtml:
IR35 (the <tspan>Intermediaries Legislation</tspan>) is the UK’s anti-avoidance
          regime preventing individuals from avoiding employee taxes by interposing a <tspan>Personal Service Company
            (PSC)</tspan>. If the engagement “<tspan>would be employment</tspan>” absent the PSC —
          full <tspan>PAYE + NIC</tspan> applies on the deemed employment income. Originally introduced by FA 2000
          (Chapter 8 ITEPA 2003), the <tspan>off-payroll working rules</tspan> (Chapter 10 ITEPA 2003) shifted the IR35
          assessment + tax-deduction burden to the <tspan>end client</tspan> from April 2017 (public sector) and April
          2021 (medium/large private sector). <tspan>Small companies</tspan> (CA 2006 size) still apply Chapter 8
          — PSC determines own status. <tspan>Status tests</tspan> from <tspan>Ready Mixed Concrete v MoP 1968
          </tspan>: <tspan>mutuality of obligation</tspan>, <tspan>personal service / substitution</tspan>, <tspan>
            control</tspan>, plus other factors (financial risk, equipment, integration). HMRC’s <tspan>CEST tool
          </tspan> gives a (sometimes-binding) determination. <tspan>Status Determination Statement (SDS)</tspan>:
          client must issue to PSC + fee-payer (often the agency) before first payment + on change. <tspan>Penalties
          </tspan>: deemed payments triggered, PAYE/NIC due, interest + penalties on under-payment. <tspan>Practical
            impact</tspan>: many PSCs have shut down post-2021; rise of <tspan>umbrella companies</tspan> for contractor
          markets. This module covers the legal framework, status tests, SDS mechanics, CEST limitations, and the
          post-2021 contractor market shifts.

sections.title: 76.1 The basics
sections.contentHtml:

hookHtml:
A trust is a <tspan>legal arrangement</tspan> where trustees hold assets for the benefit
          of beneficiaries under terms set by the <tspan>settlor</tspan>. Four main types: <tspan>bare trust</tspan>
          (transparent for tax — income/gains taxed on beneficiary), <tspan>interest in possession (IIP)</tspan>
          (beneficiary entitled to income as it arises), <tspan>discretionary trust</tspan> (trustees decide what/when
          to distribute), <tspan>accumulation trust</tspan> (income reinvested for future generations). <tspan>Tax
            treatment</tspan>: IIP — income taxed on beneficiary (45% if over band), trustees pay 20%/8.75% then
          beneficiary credits. Discretionary trusts — trustees pay <tspan>45% income tax</tspan> + 39.35%
          dividends, beneficiaries get tax credit on distribution. <tspan>Capital gains</tspan>: trustees pay 20% (24%
          residential), £1.5k AEA (half individual). <tspan>IHT treatment</tspan>: <tspan>relevant property regime
          </tspan> — 10-year periodic charge up to 6%, exit charges, entry CLT at 20% if above NRB. <tspan>Trust
            Registration Service (TRS)</tspan> mandatory for most trusts since 2022. <tspan>Common uses</tspan>: protect
          minor inheritance, vulnerable beneficiary, family wealth preservation, charitable giving, IHT planning.
          <tspan>Settlor-interested trust</tspan>: anti-avoidance — income taxed on settlor. <tspan>Practitioner
            role</tspan>: trust accounts, trustees’ SA900 return, distribution planning. This module covers types,
          tax, TRS compliance, and the planning angles.

hookHtml:
The <tspan>non-dom regime</tspan> was abolished from 6 April 2025 — but legacy
          planning for clients who relied on it continues for years to come. <tspan>Pre-2025</tspan>:
          UK-resident-but-non-UK-domiciled individuals could elect <tspan>remittance basis</tspan> — UK tax only
          on UK-source income/gains + amounts remitted to UK. <tspan>Remittance basis charge (RBC)</tspan>:
          £30k/year if UK resident 7 of last 9 tax years, £60k if 12 of 14. <tspan>Deemed domiciled</tspan>:
          long-term residents (15 of last 20) treated as UK-dom for IT/CGT/IHT. From <tspan>April 2025</tspan>: replaced
          by <tspan>4-year FIG regime</tspan> (Foreign Income & Gains) for new arrivals with 10+ years overseas
          — first 4 years UK-resident, foreign income/gains exempt. <tspan>Existing non-doms transition</tspan>:
          <tspan>50% rebasing election</tspan> for capital assets, <tspan>Temporary Repatriation Facility (TRF)</tspan>
          — bring offshore funds at 12% (2025/26-2026/27) then 15% (2027/28). <tspan>IHT shift</tspan>: long-term
          residents (10+ years) face IHT on worldwide assets — major hit for offshore trusts. <tspan>Excluded
            property trust</tspan> protection lost. <tspan>Planning</tspan>: trust restructuring, asset sales pre-2025
          for old base costs, FIG elections, family relocation. This module covers the legacy regime, transition rules,
          FIG election mechanics, and current planning considerations.

          immunity for full disclosure, otherwise penalty regime (M82) applies. This module covers enquiry types, time

hookHtml:
UK accountancy ethics is governed by the <tspan>IESBA Code of Ethics</tspan>
          (International Ethics Standards Board for Accountants) implemented by professional bodies (ICAEW, ACCA, AAT,
          CIOT, CIMA). Five <tspan>fundamental principles</tspan>: (1) <tspan>Integrity</tspan> — straightforward
          and honest in professional/business relationships; (2) <tspan>Objectivity</tspan> — no bias, conflict of
          interest, undue influence; (3) <tspan>Professional Competence + Due Care</tspan> — maintain knowledge,
          apply diligently; (4) <tspan>Confidentiality</tspan> — protect client information unless legal duty /
          authorised; (5) <tspan>Professional Behaviour</tspan> — comply with laws + avoid discrediting the
          profession. <tspan>Conceptual framework</tspan>: identify threats → evaluate significance → apply
          safeguards → if not at acceptable level, decline / withdraw. <tspan>Threats</tspan>: self-interest,
          self-review, advocacy, familiarity, intimidation. <tspan>Safeguards</tspan>: regulatory (CPD, supervision),
          firm-level (engagement quality reviews, second partner reviews), engagement-level (rotation, partners-only
          meetings). <tspan>Common dilemmas</tspan>: <tspan>conflicts of interest</tspan>, <tspan>client pressure to
            participate in tax avoidance</tspan>, <tspan>discovery of client fraud</tspan>, <tspan>fee dependency
          </tspan>. <tspan>PCRT</tspan> applies to tax specifically. <tspan>Whistleblowing</tspan>: protected disclosure
          under PIDA 1998. This module covers principles, conceptual framework application, common dilemmas, and the
          disciplinary process.

hookHtml:
The engagement letter is the <tspan>contractual foundation</tspan> of every accounting
          relationship — required by all professional bodies (ICAEW, ACCA, AAT, CIOT). Without one, professional
          indemnity insurance may not respond, fee recovery is harder, and scope disputes become acrimonious. <tspan>
            Standard contents</tspan>: parties, scope of services, fee basis, payment terms, <tspan>respective
            responsibilities</tspan> (client’s vs accountant’s), <tspan>information & record
            requirements</tspan>, confidentiality, complaints procedure, <tspan>limitation of liability</tspan>,
          termination, governing law. <tspan>Scope precision</tspan> matters: separate letters for audit, statutory
          accounts, tax, payroll, advisory. <tspan>Tax-specific clauses</tspan>: PCRT compliance, who initiates HMRC
          contact, post-cessation responsibilities. <tspan>Fee mechanisms</tspan>: hourly, fixed-fee, value-based,
          retainer. <tspan>Limitation of liability</tspan>: cap typically 2-3x annual fee or specific amount per ICAEW
          guidance. <tspan>Annual review</tspan> + update for scope or fee changes. <tspan>Disengagement letter</tspan>
          when relationship ends. <tspan>Reliance letter</tspan> when third party (bank) wants comfort. <tspan>
            Sub-contracting</tspan>: notify client + maintain confidentiality + check supervisor permissions. <tspan>
            Specimen letters</tspan> from ICAEW, ACCA available. This module covers structure, key clauses, fee
          mechanisms, liability caps, and the engagement lifecycle.

hookHtml:
PII is the <tspan>mandatory practice insurance</tspan> covering professional negligence,
          errors, breach of duty and the resulting client claims. Required by all UK accountancy bodies (ICAEW, ACCA,
          AAT, CIOT). <tspan>ICAEW minimum cover</tspan>: 2.5x fee income, £1.5m floor, £5m max. <tspan>ACCA
          </tspan>: similar tiered structure. <tspan>Cover scope</tspan>: civil liability arising from professional
          services rendered — includes errors, omissions, breach of confidentiality, dishonesty of employees.
          <tspan>Common exclusions</tspan>: criminal acts, intentional dishonesty by principal, war/terrorism, asbestos,
          regulatory fines. <tspan>Claims-made basis</tspan>: cover applies when claim made (not when act committed)
          — continuous cover essential including <tspan>run-off cover</tspan> (typically 6+ years) when practice
          closes. <tspan>Premium drivers</tspan>: fee income, claims history, services offered (advisory + tax higher),
          staff numbers, supervisor type. <tspan>Excess/deductible</tspan>: amount practice pays per claim. <tspan>
            Claims process</tspan>: notify insurer immediately of circumstance + claim, do not admit liability,
          cooperate fully. <tspan>Practical points</tspan>: maintain accurate disclosure on renewal, declare past
          claims, review limits annually, consider cyber + employers liability + management liability add-ons. <tspan>

hookText:
PII is the mandatory practice insurance covering professional negligence,
          errors, breach of duty and the resulting client claims. Required by all UK accountancy bodies (ICAEW, ACCA,
          AAT, CIOT). ICAEW minimum cover: 2.5x fee income, £1.5m floor, £5m max. ACCA
          : similar tiered structure. Cover scope: civil liability arising from professional
          services rendered — includes errors, omissions, breach of confidentiality, dishonesty of employees.
          Common exclusions: criminal acts, intentional dishonesty by principal, war/terrorism, asbestos,
          regulatory fines. Claims-made basis: cover applies when claim made (not when act committed)
          — continuous cover essential including run-off cover (typically 6+ years) when practice
          closes. Premium drivers: fee income, claims history, services offered (advisory + tax higher),
          staff numbers, supervisor type. Excess/deductible: amount practice pays per claim. 
            Claims process: notify insurer immediately of circumstance + claim, do not admit liability,
          cooperate fully. Practical points: maintain accurate disclosure on renewal, declare past
          claims, review limits annually, consider cyber + employers liability + management liability add-ons. 
            Without PII: cannot practice + supervisor disciplinary + personal liability for losses. This module
          covers requirements, cover, exclusions, premium drivers, and the claims process.
